1.overview:
On the plains of Moab in the fortieth year, Moses opens his farewell speeches by retelling the road from Horeb. God told Israel it had stayed at the mountain long enough. Moses, unable to carry the people alone, had the tribes choose wise men to serve as captains and judges. At Kadesh-barnea twelve spies brought back fruit, but the people would not go up. Afraid of the tall Anakim, they said the LORD hated them. God swore that none of that generation but Caleb would see the land; Joshua would lead their children in. The people, attacking too late, were chased back to Hormah.

Moses tells the story his own way. In Numbers the LORD orders the spies sent (Numbers 13:1–2); here the people ask for them (v. 22). And Moses places his own exclusion at Kadesh, “for your sakes” (v. 37), where Numbers ties it to the water at Meribah years later (Numbers 20:12).

1.hermeneutics:
Hittite treaties of the 14th and 13th centuries BC open with history: what the great king had done for his vassal, and how the vassal and his fathers had behaved in return. The treaty of Mursili II with Duppi-Teshub of Amurru, for example, recalls the loyalty of Duppi-Teshub's grandfather Aziru before it sets out the new king's duties. Deuteronomy 1–3 does the same work at greater length. Moses sets the LORD's care (vv. 30–33) beside Israel's refusal, so the laws that follow reach a generation that knows what its parents' disloyalty cost.

Egyptian kings also reformed their courts in writing. The edict of Horemheb, carved at Karnak in the late 14th century BC, names judges for the land and orders them not to take gifts or favor anyone. Moses' charge in vv. 16–17 belongs to this world of instructions to judges, with two changes: the people choose the men from their own tribes (v. 13), and the judges answer to God, because “the judgment is God's.”

Papyrus Anastasi I, a satirical Egyptian letter of the 13th century BC, quizzes a scribe on the roads of Canaan. It warns of narrow passes where Shasu nomads hide in the brush, some, in one reading, four or five cubits tall and fierce of face. Egyptian scribes, like the spies, pictured Canaan's hill country as a place of walled towns and frightening men. Moses' reply in vv. 29–31 grants the size of the enemy and points to the size of their God.

rows.text: Kadesh: the spies and the refusal

notes: **Go up:** the Hebrew verb *alah* occurs 9 times, all in vv. 21–43. Israel is told to go up (v. 21), will not go up (v. 26), then goes up after God has said not to (vv. 41–43).
**“Long enough”:** God's first words, *rav lakhem* (v. 6), return at 2:3 when Israel leaves Seir and, said to Moses alone, at 3:26. The phrase marks the stages of chs. 1–3.
**Fear:** “fear not” (v. 21) and “dread not” (v. 29) bracket the spies' report. Each time the people answer with fear.

Verses 1–5 head both the book and Moses' first address, which runs to 4:43. Chapters 1–3 tell the journey from Horeb to the valley opposite Beth-peor (3:29) in Moses' own voice; at 4:1 “Now therefore” turns the history into exhortation.
**Backward:** Numbers 13–14 tells the Kadesh story from the narrator's side. **Forward:** Psalm 95:8–11 and Hebrews 3:7–4:11 build on the oath of vv. 34–35.

traditions.text: Rebuking his brothers on the shore of Bountiful, Nephi recalls Israel in the wilderness: the Lord went before them, leading by day and giving light by night, yet they hardened their hearts and reviled against Moses and God. He adds that the Lord straitened them in the wilderness with his rod. His summary is the same charge Moses lays in vv. 30–33, where the God who went before them in fire and cloud was still not believed. Nephi uses the story to explain why his own family's journey in the wilderness was hard.

A revelation on priesthood says Moses sought to sanctify his people so they could behold the face of God, but they hardened their hearts. The Lord in his wrath then swore that they should not enter into his rest while in the wilderness, a rest the revelation defines as “the fulness of his glory.” Read this way, the oath of vv. 34–35 cost that generation more than a homeland. The next verse adds that the Lord then took Moses and the holy priesthood out of their midst.

The Sifre reads the place names of v. 1 as quiet reproofs. Tophel recalls the complaints about the manna, Hazeroth the punishment of Miriam, and Di-zahab, “enough gold,” the golden calf, a reading Onkelos builds into its Aramaic translation. Rashi notes that Moses rebuked them by allusion out of regard for Israel's honor. The Sifre also preserves a dissent: Rabbi Yose ben Dormasqit protests that scripture's place names record real places and events.
traditions.cite: Sifre Deuteronomy 1; Targum Onkelos Deuteronomy 1:1; Rashi on 1:1

traditions.text: Why mention that Horeb was eleven days from Kadesh (v. 2)? The Sifre answers that had Israel been worthy, they would have entered the land in eleven days. Because they refused, God exacted a year for each of the forty days the spies were in the land (Numbers 14:34), while Rabbi Judah goes further and counts it a three-day journey, citing the ark that went three days ahead of the camp (Numbers 10:33). Either way, forty years are set against a trip of days.

The Sifre reads the three nouns of v. 12 as three complaints. “Cumbrance” means the people were litigious: a man losing a case would call for more witnesses, a delay, or more judges. “Burden” means they were cynical about Moses himself, suspecting him if he left his tent early and plotting if he left it late; “strife” means they were quarrelsome traders.

On the qualities Moses asked for in v. 13, the Sifre records a convert named Arius asking Rabbi Yose the difference between “wise” and “understanding.” The wise man, Yose answers, is like a rich money changer who examines coins whether or not anyone brings him any. The understanding man is like a poor one, who examines what is brought and otherwise sits idle. The Sifre adds that “known among your tribes” (v. 13) means men the tribes themselves can vouch for, since Moses cannot tell one cloaked stranger's tribe from another's.

On “ye shall hear the small as well as the great” (v. 17), Resh Lakish taught that a lawsuit over a perutah, the smallest coin, must matter to a judge as much as one over a hundred maneh. The Talmud draws a practical rule from it: a small claim may not be pushed aside to hear a larger one first. The same passage ties the rule to the charge in v. 16 to judge rightly between brothers and strangers.

Rashi explains the image of the Amorites chasing Israel “as bees do” (v. 44) from an earlier midrash. A bee dies once it stings; so the Amorites who struck Israel at Hormah died soon after. Numbers 14:45 names Amalekites and Canaanites at Hormah, and Deuteronomy calls the attackers Amorites, its usual name for the hill-country peoples.

Hebrews asks with whom God was grieved for forty years and to whom he swore they should not enter his rest, and answers: that they could not enter in because of unbelief. It is the charge of v. 32, where Israel did not believe the God who had carried it like a son. Hebrews turns it into a warning for Christians, and D&C 84 above reads the same oath of exclusion from God's rest.

In Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch, God “suffered their manners” in the wilderness for forty years. Greek manuscripts divide here by one letter: some read that God bore with Israel's ways, others that he nursed or carried them. The second reading matches the Greek Septuagint of v. 31, where God bears Israel as a man carries his son. Either way, Paul's sermon opens Israel's story the way Moses does here, with God's patience in the wilderness.

2.overview:
After many days circling Mount Seir, God turns Israel north and forbids three wars. Israel must not take land from Edom, Moab, or Ammon, kin peoples whose lands God himself has given them. Short notes recall the giant peoples those nations displaced long before. At the brook Zered, thirty-eight years after Kadesh, the last of the fighting men have died. Then God hands over Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, who refuses Israel passage; Israel defeats him at Jahaz and devotes his towns to destruction.

Set this beside Numbers. There Edom refuses passage and comes out armed (Numbers 20:18–21); here the sons of Esau sell Israel food and water (vv. 6, 29), and Moab does the same, though 23:4 later says Moab and Ammon met Israel with no bread. Moses' version stresses that God assigns every nation its land.

2.hermeneutics:
The Mesha Stele, set up about 840 BC by a king of Moab, speaks the language of this chapter. Chemosh, Moab's god, was angry with his land and let Omri of Israel occupy it; later Chemosh drove the king of Israel out of Jahaz, where Sihon fell in v. 32. Mesha boasts that he devoted a town's people to his god and built the road through the Arnon. Moabites and Israelites alike believed a god gives his people land, as Jephthah says to Ammon in Judges 11:24. This chapter claims more: Israel's God gave Seir to Esau and Ar to Lot's sons (vv. 5, 9, 19).

Egyptian frontier reports know Edom as herders who crossed borders by leave. In Papyrus Anastasi VI, from the late 13th century BC, an official reports letting Shasu tribes of Edom past a border fort in the eastern Delta to reach water for themselves and their flocks. Passage, water, and payment were the ordinary business of travelers at a frontier, and they are exactly what Israel offers in vv. 6 and 27–28.

The notes in vv. 10–12 and 20–23 read like an ancient geographer's asides. Caphtor (v. 23) is the land Egyptian texts call Keftiu and Mari texts Kaptara, usually identified with Crete; Amos 9:7 names it as the Philistines' homeland. The notes set Israel's conquest in a series: Esau replaced the Horim, Moab the Emim, Ammon the Zamzummim, and the Caphtorim the Avim. Every people on this map holds land that once belonged to someone else.

notes: **Possession:** *yerushah* “possession” occurs 6 times, all in vv. 5–19, for the lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon and once (v. 12) for Israel's own.
**The formula:** each displacement is told the same way: the newcomers destroyed the old people “and dwelt in their stead” (vv. 12, 21, 22, 23).
**The turn:** at v. 24 the refrain flips. God has not given Sihon's land to anyone else; “I have given into thine hand Sihon,” and Israel must “begin to possess” (vv. 24, 31).
Chapter 2 is the middle of the retold journey (1:1–3:29). It opens by obeying the order of 1:40 to turn toward the Red Sea and closes with Sihon, whose land is given to Reuben and Gad in 3:12–17.
**Forward:** Jephthah argues Israel's claim to Sihon's land from this history in Judges 11:15–26, and Psalms 135:11 and 136:19–20 sing of Sihon and Og among God's mighty acts.

traditions.text: Nephi asks his brothers whether the peoples Israel drove out of the promised land were righteous, and answers no. Israel was not chosen for being more choice, since “the Lord esteemeth all flesh in one”; the land's people had rejected God and were ripe in iniquity. He adds that God made the earth to be inhabited and leads the righteous into precious lands. Like the notes in vv. 10–23, Nephi treats land as God's to give and to take back.

The midrash explains why Edom was off limits by Esau's devotion to his father: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel confesses that Esau honored Isaac more than he honored his own father, putting on his finest clothes to serve him. When Israel approached Seir, God showed Moses the mountain where the patriarchs were buried and said Esau was still owed the reward for honoring them, so the people must turn north (v. 3). Another voice in the same midrash warns that harming Esau would endanger Jacob's own blessings.

Genesis 15:19–21 promised Abraham ten peoples, but Israel received only seven. Genesis Rabbah says the other three, the Kenites, Kenizzites, and Kadmonites, were deferred to the future. Rashi identifies them with Seir, Moab, and Ammon, which explains why God calls their lands a gift in vv. 5, 9, and 19: the promise was real but kept for later. On v. 10 Rashi adds that Moab's land had once belonged to Rephaim, yet it was not the Rephaim country promised to Abraham.

Rashi meets the conflict with Numbers head on. When Moses tells Sihon to deal with him as the children of Esau did (v. 29), he means selling food and water, not letting Israel pass, because Edom had refused passage (Numbers 20:18). On v. 7 Rashi adds a point of manners: since God had blessed them, Israel should pay like the rich and not act poor before Esau.

God never told Moses to offer Sihon peace, so why did he send words of peace from Kedemoth (v. 26)? Rashi plays on the name, which sounds like “before”: Moses learned from the Torah that existed before the world. God offered it first to Esau and Ishmael, knowing they would refuse, and so Moses offered peace to a king he knew would not accept.

Moses reasoned that if Israel was told to strike the Midianites for helping Moab (Numbers 25:17), Moab itself deserved war. God replied that he had two good doves to bring out of these peoples: Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite, mothers of David's line. The Talmud also notes the difference between vv. 9 and 19: Moab may be harassed though not fought, while Ammon may not even be provoked.

The Talmud says the fifteenth of Av became a festival because on that day the deaths in the wilderness ended. As long as the generation was dying, God's speech did not come to Moses; only “when all the men of war were consumed” did the LORD speak to him (vv. 16–17). Rashi adds that during the thirty-eight years God spoke to Moses, but never with affection or face to face.

From v. 25, where God begins to put the dread of Israel on all nations under heaven, the Talmud teaches that the sun stood still for Moses as it later did for Joshua. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani asks when the nations ever trembled because of Moses and answers: when the sun stopped for him. Rashi places the miracle at the battle with Og, the next victory after Sihon (3:1–3).

Josephus has Moses offer Sihon any security he asked and a good price for supplies, even for water. When Sihon refused, Moses asked God's leave to fight, partly to cure the Hebrews of the idleness that had bred their earlier revolts. He describes Sihon's land as almost an island, bounded by the Arnon, the Jabbok, and the Jordan, and fruitful enough to feed a great people.

Josephus explains Balak's alarm in Numbers 22 by his ignorance of this chapter's rule. Balak, he says, did not know that the Hebrews would not meddle with any other country, “God having forbidden them to go any farther” than Canaan. The restraint shown to Moab in v. 9 thus becomes, in Josephus, the fact Moab's king failed to grasp.

3.overview:
Israel turns north to Bashan, where King Og comes out to fight at Edrei. God says “Fear him not,” and Israel takes sixty walled cities in the region of Argob. Og, last of the Rephaim, is remembered by his iron bedstead, nine cubits long, still on show at Rabbath of Ammon. Moses gives the land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, on condition that their men cross armed with their brothers. He tells Joshua the LORD will fight for him, then pleads to cross over and see the good land.

The plea is told only here. Numbers 27:12–14 has God send Moses up to view the land; Deuteronomy lets us hear Moses ask and God refuse: “Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter” (v. 26). As at 1:37, Moses says the anger fell on him “for your sakes.”

3.hermeneutics:
At Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, the Rephaim were the honored royal dead, invoked in a 13th-century BC funeral liturgy for a king. Another Ugaritic text (KTU 1.108) calls on Rapiu, “king of eternity,” a god who dwells in Ashtaroth and rules in Edrei, the two cities of Og (1:4; Joshua 12:4). For a listener who knew that lore, Og was no ordinary king. He was the last of a legendary race tied to the realm of the dead, and his defeat ends that story (v. 11).

Iron was rare and costly in the Late Bronze Age. In the Amarna letters, kings of Mitanni send the pharaoh iron jewelry and an iron-bladed dagger as royal gifts. An iron bed would be a treasure, which may be why it was kept in Rabbath as a trophy. Scholars read it in two ways: a wooden royal bed fitted with iron (Alan Millard), or a basalt coffin of the kind the dolmen fields of Bashan suggest. Either way, nine cubits by four, about 13 by 6 feet, measures a legend.

The aside in v. 9 is accurate. Ugaritic poems pair Lebanon with Sirion, and Psalm 29:6 does the same. Assyrian annals of Shalmaneser III, about 841 BC, name the mountain where he fought Hazael of Damascus as Saniru, matching the Amorite name Shenir. Moses' speech knows the mountain's names in three languages.

notes: **“At that time”:** the phrase opens or marks 6 of the chapter's scenes (vv. 4, 8, 12, 18, 21, 23), out of 10 uses in chs. 1–3. Moses is dating each memory against the conquest.
**Fear:** “Fear him not” (v. 2) and “Ye shall not fear them” (v. 22) frame the conquest and settlement.
**“Long enough”:** God's refusal, *rav lakh* (v. 26), echoes his “long enough” to the whole people at 1:6 and 2:3. This time the words stop Moses instead of sending Israel forward.

Chapter 3 brings the retold journey (1:1–3:29) to the place where Moses is speaking, “the valley over against Beth-peor” (v. 29). The same location introduces the law at 4:46, and chapter 4 turns from history to exhortation.
**Forward:** Joshua 1:12–15 and 22:1–4 show the eastern tribes keeping the promise of vv. 18–20, and Deuteronomy 34:1–4 carries out v. 27 on the top of Pisgah.

traditions.text: This revelation says that because Israel hardened their hearts and could not endure God's presence, the Lord “took Moses out of their midst, and the Holy Priesthood also.” Like v. 26, it places the reason for Moses' loss on the people, though the revelation is speaking of the whole wilderness period rather than one scene. Deuteronomy pictures Moses kept from the land; the revelation pictures Israel losing Moses and the higher priesthood with him.

Why does God tell Moses “Fear him not” about Og (v. 2) and not about Sihon? The Talmud answers that Moses feared Og had merit with Abraham. Og, it says, was the one who escaped the flood and brought Abram word of Lot's capture (Genesis 14:13); it also calls Sihon and Og brothers. Rashi links the escape to v. 11, where Og alone remains of the Rephaim struck in Genesis 14:5.

A tradition with no verse behind it, the Talmud admits, tells how Og died. Seeing that Israel's camp was three parasangs wide, Og tore up a mountain of that size to throw on it, but God sent insects to bore through it, and it fell around his neck. Moses, ten cubits tall, took an axe ten cubits long, leapt ten cubits, and struck Og on the ankle.

This Aramaic paraphrase expands v. 11: Og was left “of the remnant of the giants who perished in the deluge.” His iron bed is not merely in Rabbath but laid up in its archive house, as if in a royal museum. The Talmud's Og who escaped the flood (above) and the Targum's Og share the same backstory.

Josephus describes Og as a king with few equals in size or looks, quick and strong with his hands. Men could guess his size, he says, when they took his bed at Rabbath, the Ammonite royal city: “Its structure was of iron,” four cubits broad and a cubit more than double that in length. He calls Og king of Gilead and Gaulanitis, using the Greek names of his own day.

Why did Moses pray “at that time” (v. 23)? The Sifre gives a parable: a town waits to petition the king until he has just beaten two enemies. When Moses saw Sihon and Og fall, he judged the moment right to ask to enter the land. Rashi adds that Moses hoped the decree had lapsed, since he had already entered Sihon's and Og's land, counted as part of the inheritance, and the next Sifre section has him plead that he learned to pray from God's own “let me alone” at the golden calf.

The Talmud hears measure for measure in God's *rav lakh* (v. 26). Rabbi Levi notes that Moses had rebuked Korah's company with the same word, *rav*, “ye take too much upon you” (Numbers 16:7), and he was answered with it. Other readings: *rav* means Moses now has a master to succeed him, Joshua; or God cut the plea short so that people would not say the Master was harsh and the disciple stubborn.

The Sifre reads *rav lakh* a second way, as “there is much for you”: great reward is stored up for Moses in the world to come. It also notes that for all his deeds Moses was never told to go up, but in answer to this prayer he was told to climb Pisgah (v. 27). From that, Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob taught that one prayer is better than a hundred good deeds.

Why does v. 9 bother to give Hermon's other names? Rashi, following the Sifre, counts four (with “Sion” in 4:48) and says each kingdom wanted the mountain named after itself. The names are recorded to praise the land of Israel, a land that four kingdoms boasted of.

Moses promises the eastern tribes they may go home once the LORD has given their brothers rest (v. 20), and he charges Joshua to lead the people in (v. 28). Hebrews answers that if Joshua had truly given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day. The rest Joshua won in Canaan, which Joshua 22:4 says the eastern tribes saw come, becomes for Hebrews a sign of a rest still to come for the people of God.

4.overview:
Moses turns from history to appeal. Israel must keep the statutes he teaches, adding nothing and taking nothing away; the law will make them wise before the nations. He recalls Horeb, where God spoke out of the fire: they heard a voice but saw no form, so they must make no image and must not worship the sun, moon, and stars. If they do, they will be scattered among the nations, yet if they seek the LORD there, they will find him. No other people has heard God speak and lived; the LORD alone is God. Moses then sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan.

The argument rests on one fact about Horeb: “ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude” (v. 12). Because God showed no form, Israel must give him none. What they received at the mountain was words, and words are what Moses now asks them to keep.

4.hermeneutics:
Hittite and later Assyrian treaties close with a list of witnesses: the gods of both parties, then mountains, rivers, springs, the sea, heaven and earth. Moses calls heaven and earth to witness (v. 26) because there are no other gods to call. The treaty pattern also shows in the chapter's parts: history (vv. 10–14, 32–38), the basic demand of loyalty (vv. 15–24, 39–40), and the curse of exile (vv. 25–28).

Ancient lawgivers guarded their texts. The epilogue of Hammurabi's laws, about 1750 BC, curses any later king who changes his words or erases his name. Esarhaddon's succession treaties of 672 BC curse anyone who alters, burns, or destroys the tablet itself. Verse 2 aims the same clause at the hearers: it is Israel, not a rival king, that must neither add to the word nor take from it.

In Mesopotamia the sun, moon, and planet Venus were great gods: Shamash, Sin, and Ishtar. Shamash was the god of justice who handed Hammurabi his laws, and the moon god Sin was worshiped at Ur and Harran. By the 7th century BC Judah had priests burning incense to the sun, moon, and planets, whom Josiah removed (2 Kings 23:5). Verse 19 names exactly these as the temptation once Israel settles, and it says something bolder about them: the LORD himself has allotted the host of heaven to the nations.

notes: **Fire:** *esh* “fire” occurs 7 times in vv. 11–36, and “out of the midst of the fire” 4 times (vv. 12, 15, 33, 36). The voice from the fire is the chapter's main evidence.

**Creation reversed:** the forbidden likenesses in vv. 16–19 run from “male or female” (the words of Genesis 1:27) to beasts, birds, creeping things, fish, and finally the sun, moon, and stars, roughly Genesis 1 in reverse order. *Tavnit* “likeness” occurs 5 times in vv. 16–18.
**Hear:** *shama* “hear” occurs 11 times. Israel heard; it did not see.

Verses 1–40 close Moses' first address with exhortation. Verses 41–43 are a short narrative bridge, and vv. 44–49 open the second address with a new heading, “this is the law,” which runs to 28:68 and begins with the Ten Commandments in chapter 5.
**Forward:** the warning of scattering and return (vv. 25–31) returns at 28:64 and 30:1–3, where Moses promises that God will gather Israel from all the nations.

traditions.text: A thematic link: in the Kirtland Temple, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery record that Moses appeared and “committed unto us the keys of the gathering of Israel.” The Moses of vv. 27–31, who foretells Israel's scattering among the nations and its return in the latter days (v. 30), is in Restoration scripture the one who hands on the authority to gather it. The same verse adds the leading of the ten tribes from the land of the north.

A thematic link: Nephi records the Lord rebuking those who say a Bible is all the word they need. God speaks to more than one nation, and having spoken one word does not mean he cannot speak another, for “my work is not yet finished.” Verse 2 forbids Israel to add to or take from Moses' commandments; 2 Nephi 29 insists that God himself may add.

Among the changes the Talmud says the seventy-two elders made when they translated the Torah into Greek for King Ptolemy is one in v. 19. To keep the king from thinking God had given the nations the sun and moon to worship, they wrote that God had allotted them “to give light” to all peoples. Rashi offers both this reading and another: God let the nations stray after the heavenly bodies.

The Mishnah notes that the three cities Moses set apart (vv. 41–43) could not shelter anyone until Joshua named the three west of the Jordan. Why set them apart early? The Talmud applies to Moses the proverb “he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver”: a lover of commandments takes any one he can keep, even one that will not take effect in his lifetime.

Rabbi Simlai read “toward the sunrising” in v. 41 as God telling Moses to make the sun rise for those who killed by accident, giving them hope of rescue. Rabbi Yohanan noted that the list of refuge cities (v. 43) is followed at once by “this is the law” (v. 44). From the pairing he taught that words of Torah also give refuge, so that a manslayer who studies them is protected from the avenger.

Rashi gives concrete examples of adding to the commandments (v. 2): putting five passages in the tefillin instead of four, using five species instead of four with the lulav, or tying five fringes on a garment. Taking away works the same way in reverse, as in using three passages or three fringes. For him the verse guards the exact shape of each commandment as well as their number.

traditions.text: In Justin's Dialogue, the Jewish speaker Trypho reads v. 19 at face value: the sun and moon are what God gave the nations to worship as gods. Clement goes further, saying God gave the nations the heavenly bodies to worship “that they might not become altogether atheistical.” Both readings stand opposite the softened Greek wording the Talmud credits to Ptolemy's translators (above).

traditions.text: Hebrews ends its comparison of Sinai and Mount Zion with the words of v. 24: “For our God is a consuming fire.” In Deuteronomy the phrase warns against images; in Hebrews it warns against refusing the one who now speaks from heaven. The same chapter of Hebrews recalls the burning mountain and the voice that the people could not bear, then contrasts the earth shaken at Sinai with a kingdom that cannot be moved.

Jesus tells his opponents that the Father has borne witness of him, yet they have never heard the Father's voice “nor seen his shape.” The words echo v. 12, where Israel heard the voice at Horeb but saw no form. In John even the hearing is denied to those who reject the one the Father sent, and Jesus adds that God's word does not abide in them.

The last chapter of the New Testament closes with a warning shaped like v. 2: whoever adds to the words of the prophecy will have the plagues of the book added to him, and whoever takes away will lose his part in the holy city. Moses' rule for the law becomes John's seal on his own book. Like Deuteronomy, Revelation is meant to be read aloud, and the curse falls on every hearer who tampers with it.

5.overview:
Moses tells Israel the covenant made at Horeb was made with the people standing before him, not just with their parents. He repeats the Ten Commandments the LORD spoke out of the fire and recalls that God wrote them on two tablets and “added no more.” The leaders, afraid the fire would consume them, begged Moses to go near, listen for them, and report back, and they promised to obey. God approved, wished they would always have such a heart, and kept Moses with him to receive the rest of the law.

The commandments are not repeated word for word. The Sabbath is to be kept as well as remembered (v. 12), and its reason is Israel's slavery in Egypt, where Exodus gives God's rest at creation (v. 15; Exodus 20:11). The day of rest is turned toward those who most need it: “that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou” (v. 14).

5.hermeneutics:
Ancient treaties bound more than the people who swore them. Esarhaddon's succession treaties of 672 BC made vassals swear for their sons and grandsons not yet born, and Hittite kings reissued a treaty when a vassal's son took the throne, restating the father's terms in the son's name. Verse 3 does both at once: the covenant at Horeb is “with us, even us,” the living, though most who stood at Horeb have died (2:14–16). Each generation stands at the mountain again.

Babylonian texts know a day called *shapattu*, the fifteenth of the month, when the moon was full, described as a day for quieting the god's heart. It was a lunar feast, not a weekly rest for workers. Israel's Sabbath counts sevens without regard to the moon, and Deuteronomy gives it a social reason: servants, foreigners, and working animals rest because Israel itself was a slave in Egypt (vv. 14–15). Where law collections like Hammurabi's treated slaves as property, this command gives them a day of their own.

Letters from Mari in the 18th century BC show how a god's word usually reached people: a prophet received it, and an official wrote it down and sent it on to the king. Horeb begins the other way round. The whole assembly hears God directly (vv. 4, 22), and only afterward, at the people's request, does Moses become the go-between (vv. 23–27), with God's approval (v. 28). Deuteronomy grounds Moses' role as mediator in this request, as 18:16–18 recalls.

The unit begins with the new heading at 4:44 and ends at 5:33, once Moses has explained why he, not God, now speaks the statutes. At 6:1 “Now these are the commandments” opens the teaching that follows.

traditions.text: When Abinadi reads the commandments to King Noah's priests, his wording follows Exodus, not this chapter. He says “Remember the sabbath day,” grounds it in the six days of creation, and puts the neighbor's house before his wife. The Book of Mormon's one full recital of the commandments thus preserves the Exodus 20 form, though Abinadi is speaking to Nephites who also had the five books of Moses on the brass plates (1 Nephi 5:11).

This revelation says that without the higher priesthood no one can see the face of God and live, and that Moses plainly taught this to Israel and sought to sanctify them so that they might behold his face. Deuteronomy's people say they have seen that God talks with man and he lives (v. 24), yet they ask Moses to go near in their place (v. 27). The revelation reads that retreat as the people's failure to endure God's presence.

How can Exodus say “Remember” and Deuteronomy “Keep” (v. 12)? A teaching quoted in the Talmud answers that God spoke both words in a single utterance, which no human mouth could say and no human ear could hear. Rav Adda bar Ahava drew a rule from the pairing: since women must keep the Sabbath, they are also bound to remember it with the blessing over the day.

Only Deuteronomy adds “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee” to the Sabbath (v. 12). Commanded when? The Talmud, followed by Rashi, says at Marah, where God made a statute for Israel before they reached Sinai (Exodus 15:25). On v. 15 Rashi adds that God freed Israel on condition that they serve him and keep his commandments.

The rabbis compared the animals in both lists. Exodus says “thy cattle”; Deuteronomy says “thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of thy cattle” (v. 14), and the Talmud draws rulings from each word, linking the ox to the law of muzzling and the ass to the law of unloading a burden. It also reads the closing clause, that servants may rest as well as their master, as limiting the comparison: people and animals are treated alike only in resting on the Sabbath.

Rabbi Hanina ben Agil asked why the word “good” appears with the parents command here (“that it may go well with thee,” v. 16) but not in Exodus. The answer he finally received: the first tablets were destined to be broken. Rav Ashi explained that if “good” had been written on them, good would have ended for Israel when they shattered.

A Qumran manuscript of Deuteronomy, probably a study or liturgical text, gives the Sabbath command both reasons. After the Egypt reason of v. 15 it adds the Exodus reason, that the LORD made heaven and earth in six days. Its scribe joined the two versions instead of choosing between them, much as the rabbis held “Remember” and “Keep” together (above). The manuscript is one of the clearest signs that early readers noticed the differences between the two Decalogues.

God says the people “have well said” (v. 28), but Rashi hears disappointment in Moses' telling. When they ask him to go near and speak to them (v. 27), the Hebrew uses an unusual pronoun, and Rashi says it shows they had weakened Moses, who grieved that they did not want to learn from God's own mouth out of love. Would it not have been better, Moses asks, to hear from God than from me?

Paul calls the command to honor father and mother the first commandment with promise, and gives the promise as “That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long.” The first half is Deuteronomy's addition (v. 16), also found in the Greek Septuagint of Exodus 20:12. His wording links the rabbis' question about “good” (above) to the version Christians read.

Hebrews recalls the mountain that burned with fire, the darkness, and the voice which those who heard begged not to hear any more. The detail matches v. 25, where the people fear that hearing the voice “any more” will kill them, and the retelling in 18:16. Hebrews sets that fear against Christians' approach to Mount Zion and to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, a mediator greater than the one the people asked for in v. 27.

6.overview:
Moses explains why the commandments are given: so that Israel, their children, and their grandchildren will fear the LORD and live long in the land. Then comes the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD,” with the command to love him with all the heart, soul, and might. These words are to be on the heart, taught to children, talked of at home and on the road, bound on the hand and between the eyes, and written on doorposts and gates. Moses warns that cities, houses, and vineyards Israel did not build or plant could make them forget the God who brought them out of Egypt, and he forbids tempting the LORD as at Massah.

The chapter is framed by a child. Verse 7 says to teach these words to your children, and v. 20 imagines the child asking what they mean. The father answers with a story: “We were Pharaoh's bondmen in Egypt.”

6.hermeneutics:
In the Amarna letters of the 14th century BC, Canaanite kings assure Pharaoh of their loyalty in the language of love, and William Moran showed in 1963 that “love” was the ordinary word for a vassal's faithfulness to his overlord. The succession treaty that Esarhaddon of Assyria imposed on his subjects in 672 BC orders them to love his heir Ashurbanipal as they love themselves (§24). Read against that background, v. 5 asks for more than a feeling. To love the LORD with heart, soul, and might is to give him undivided loyalty that shows in conduct. That is why the next verses turn at once to words kept, taught, spoken, and displayed.

Inscriptions from about 800 BC at Kuntillet Ajrud, a way station in the Sinai desert, bless travelers by “YHWH of Samaria” and by YHWH of Teman, a region to the south. Some Israelites, it seems, spoke of the LORD in local forms tied to particular places, much as Canaanites worshiped many local Baals. Against that background, “The LORD our God is one LORD” (v. 4) can be heard as a claim that there are not several LORDs of several places. The Hebrew *echad*, “one,” can mean both single and unique, and the verse allows either. The same concern drives chapter 12, which gathers Israel's sacrifices to a single chosen place.

notes: **Fear at each turn:** the verb “fear” comes 3 times, at the opening (v. 2), in the warning (v. 13), and in the father's answer (v. 24).
**Keep:** the verb *shamar* appears 6 times (vv. 2, 3, 12, 17 twice, 25). In v. 12 it is the “beware” of “beware lest thou forget.”
**The oath:** the land is what the LORD “sware” to the fathers (vv. 10, 18, 23), and in v. 13 Israel is to swear by his name. Verse 4 has six Hebrew words, and v. 5 has ten.

Chapters 6–8 form one unit. In 5:31 God tells Moses he will give him “the commandments, and the statutes, and the judgments” to teach, and 6:1 opens with that same phrase. Before any detailed law (chs. 12–26), Moses spends three chapters preaching the first commandment: one LORD, loved and not forgotten.

**Forward:** the warning of vv. 10–12, eaten and full and then forgetting, returns at length in 8:10–14. The father's answer in vv. 21–23 is a short creed of the Exodus, like the confession Israel will make over the firstfruits in 26:5–9.

traditions.text: Restoration scripture echoes v. 5 again and again, usually with “mind” added to the list, as Jesus adds it in Mark 12:30. The first revelation to Joseph Smith Sr. asks those who embark in God's service to serve him “with all your heart, might, mind and strength” (D&C 4:2). Nephi says to worship Christ with all might, mind, and strength and the whole soul, and Moroni's last exhortation promises that those who love God this way will find his grace sufficient to make them perfect in Christ.

The Church's footnotes to v. 4 point to passages that call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost “one God” (2 Nephi 31:21; Mosiah 15:4). The 1830 articles of the Church say the same: “Which Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are one God.” In the Church's teaching, the three members of the Godhead are separate beings who are one in purpose and doctrine.

The schools of Shammai and Hillel argued over v. 7. Shammai's followers said one must lie down to recite the Shema at night and stand to recite it in the morning, since the verse says “when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.” Hillel's followers answered that the verse also mentions walking by the way, so it sets the time of recitation, and anyone may say it in any posture. Rabbi Tarfon once lay down by the road to follow Shammai and was nearly attacked by bandits.

The Mishnah reads each phrase of v. 5. All the heart means with both inclinations, the good and the evil; all the soul means even if God takes your life; all the might means with all your money. The Talmud tells how Rabbi Akiva, executed by the Romans, recited the Shema while his flesh was torn and told his students he had waited all his life to fulfill “with all thy soul.” He drew out the final word, “one,” until he died.

This early rabbinic commentary asks why v. 4 addresses “Israel” and answers with Jacob, whose other name was Israel. On his deathbed Jacob feared that one of his sons might doubt God, as Abraham had fathered Ishmael and Isaac had fathered Esau. His sons replied: Hear, Israel our father, as there is no doubt in your heart, there is none in ours; the LORD is our God, the LORD is one. The Shema is read back into the scene of Genesis 49.

Rabbi Meir matches the three phrases of v. 5 to the three patriarchs. Love with all your heart, like Abraham, whom God calls “my friend” (Isaiah 41:8); with all your soul, like Isaac, who bound himself on the altar; with all your might, by giving thanks as Jacob did when he said he was not worthy of all God's mercies (Genesis 32:10). Each kind of love has a model in Israel's own family.

Rashi notices that v. 4 names the LORD twice and reads two claims in it: the LORD is now our God and not yet the God of the other nations, but in time he will be the one LORD of all. He supports this with Zephaniah 3:9 and Zechariah 14:9, “in that day shall there be one LORD, and his name one.” On v. 7 he reads “thy children” as disciples, since teachers in scripture are called fathers.

In his treatise on justice Philo reads vv. 6–9 as figures. Laying the words on the heart means stamping them on the mind, not trusting them to the ears; binding them on the hand means acting on them without delay, since the hand stands for deeds. Teaching them at home and on the road, lying down and rising up, means filling the whole soul with justice, and writing them on gates means every passerby should be reminded of what is right.

Asked which commandment is first, Jesus quotes vv. 4–5, and in Mark he begins with “Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord.” He pairs it with Leviticus 19:18 on loving one's neighbor and says all the law and the prophets hang on the two. Both Gospels add “mind” to the list in v. 5, the same addition found in the Restoration passages above.

In the wilderness Jesus answers the devil three times from Deuteronomy, twice from this chapter. Urged to throw himself from the temple, he quotes v. 16, “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” Offered the kingdoms of the world, he quotes v. 13 with “worship” for the Hebrew “fear” and an added “only.” His third answer comes from 8:3.

Two New Testament letters build on the confession of v. 4. Paul, writing about food offered to idols, says there are gods many and lords many, “but to us there is but one God, the Father,” and one Lord Jesus Christ; many scholars read his line as the Shema expanded. James grants that believing God is one is good but says the devils believe it too, and tremble.

7.overview:
Moses tells Israel that when the LORD brings them into the land, they are to destroy the seven nations living there, make no covenant or marriages with them, and break down their altars, images, and groves. The reason is Israel's holiness: the LORD chose them as his special people. Obedience will bring blessing on womb, field, and flock, and freedom from the diseases of Egypt. Israel need not fear nations stronger than itself. The LORD who struck Egypt will send the hornet and drive them out little by little, and the images of their gods must be burned, with none of their silver or gold kept.

Verse 7 removes any pride in being chosen. Israel was “the fewest of all people,” and the only causes Moses gives are the LORD's love and the oath he swore to the fathers (v. 8).

7.hermeneutics:
Verse 13 promises blessing on “the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep.” The Hebrew words are *sheger* and *ashterot*, and both are also names of deities. A plaster inscription from Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, from about 800 BC, names a goddess pair called Shagar-and-Ashtar, and Ashtart, or Astarte, was a great goddess of Canaan. In the land Israel was entering, the births of the herds could be credited to such powers. Deuteronomy uses their names as plain farm words and puts the fertility of the flocks in the LORD's hands.

When Assyrian armies took a city, they often carried off its gods. Palace reliefs show soldiers bearing statues of conquered gods on their shoulders, and Assyrian kings boast of removing them to Assyria as trophies or hostages. Such statues were wood or stone overlaid with silver and gold, precious booty in their own right. Verse 25 forbids the same profit: Israel must burn the images and may not covet or take the metal on them, “for it is an abomination.” The gods of the land were not to be kept, even as prizes.

Two small silver scrolls found in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from about 600 BC, were rolled up as amulets. One carries the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26. The other has lines close to v. 9: God keeps covenant and mercy with those who love him and keep his commandments. The confession of this chapter was already being written down and carried in Judah before the exile.

notes: **Devoted:** the verb *haram*, “utterly destroy,” comes twice in v. 2, an emphatic doubled form, and the noun *herem*, “a cursed thing,” twice in v. 26. The chapter that opens with the nations devoted to destruction ends by warning that an Israelite who brings an idol home becomes devoted like it.
**Love and oath:** the LORD's love is named in vv. 7, 8, and 13, and the oath he “sware” to the fathers in vv. 8, 12, and 13.
**The LORD thy God:** the divine name YHWH occurs 20 times in 26 verses; the conquest is his act from first verse to last.

Chapter 7 sits in the middle of the sermon of chapters 6–8 on the first commandment. Chapter 6 warns against “the gods of the people which are round about you” (6:14); chapter 7 applies that warning to the nations of Canaan; chapter 8 turns to the danger inside Israel, a full stomach and a proud heart.

**Backward and forward:** the list of nations, the hornet, and the slow conquest come from Exodus 23:23–33. Solomon broke v. 3, and 1 Kings 11:2 quotes its warning that foreign wives “will turn away your heart after their gods.”

traditions.text: When his brothers claim the people of Jerusalem are righteous, Nephi asks whether the nations driven out of Canaan were righteous, and answers no. Had they been righteous, he says, Israel would not have been more choice than they, for “the Lord esteemeth all flesh in one,” and he that is righteous is favored of God. Those nations were ripe in iniquity, so the land was cursed to them and blessed to Israel. The Church's footnote to v. 10 points to this passage, which, like vv. 7–8, refuses to make the conquest a reward for Israel's superiority.

After the return from exile, Judah's leaders apply vv. 1–3 to their own day. The princes report to Ezra that the people have not separated from the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and others, and have taken their daughters as wives. Nehemiah makes men swear not to give their daughters to foreign sons or take foreign daughters, in the wording of v. 3, and points to Solomon, whom foreign wives led into sin. The returned community read the old list of Canaanite peoples as a warning about the neighbors of their own time.

Philo paraphrases v. 3 as a command not to marry anyone of another nation, and takes his reason from v. 4. A spouse from outside, he says, may draw children into foreign customs until they forget the honor due to the one God. He adds that even children trained from youth in the sacred laws give their parents real cause for fear. In his reading the ban protects the household's worship of the one God, which is the concern of v. 4.

In his version of Moses' farewell, Josephus has Moses warn that if the laws are broken Israel will be scattered as slaves over sea and land. To keep the laws, he advises, they must leave none of their enemies alive, “lest if you permit them to live, you taste of their manners.” They are also to overthrow the altars and groves and burn all such things with fire. Josephus gives the danger to Israel's way of life as the reason, as v. 4 does.

The Talmud reads v. 3 as making a marriage with a non-Jew legally void, and v. 4 as the source for the rule that a child's status follows the mother. Rabbi Yohanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, notes that the verse fears that the foreign husband will turn away “thy son”: the child of your daughter is still called your son. A gentile mother's child, by contrast, is called her son and not yours.

The words “nor shew mercy unto them” (v. 2) are read three ways from the Hebrew spelling: do not praise them, do not give them free gifts, and do not give them a foothold to settle in the land. On v. 25 the rabbis notice a tension: the verse forbids coveting the silver on an idol, yet goes on to speak of taking it. Their answer is that once its gentile owner annuls the image as a god, the metal may be used.

Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose the Galilean reads v. 7 against its plain sense: God says he loves Israel because, when he gives them greatness, they make themselves small. Rashi, quoting him, lists Abraham's “which am but dust and ashes” and Moses and Aaron's “what are we?” against the boasts of Nebuchadnezzar, Sennacherib, and Hiram of Tyre. Rashi first notes the plain meaning: Israel really was the smallest people.

The Greek of v. 6 calls Israel a *laos periousios*, a “peculiar people,” the LORD's own possession. Titus 2:14 uses the phrase for those Christ redeems and purifies, and 1 Peter 2:9 joins it to the titles of Exodus 19:6 for the church: “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation.” The language of vv. 6–8 is carried over to the Christian community.

A monk of southern Gaul, Cassian reads the seven nations of v. 1 as the soul's chief vices, which are “greater and mightier” than the monk himself. Egypt, already left behind, stands for gluttony, making eight in all. The promise that the LORD will drive them out “by little and little” (v. 22) becomes a rule of spiritual struggle: fight one vice at a time and trust God for the victory. He quotes 8:12–15 against pride once a vice is beaten.

8.overview:
Moses calls Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness. God humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna, to teach that man does not live by bread only but by every word from the LORD's mouth. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell, and like a father he was training a son. Now he is bringing them into a good land of brooks and springs, wheat and barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olives, and honey, with iron in its stones and copper in its hills. When they have eaten and are full, they must bless the LORD. They must not forget him or claim that their own power earned their wealth, or they will perish like the nations.

Moses fears plenty more than hunger. The wilderness taught Israel to depend on God; the good land could teach them to forget him (vv. 12–14, 17).

8.hermeneutics:
The Egyptian Story of Sinuhe, from about 1900 BC, tells of an official who fled Egypt and settled in Retenu, the region of Syria and Canaan, where a local ruler gave him a district called Yaa. He describes it as a catalogue of plenty: figs and grapes, more wine than water, abundant honey and oil, fruit on every tree, barley and emmer, and cattle without number. To an Egyptian raised on the Nile, the hill country's mixed farming looked rich. Verses 7–9 use the same kind of list. But Canaan has no Nile, and the list begins with its water: brooks, fountains, and depths that spring out of valleys and hills, water that comes as a gift and cannot be managed from a river bank.

Verse 9 promises a land “whose stones are iron,” with hills where “thou mayest dig brass.” The KJV's “brass” is copper. Copper was mined and smelted on a large scale at Faynan and Timna in the Arabah, the rift valley south of the Dead Sea, and the slag heaps at Faynan date to the 10th and 9th centuries BC. Iron ore from Mugharat al-Warda in the Ajlun hills of Gilead was smelted at nearby Tell Hammeh from early in the Iron Age. Hearers who knew those places would hear v. 9 as a description of real mines, and of wealth that could tempt them to say “my power” (v. 17).

notes: **Forget and remember:** the verb “forget” comes 4 times (vv. 11, 14, and twice in the emphatic form of v. 19), and “remember” twice (vv. 2, 18). The whole chapter turns on which of the two Israel will do.
**Humbled:** the verb comes 3 times, all of the wilderness (vv. 2, 3, 16); manna appears twice (vv. 3, 16). The B and B′ panels share both.
**Eat:** “eat” comes 5 times (vv. 3, 9, 10, 12, 16), and “be full” twice (vv. 10, 12), once leading to blessing and once to a proud heart.

Chapter 8 closes the sermon of chapters 6–8. It returns to the warning of 6:10–12, a people eating from houses and vineyards it did not build, and expands it into a whole chapter. Chapter 9 opens a new unit with a second “Hear, O Israel” (9:1).

**Backward:** At Kadesh Israel complained that the wilderness had no seed, figs, vines, or pomegranates (Numbers 20:5); v. 8 promises a land that has all four. **Forward:** Hosea 13:5–6 describes the same sequence the chapter fears: fed, filled, heart exalted, God forgotten.

traditions.text: The revelation on priesthood closes by telling the elders to beware concerning themselves and give diligent heed to the words of eternal life. It then quotes v. 3 in the form Jesus used: you “shall live by every word,” adding “forth” to “proceedeth.” It goes on to say that the word of the Lord is truth, light, and Spirit, the Spirit of Jesus Christ. The Church's footnote to v. 3 points to this passage.

Mormon, abridging the Nephite record, stops to draw a lesson that matches vv. 11–17. At the very time the Lord prospers his people, in fields, flocks, herds, gold, and silver, they harden their hearts and forget him, “because of their ease, and their exceedingly great prosperity.” Unless the Lord chastens them with affliction, he adds, they will not remember him, an echo of the father's chastening in v. 5. The Church's footnote to v. 11 points here.

Verse 10 is the rabbinic source for grace after meals as a commandment of the Torah. A teaching in the Talmud divides the verse into the blessings of the grace: “bless” for the blessing over food, “the LORD thy God” for the invitation to bless, “the land” for the blessing of the land, and “good” for the blessing of Jerusalem. Rav Nahman says Moses composed the first blessing, “who feeds all,” when the manna came down.

Verse 16 says the manna was given “that he might humble thee,” and the rabbis ask how food from heaven could be an affliction. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi offer two answers. One says a man with bread in his basket for tomorrow is not like a man without it, and the manna never left any over. The other says it is not the same to eat food one can see as food one cannot, since the manna tasted of anything but always looked the same.

Several rabbis comment on v. 5, “as a man chasteneth his son.” Rabbi Yose son of Judah calls sufferings precious, because the name of God is set on the one who bears them. Rabbi Nathan says a covenant is made with sufferings just as a covenant is made with the land, and links v. 5 to v. 7, the good land that follows. The father's discipline is read as part of the covenant, not a break in it.

Philo quotes v. 3 and reads the manna as the word of God, which nourishes the soul; the more perfect soul is fed by the whole word, others by a portion of it. Elsewhere he quotes vv. 12–17 against the forgetful person who credits himself with his success. Remember your own nothingness, he says, and you will remember the greatness of God.

traditions.text: On v. 4 Rashi explains how clothes could last forty years. The clouds of glory rubbed the dirt from their garments and kept them white, and as the children grew their clothes grew with them, like the shell of a snail. Their feet did not swell, as the feet of those who walk barefoot do. Justin Martyr, below, tells the same story of the growing clothes centuries earlier.

After forty days of fasting in the wilderness, Jesus is hungry, and the tempter tells him to turn stones into bread. He answers with v. 3, “Man shall not live by bread alone,” and Matthew gives the rest of the verse as well: every word from the mouth of God. Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness, with hunger and manna, are echoed in his forty days.

In his dialogue with the Jewish teacher Trypho, Justin lists God's gifts to Israel in the wilderness: manna, quails, water from the rock, and the cloud for shade. Among them, the latchets of their shoes did not break and their garments did not wear out, “but even those of the children grew along with them.” It is the same tradition Rashi records on v. 4, here in a Christian writer of the 2nd century.

Arguing for the resurrection of the body, Tertullian lists the clothes and shoes of Israel that stayed unworn and fresh for forty years, citing the parallel verse 29:5. With them he puts the three Hebrews unharmed in the furnace, Jonah coming out of the fish, and Enoch and Elijah taken up alive. These, he says, are figures written so that we may believe God can preserve the flesh, since he preserved even its clothes and shoes.

9.overview:
Israel is about to cross the Jordan against walled cities and the tall sons of Anak, and Moses promises that the LORD will go ahead of them as a consuming fire. Then he warns them not to think the land is a reward for their righteousness. It comes because of the nations' wickedness and the LORD's oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for Israel is a stiffnecked people. As proof Moses retells Horeb: forty days on the mountain, the tablets written by God's finger, the molten calf, the broken tablets, and forty more days face down before the LORD, praying for the people and for Aaron. He adds Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and Kadesh-barnea, and ends with the words of his prayer.

Here the calf story serves an argument about the land. Moses tells it so that Israel will never say “For my righteousness” (v. 4); only the oath and the intercession stand on Israel's side.

9.hermeneutics:
In Mesopotamia an agreement lived on a clay tablet. When a loan was repaid, the tablet recording it was usually broken, and the obligation ended with it. Moses says he broke the tablets of the covenant “before your eyes” (v. 17), and in that world a broken tablet looked like a cancelled agreement. The people had already broken the covenant by making the calf; Moses' act made the breach visible. That is why chapter 10 begins with new tablets and the same words written on them again.

Peoples of the region explained disaster as the anger of their own god. Mesha of Moab says on his stele (about 840 BC) that Omri of Israel oppressed Moab for many years because Chemosh was angry with his land. Esarhaddon's inscriptions on rebuilding Babylon say that the god Marduk in his anger decreed seventy years of ruin for the city, then, his heart soothed, reversed the numbers to eleven. Moses' prayer (vv. 26–29) uses the same way of thinking but turns it. He fears that Egypt will read Israel's death in the wilderness as the LORD's weakness or hatred (v. 28), and he pleads the LORD's own honor, his oath to the fathers, and Israel as his inheritance.

notes: **Forty days and forty nights:** the phrase comes in vv. 9, 11, 18, and 25, and once more in 10:10.
**Destroy:** the verb *shamad* appears 6 times (vv. 3, 8, 14, 19, 20, 25). In v. 3 the LORD will destroy the nations; in every later use it is Israel, or Aaron, whom he threatens to destroy.
**Stiffnecked:** Moses' charge in v. 6 repeats God's own words in v. 13. The same expression returns in 10:16 as a command: “be no more stiffnecked.”

A new unit opens with a second “Hear, O Israel” (9:1; compare 6:4) and runs to 10:11, when the LORD sends Moses to lead the people on. Chapter 9 is the case against Israel; 10:1–11 shows the covenant restored with new tablets and the ark.

**Backward:** Exodus 32 tells the calf story in order of events. Deuteronomy arranges it as evidence and moves the forty days of prayer after the breaking of the tablets. Moses' plea in v. 28 repeats the argument he made at Kadesh, that the nations would say the LORD was not able to bring Israel in (Numbers 14:16).

traditions.text: Nephi makes the argument of vv. 5–7 to his own rebellious brothers. Israel in the wilderness hardened their hearts and reviled against Moses and against God, he says, yet the Lord loved their fathers, covenanted with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and remembered his covenants. So Israel was led by his “matchless power into the land of promise.” As in vv. 5–7, the people's record and the fathers' covenant stand side by side, and the covenant decides the outcome.

Philo quotes vv. 4–5 against anyone who thinks he deserved the good things he enjoys. The land is given, he notes, first because of the nations' wickedness and second to confirm the covenant sworn to the fathers. He reads the covenant as a figure for God's graces, which are complete gifts and not wages. Forgetfulness, ingratitude, and self-love are what he tells his readers to discard.

traditions.text: This Aramaic paraphrase turns the anger and hot displeasure of v. 19 into destroying angels: “five destroying angels were sent from the Lord to destroy Israel,” among them Wrath and Burning. When Moses called on the divine Name, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rose from their tomb to pray, and three of the angels were held back. Moses prayed on until the last two were restrained, and he buried them in the land of Moab. The legend acts out Moses' plea in v. 27 that God remember his servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The Mishnah dates two of this chapter's events in Israel's calendar of mourning. On the seventeenth of Tammuz, it says, Moses broke the tablets when he saw the calf (v. 17), the first of five disasters on that day, which include the breaching of Jerusalem's walls. On the Ninth of Av it was decreed that the wilderness generation would die without entering the land, the punishment for the refusal at Kadesh-barnea that v. 23 recalls. Both days became fasts.

Moses broke the tablets (v. 17) on his own judgment, the Talmud says, and God agreed. He reasoned that if no apostate Israelite may eat the Passover, one of the 613 commandments, then people worshiping a calf were not fit to receive the whole Torah. God's approval is found in the phrase “which thou brakest,” read by Resh Lakish as a blessing on Moses for breaking them. The same phrase recurs in 10:2.

On v. 20, where the LORD was angry with Aaron “to have destroyed him,” Rashi says Aaron was blamed because he listened to the people. He takes “destroy” to mean the cutting off of a man's children, citing Leviticus Rabbah. Moses' prayer for Aaron atoned for half, Rashi says: two of Aaron's four sons died (Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus 10) and two lived.

Paul sets out the righteousness that comes by faith with the words “Say not in thine heart,” the opening of v. 4 in the Greek Bible, and then continues with 30:12–14. Verse 4 had warned Israel not to say in its heart that the land came by its own righteousness. Paul, who has just spoken of those who go about to establish their own righteousness (Romans 10:3), joins the two passages to set righteousness by faith against a righteousness of one's own.

Writing to the divided church at Corinth, Clement retells vv. 12–14: Moses after forty days of fasting is told to go down, for the people are stiffnecked, and God offers to make of him a great nation. Moses refuses and asks to be blotted out with them instead (Exodus 32:32), which Clement praises as mighty love and unsurpassable perfection. He then urges whoever caused the strife at Corinth to step aside for the good of the flock, as Moses was willing to do.

Describing the terror of Sinai, Hebrews says Moses himself said, “I exceedingly fear and quake.” Exodus records no such words at the giving of the law. The closest source is v. 19 in the Greek Bible, *ekphobos eimi*, “I am terrified,” spoken by Moses when he feared the LORD's anger after the calf.

Jesus fasts “forty days and forty nights” in the wilderness, the phrase used of Moses on the mountain in vv. 9 and 18. Moses neither ate bread nor drank water while he received the covenant and while he interceded for Israel. Matthew's wording sets Jesus' fast alongside Moses' as he begins his ministry.

10.overview:
The LORD tells Moses to cut two new tablets like the first and to make an ark of wood. Moses makes the ark, climbs the mountain with the tablets, and the LORD writes the Ten Commandments on them again; Moses brings them down and puts them in the ark, “and there they be.” A travel note follows. Aaron dies at Mosera, Eleazar succeeds him, and the tribe of Levi is set apart to carry the ark and bless in the LORD's name. Then Moses asks what the LORD requires: fear, walking in his ways, love, service, and obedience. The God of gods loves the fatherless, the widow, and the stranger, and Israel must love the stranger too, for they were strangers in Egypt.

The chapter turns from story to sermon at v. 12, “And now, Israel.” A people called stiffnecked in chapter 9 is told to “circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (v. 16).

10.hermeneutics:
Kings across the ancient Near East claimed to protect the weak. Hammurabi's epilogue says he set up his laws “that the strong might not injure the weak” and to protect widows and orphans, and in the Ugaritic poem of Aqhat the good king Danel sits at the city gate judging the cause of the widow and the orphan. Verses 17–18 give that royal role to the LORD, “God of gods, and Lord of lords,” who takes no bribe. Then they add a third person under his care, one not usually on the royal list: he loves the stranger, and Israel must love the stranger too (v. 19).

Israel was not the only people that practiced circumcision. A tomb relief at Saqqara from Egypt's Old Kingdom shows the operation, Herodotus says the Egyptians had circumcised “from the first” and that the Phoenicians and Syrians of Palestine learned it from them, and Jeremiah 9:25–26 lists Egypt, Edom, Ammon, and Moab with Judah among the circumcised. A sign that neighbors shared could not by itself mark Israel as the LORD's. Verse 16 moves the cut inward, to the heart. The image is of removing whatever covers the heart and keeps it from hearing, which is why the same verse adds, “be no more stiffnecked.”

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from the end of the calf story (vv. 1–11) to a new exhortation (vv. 12–22).
notes: **Five duties:** vv. 12–13 ask Israel to fear, to walk in his ways, to love, to serve, and to keep. Verse 20 repeats the list in short form: fear, serve, cleave, swear by his name.
**Love:** the verb *ahav* comes 4 times in vv. 12–22. Israel is to love the LORD (v. 12), the LORD loved the fathers (v. 15), he loves the stranger (v. 18), and Israel must love the stranger (v. 19).
**Stiffnecked:** the word that condemned Israel in 9:6 and 9:13 appears a third time in v. 16, now as a command to stop.

Chapter 10 straddles two units. Verses 1–11 finish the story begun in 9:1: the tablets restored, Levi set apart, and Israel sent on toward the land. At v. 12, “And now, Israel,” Moses turns to exhortation, and that unit runs to the blessing and curse set before Israel in 11:26–32.

**Echoes:** Micah 6:8 asks the same question as v. 12, “what doth the LORD require of thee,” and answers with justice, mercy, and humility. When Solomon brings the ark into the temple, there is nothing in it but the two tablets Moses put there at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote to v. 2 gives the Joseph Smith Translation: the Lord will write on the new tablets the words of the first, “save the words of the everlasting covenant of the holy priesthood.” The change agrees with the JST of Exodus 34:1–2 and with D&C 84:23–27, which teach that the higher priesthood was taken from Israel after the calf. In this reading the second tablets carried a lesser law than the first.

Verse 8 sets Levi apart to bear the ark, minister, and bless. When John the Baptist conferred the Priesthood of Aaron on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery in 1829, he said it would remain on the earth “until the sons of Levi do offer again an offering” in righteousness. D&C 84 speaks of the sons of Moses and of Aaron offering an acceptable offering in the Lord's house, and says the faithful who obtain both priesthoods become those sons. The link to v. 8 is thematic.

Rashi asks why vv. 6–7 interrupt the calf story with a journey, and why Aaron dies at Mosera when Numbers 20 puts his death on Mount Hor. His answer, drawn from earlier midrash, is that this too is rebuke: after Aaron's death Israel lost heart, turned back eight stations toward Egypt, and mourned Aaron at Mosera as if he had died there. He adds that the death is placed next to the broken tablets to teach that the death of the righteous is as grievous to God as the day the tablets were broken.

Rabbi Hanina asks how v. 12 can call the fear of heaven a small request, and answers that for Moses it was: a large vessel seems small to the one who owns it. The same page tells of a prayer leader who heaped up adjectives for God. Rabbi Hanina stopped him, saying that even “the great, the mighty, and the terrible” could be said in prayer only because Moses said them in v. 17.

Philo paraphrases v. 12: God asks nothing hard of the mind, only to love him as a benefactor, or at least fear him as ruler, and to walk in his ways and serve him with the whole soul. On v. 16 he says those with hard hearts are uncircumcised in heart, and reads the command as an order to cut away the arrogance of the ruling part of the soul. Stiff necks, he adds, mean a mind that will not bend.

Philo reads the stranger of vv. 18–19 as the proselyte, who has left kin, country, and ancestral gods for the worship of the one God. Moses, he says, commands Israel to love such strangers not only as friends and relatives but as themselves. In another treatise he quotes v. 17 and notes that the great God gives judgment for the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, the people with no powerful allies.
traditions.cite: On the Virtues 102–103; On the Special Laws 4.176–178

traditions.text: Paul writes that circumcision is “that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter,” and that the true Jew is one inwardly. Stephen, on trial in Jerusalem, calls his accusers stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, joining the two charges that sit side by side in v. 16. Both draw on the inward circumcision commanded in v. 16 and promised in 30:6.

Peter, in the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius, says he now perceives that “God is no respecter of persons,” the phrase v. 17 uses of the LORD. The title “Lord of lords” from the same verse is given to God in 1 Timothy 6:15 and to the Lamb in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16, paired with “King of kings.”

Barnabas quotes v. 16 in its Greek form, “Be ye circumcised in the hardness of your heart,” with its warning against a hardened neck, and argues that God never wanted a circumcision of the flesh. Answering the objection that circumcision was Israel's seal, he points out that Syrians, Arabians, the priests of idols, and Egyptians are circumcised too. His argument rests on the same fact that gives v. 16 its force: the outward mark was shared with the neighbors.

In his dialogue with Trypho, Justin quotes vv. 16–17 together: circumcise the hardness of your hearts and stiffen the neck no more, for the LORD is Lord of lords and regards not persons. He sets beside them Leviticus 26:41 on the uncircumcised heart. For Justin these verses show that God asked for a changed heart from the beginning, and he treats the fleshly sign as a mark that set Israel apart.

11.overview:
Moses calls Israel to love the LORD and keep his charge, and he points to what this generation saw with its own eyes: the signs in Egypt, the Red Sea closing over Pharaoh's chariots, the earth swallowing Dathan and Abiram. Then he describes the land ahead. Egypt was watered by the farmer's foot, but Canaan drinks the rain of heaven, and that rain will come in its season only while Israel stays loyal; serving other gods will shut the sky. These words are to be bound on the hand, taught to children, and written on doorposts. The chapter ends by setting a blessing and a curse before the people, to be pronounced on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal across the Jordan.

Listen for “this day.” The Hebrew *hayyom* comes eight times between v. 2 and v. 32. The choice between blessing and curse is put to the people standing in Moab now, before they cross.

11.hermeneutics:
Egypt's farmers did not wait for rain. Herodotus, who visited in the 5th century BC, reports that below Memphis the river rose and watered the fields by itself, and the farmer simply sowed and turned his pigs in to tread the seed down. The Egyptian priests told him the Greeks were the ones at risk: they had no water except what Zeus sent, and if he withheld it they would starve. Deuteronomy turns that comparison around. Egypt is the land watered “with thy foot” (v. 10), most likely by opening and closing irrigation channels, and Canaan is the land that “drinketh water of the rain of heaven” (v. 11). What an Egyptian counted a weakness becomes the point of the land: its water cannot be managed, only given, so the harvest depends on the LORD who watches it all year (v. 12).

In Canaan the rain had a god already. The Ugaritic texts from Ras Shamra (14th–13th centuries BC) call Baal “rider of the clouds.” In his myth a window is built into his palace so he can thunder and send rain in its season, and in the Aqhat epic a curse wishes that Baal fail for seven years, with no dew and no showers. Verses 13–17 claim the early and latter rain for the LORD and name serving other gods as the thing that shuts the sky. The rival being warned against is the very god farmers credited with rain. The stories of Elijah and Ahab later stage that contest as a drought (1 Kings 17–18).

**Two outcomes, one day:** *Hayyom*, “this day,” occurs 8 times. “Blessing” and “curse” each occur 3 times in vv. 26–29, and the curse falls on those who “go after other gods,” the same danger as v. 16.

Chapter 11 ends the long exhortation of chs. 5–11 that stands before the laws. Verse 32 hands over to the heading at 12:1, “These are the statutes and judgments,” where the detailed laws of chs. 12–26 begin. The blessing and curse of vv. 26–32 return in chs. 27–28, so the two Gerizim and Ebal passages bracket the law code.

**Later echoes:** Joshua builds an altar on Ebal and reads the blessings and cursings with half the people facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal (Joshua 8:30–35). Elijah's drought under Ahab (1 Kings 17:1) plays out the shut heaven of vv. 16–17.

traditions.text: A thematic link, not a quotation. Lehi describes the land of promise in terms close to vv. 8–17: those who keep the commandments will prosper in it and be kept from other nations, and if iniquity abounds the land will be cursed for their sakes. Moroni's abridgment of the Jaredite record states the same decree more sharply, that whoever possesses the land must serve God or be swept off when they are ripe in iniquity. Like Deuteronomy, both tie a people's hold on a chosen land to their loyalty.

Given in Missouri, this revelation restates the great command with the two verbs of v. 13 joined: love the Lord “with all thy heart,” and serve him. It adds might, mind and strength, and says the service is to be rendered in the name of Jesus Christ.

Verses 13–21 became the second paragraph of the Shema, recited morning and evening after 6:4–9 and before Numbers 15:37–41. Rabbi Joshua ben Korha explains the order: one first accepts the yoke of the kingdom of heaven in 6:4–9, and only then the yoke of the commandments in this passage. This paragraph also comes before the one on fringes, the Mishnah adds, because its commands apply by night as well as by day.

Verses 18–20 were taken literally. The mezuzah on the doorpost holds two passages, 6:4–9 and 11:13–21, and the phylacteries hold those two plus Exodus 13:1–10 and 13:11–16. If even one letter is missing, the Mishnah rules, none of the passages fulfills the command.

In his summary of the laws Moses gave in Moab, Josephus says Israel is to remember the deliverance from Egypt twice a day, at its start and at bedtime. They are also to write the chief blessings on their doors and to bear on the forehead and the arm “those wonders which declare the power of God.” He treats the practice as public thanksgiving.

The rabbis read v. 10 as praise of the land of Israel over Egypt, the most fertile land they knew. Egypt drinks from below, from the Nile, and yields only to mattock and spade and lost sleep, while Israel drinks from above. Other lands have servants to water them, the Nile for Egypt and canals for Babylonia, but in Israel people sleep in their beds and God brings the rain, like a king who resolves to feed a favored man with his own hands.

A teaching on v. 13 asks what service is done with the heart, and answers that it is prayer. Because the next verse promises rain in its season, the rabbis tied the prayer for rain to the Amidah, the daily standing prayer. The phrase “service of the heart” became a standard rabbinic name for prayer.

The rabbis argue over where v. 30 puts the two mountains. One view links “the plains of Moreh” to Shechem through Genesis 12:6, and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose accuses the Samaritans of forging their Torah by writing that link into the text. The Samaritan Pentateuch does read “opposite Shechem” here, and Samaritans still worship on Gerizim (see John 4:20).

Josephus retells the command of vv. 29–30 with details of his own. The altar is to face the rising sun near Shechem, with Gerizim on the right hand and Ebal on the left, and six tribes stand on each mountain to answer one another with blessings and curses. He adds that Moses wrote the blessings and curses on both sides of the altar.

Jesus faults scribes and Pharisees who “make broad their phylacteries,” the leather cases worn in obedience to v. 18 and 6:8, and who lengthen the fringes of their garments. His complaint is that they do it to be seen of men, turning a sign meant for the wearer into a display. The Mishnah's careful rules and Josephus' public reading of the practice show how visible it already was.

James borrows the farmer of v. 14 to teach patience: the husbandman waits for his crop “until he receive the early and latter rain.” The pair are the autumn rains that soften the ground for sowing and the spring rains that fill out the grain, the two the LORD promises here. For James the farmer's long wait becomes a picture of waiting for the coming of the Lord.

12.overview:
Moses orders the Canaanite shrines destroyed: the high places on hills and under green trees, the altars, pillars, and carved images. Israel is not to worship its God that way. Offerings, tithes, vows, and firstlings must go to one place, the place the LORD will choose out of all the tribes to put his name, and there households, servants, and Levites are to eat and rejoice together. Because that place may be far off, ordinary meat may now be killed and eaten at home like gazelle or deer, as long as the blood is poured on the ground. The chapter closes with a warning not to copy the nations, who even burned their children, and a charge to add nothing and take nothing away.

The place is never named. Six times the chapter speaks of the place the LORD “shall choose,” and readers have found it at Shiloh, at Jerusalem, and, among the Samaritans, at Gerizim.
