12.hermeneutics:
Archaeology shows what vv. 2–4 and 13 are aimed at. Inside the royal fortress at Arad in the Negev, excavators found a small Judahite shrine of the Iron Age, with an altar in its courtyard and a standing stone in its inner niche. The shrine was later put out of use, and its excavators tied that to the reforms of Hezekiah or Josiah, though the dating is disputed. Worship of Israel's God at local shrines was normal practice, and 2 Kings 23:8 says Josiah defiled the high places “from Geba to Beer-sheba.” Chapter 12 reads as the charter for that kind of reform.

“To put his name there” (vv. 5, 21) uses a royal idiom. In Akkadian, to place one's name meant to set up an inscription that claimed a city or a land. In the 14th century BC Abdi-Heba, ruler of Jerusalem, reminded Pharaoh that the king had set his name in Jerusalem forever and so could not abandon it (Amarna letter EA 287). Heard that way, the chosen place is the spot the LORD marks as his own, the way a king marks his territory.

Verse 31 ends with sons and daughters “burnt in the fire to their gods.” At Carthage and other Phoenician settlements, walled precincts now called tophets held thousands of urns with the burned bones of infants and young animals, many under stones dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit. Scholars still debate whether every child was sacrificed or some had died naturally, but the rite was real in the Phoenician world. Deuteronomy sets it at the end of the road that begins with asking how the nations served their gods (v. 30).

notes: **Choose:** Each block restates the one-place law from a new angle. *Bachar*, “choose,” comes 6 times (vv. 5, 11, 14, 18, 21, 26).

**Place and name:** *Maqom*, “place,” occurs 9 times: the nations' places to be destroyed (vv. 2–3), “every place that thou seest” (v. 13), and the one place the LORD chooses. “Name” comes 4 times: Israel wipes out the names of the gods (v. 3), and the LORD puts his name at his place (vv. 5, 11, 21).
**Rejoice and blood:** “Rejoice” comes 3 times (vv. 7, 12, 18), each time with the household and the Levite. “Blood” comes 5 times, all in vv. 16–27.

The heading in v. 1, “These are the statutes and judgments,” opens the law code of chs. 12–26. Its first law settles where Israel worships, and its last returns to “the place which the LORD thy God shall choose” (26:2). KJV 12:32 is 13:1 in Hebrew Bibles, where the warning against adding and taking away heads the laws on false prophets.

**Later echoes:** Solomon's temple is the house of which God said, “My name shall be there” (1 Kings 8:29; 9:3). Jeremiah reminds Jerusalem that Shiloh was where God first set his name, and that it lies in ruins (Jeremiah 7:12).

traditions.text: The Kirtland Temple dedicatory prayer speaks of a house built to the Lord's name and asks that his name be put upon his people in that house. A week later, in the vision recorded in D&C 110, the Lord says he has accepted the house and “my name shall be here.” The wording follows vv. 5 and 11 and God's answer to Solomon in 1 Kings 9:3, where the temple is hallowed to put his name there for ever.

A thematic link to v. 32. D&C 20 affirms that the restored record agrees with the revelations of John, “neither adding to, nor diminishing from” them, wording that echoes this verse and Revelation 22:18–19. In 2 Nephi 29 the Lord answers Gentiles who say they have a Bible and need no more, warning them not to suppose it holds all his words. Both passages read the warning as binding people, not as a limit on what God may reveal.

The rabbis wrote Israel's history of worship around this chapter. Private altars were allowed before the tabernacle was set up, at Gilgal, and at Nob and Gibeon, and forbidden at Shiloh and finally at Jerusalem, never to be allowed again. They read “the rest” of v. 9 as Shiloh and “the inheritance” as Jerusalem, so the verse names both places that served as the chosen sanctuary.

Josephus has Moses command one holy city in Canaan, chosen by God through prophetic revelation, with one temple and one altar, and no altar or temple in any other city. His reason is short: “For God is but one,” and the nation of the Hebrews is one. By his day the chosen place was taken for granted to be Jerusalem, and its temple was the only one most Jews recognized.

Philo gives the same reason as Josephus: since God is one, his temple also should be one. He adds that Moses forbade sacrifice at home and made worshipers travel from the ends of the earth on purpose. The long journey tests the worshiper, since no one would leave country and kin to sacrifice without a pure intent.

Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva disagree over what v. 20 changed. For Ishmael, Israel in the wilderness could eat meat only as a sacrifice, and “meat of desire” was first allowed on entering the land. For Akiva, ordinary meat was always permitted, and the verse forbade what had been allowed before, meat from an animal stabbed rather than properly slaughtered.

The Samaritan woman at the well puts the chapter's unanswered question to Jesus: her fathers worshiped “in this mountain,” Gerizim, while the Jews say Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. Jesus answers that the hour is coming when the Father will be worshiped neither on that mountain nor at Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth. The dispute he sets aside is the one the Samaritan Pentateuch's reading reflects (below).

The Jerusalem council frees Gentile converts from most of the law of Moses but keeps four rules, one of them to abstain from blood. The blood ban of vv. 16 and 23–25 is older than Sinai: God gives it to Noah for all his descendants (Genesis 9:4), which may be why the apostles kept it for every believer.

The last book of the New Testament closes with the warning of v. 32 turned on itself. If anyone adds to the words of this prophecy, God will add the plagues written in it, and if anyone takes away, God will take away his part in the holy city. Deuteronomy 4:2 gives the same warning in Moses' first address.

This early church manual of moral teaching borrows the wording of v. 32 for Christian instruction. Do not forsake the Lord's commandments, it says, but keep what you have received, “neither adding thereto nor taking away.” The phrase had become a standard way to describe faithful handing on of a teaching.

traditions.text: The Samaritans' Torah reads “the place which the LORD has chosen” throughout Deuteronomy, where the Jewish text has “shall choose.” For them the place was already chosen in Moses' day: Gerizim, the mountain of blessing in 11:29 and 27:12. The Jewish reading leaves the choice in the future, open for Jerusalem.

13.overview:
Three cases of enticement to worship other gods, each quoting the same call: let us go and serve “other gods, which ye have not known.” First, a prophet or dreamer gives a sign that comes true. Israel must still refuse him, because the LORD is testing whether they love him with all their heart, and the prophet is to die. Second, a brother, son, daughter, wife, or closest friend urges it in secret. The hearer may not pity or hide him, and his own hand is to be first in the stoning. Third, worthless men lead a whole town astray. After careful inquiry, the town is to be destroyed, burned with all its spoil, and left a heap for ever.

In the first case the sign comes to pass, and it settles nothing. A prophet is judged by where he leads, toward or away from the God who brought Israel out of Egypt (v. 5).

13.hermeneutics:
Assyrian kings bound their subjects with loyalty oaths, and the best preserved is the succession treaty Esarhaddon imposed in 672 BC to secure the throne for his son Ashurbanipal. One clause requires the oath-taker who hears an evil word against the prince to report it and not conceal it, whether it comes from his own relatives or from the mouth of a prophet, an ecstatic, or an inquirer of oracles. Another orders him to seize anyone who speaks of rebellion. Deuteronomy 13 has the same cast of characters, prophet and dreamer, brother, son and friend, and the same demand: “neither shalt thou conceal him” (v. 8). Many scholars think the chapter adapts such oaths, transferring to the LORD the total loyalty an Assyrian vassal owed his king.

Prophets were not new, and neither was checking them. Letters from Mari on the Euphrates (18th century BC) report oracles to King Zimri-Lim, and officials sometimes sent along a lock of the prophet's hair and the fringe of his garment so the message could be tested. Deuteronomy sets a different test. A sign that comes true proves nothing if the message is “let us go after other gods” (v. 2); the content of the call outweighs the wonder.

The town law uses the word of holy war, *herem*, “devoted to destruction” (vv. 15, 17). King Mesha of Moab boasts on his stele (c. 840 BC) that he took Nebo from Israel, killed its seven thousand people, and devoted it to his god Ashtar-Chemosh. Here the same treatment is turned inward, against an Israelite town that goes over to other gods, and it ends as a *tel*, “an heap for ever” (v. 16), like Ai in Joshua 8:28.

notes: **The same words three times:** Each case quotes the tempter: go and serve “other gods, which ye have not known” (vv. 2, 6, 13). *Elohim acherim*, “other gods,” occurs 3 times, once per case.

**Widening circles:** The cases move out from one inspired voice to the household and the friend “which is as thine own soul,” then to a whole city. The penalty widens with them, from one death to a town left a ruin.

**Thrust away:** The verb *nadach*, to drive or lure away, comes 3 times (vv. 5, 10, 13), once in each case, and names the crime. *Shama*, “hear” or “hearken,” comes 6 times, from refusing to hear the prophet (v. 3) to hearkening to the LORD's voice (v. 18).

Chapter 13 completes the subsection that began in ch. 12. Chapter 12 guards where Israel worships; ch. 13 guards whom, against the voices that would draw Israel to other gods. In Hebrew Bibles the chapter opens with the charge not to add or take away (KJV 12:32), so the false prophet appears as one who adds. Chapter 14 then turns to Israel as a holy people.

**Later echoes:** Deuteronomy 18:20–22 adds the second test, a prophecy that fails. Jeremiah applies it to Hananiah, who “taught rebellion against the LORD,” the charge of v. 5, and who dies the same year (Jeremiah 28:15–17).

traditions.text: Joseph Smith's revision of Jesus' Olivet discourse keeps the warning built on this chapter: false Christs and false prophets will show great signs and wonders and, if possible, deceive the very elect. It adds that the elect are those “according to the covenant.” As in v. 3, wonders are no guarantee, and the covenant people are the ones being tested.

A thematic link. Given when some in Kirtland were disturbed by people making false claims as revelators, this revelation sets a rule for the Church: none but the one appointed receives commandments and revelations for it. Members are to receive no one's teachings as revelations or commandments, “that you may not be deceived.” Like Deuteronomy 13, it guards the community against voices that claim divine authority.

Two rabbis argue over how great a sign v. 2 imagines. Rabbi Yose the Galilean says the Torah grants even idolaters power over the sun, moon, and stars, and still Israel must not listen. Rabbi Akiva recoils: God would never alter the heavens for such people, so the verse must mean a true prophet who later turned false, like Hananiah son of Azzur in Jeremiah 28.

Philo calls anyone who uses the name of prophet to lead people to other gods an impostor inventing oracles. Even a brother, son, wife, or close friend who urges it should be treated as a public enemy. The only kinship that counts, he says, is shared zeal for God, and he cites 14:1, “Ye are the sons of the Lord your God,” as the higher bond.

Josephus folds this chapter into the oath he says Moses had the whole people swear in Moab, women, children, and slaves included. If anyone of their own blood, or any city, tried to overturn the constitution, they would punish them all in general and each in particular, and overturn that city to its foundations. If they could not, they were at least to show that it was done against their will. Like the Assyrian treaties, his version treats the law as a sworn political loyalty.

The enticer of vv. 6–11 is the one offender for whom the court may hide witnesses to catch him. The Mishnah pictures his pitch: an idol in such a place that eats and drinks, does good to its worshipers and harms those who refuse it. Rabbinic law elsewhere protects the accused, so the exception shows how seriously the rabbis took v. 8, “neither shalt thou conceal him.”

One teaching holds that the condemned town of vv. 12–18 never existed and never will, and was written only to be studied for reward. Rabbi Eliezer reasons that a town with even one mezuzah cannot qualify, since v. 16 requires burning everything and 12:3–4 forbids destroying holy writing. Rabbi Jonathan disagrees: he once saw such a town and sat on its ruins.

On v. 16, Rabbi Akiva rules that the ruined town may not even become a garden or an orchard. On v. 17 the Sifre adds that no benefit may be had from anything taken from it, even a staff or a spindle. It reads the promise of mercy in the same verse as running both ways, and quotes Rabban Gamaliel: while you show mercy to others, Heaven shows mercy to you. The harshest law in the chapter ends in compassion.

In his last discourse Jesus warns that false Christs and false prophets will rise and show signs and wonders “to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect.” The pairing of prophet, signs, and wonders follows vv. 1–3, now set in the last days. The warning to the disciples is the same as Moses' warning to Israel: wonders alone prove nothing.

Paul expects the lawless one to come with “signs and lying wonders,” and Revelation's second beast makes fire fall from heaven and deceives the earth's people into worshiping an image. Both picture the danger of vv. 1–3 on a world scale: real wonders in the service of false worship.

This early church manual gives congregations rules for wandering teachers and prophets. A teacher who turns to “another doctrine” is not to be heard, and a prophet is known by whether he holds the ways of the Lord: one who stays three days, asks money for himself, or does not do what he teaches is a false prophet. Like v. 3, it judges a prophet by his ways, not by the power of his speech.

14.overview:
Israel are the children of the LORD and a holy people, so they must not gash themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead. The food laws follow in short form: ten kinds of animals that may be eaten, the two signs of a clean beast, fins and scales, the birds that may not be eaten, and bans on flying swarming things and on meat from an animal that died of itself, which may go to a resident stranger or be sold to a foreigner. Then the tithe. Each year a tenth of grain, wine, and oil is eaten before the LORD at the chosen place, turned into money first if the road is long, and shared with the Levite. Every third year it stays in town for the Levite, stranger, orphan, and widow.

The food list shortens Leviticus 11, but its frame is new. “Thou art an holy people” opens it (v. 2) and closes it (v. 21).

14.hermeneutics:
Gashing the body was how the gods themselves mourned in Canaanite myth. In the Baal cycle from Ugarit (14th–13th centuries BC), when El hears that Baal is dead he comes down from his throne, sits in the dust, scrapes his skin with a stone, and gashes his cheeks, chin, and arms; the goddess Anat mourns the same way. The prophets of Baal on Carmel cut themselves “after their manner” (1 Kings 18:28). Verse 1 forbids the rite and gives a family reason for it: Israel are the LORD's children, and their grief is not to copy the mourning for a dying god.

The kid in its mother's milk (v. 21) has a famous false parallel. In the 1930s one line of an Ugaritic ritual text was restored to read that a kid was cooked in milk, and for decades that reading was offered as the Canaanite rite the law opposed, as Maimonides had once guessed without any text. Later study of the tablet showed the key word is damaged and the restoration doubtful, and most scholars now set it aside. The reason for the law remains open; Deuteronomy places it right after “thou art an holy people.”

Tithes were normally a tax. Babylonian temples of the 6th century BC, such as the Eanna at Uruk and the Ebabbar at Sippar, collected a tenth (*eshru*) of harvests and herds, from royalty down, to fund the god's household. Deuteronomy's yearly tithe goes the other way: the farmer brings it to the chosen place and eats it there with his household and the Levite (vv. 23–27), and every third year it feeds the poor in his own town (vv. 28–29). The tithe still belongs to God, but the people who eat it are Israel and those who have no land.

rows.text: The tithe eaten before the LORD

notes: **Frame:** “Thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God” opens the food laws (v. 2) and closes them (v. 21). *Qadosh*, “holy,” occurs only in those 2 verses.
**Eat:** The verb *akhal* occurs 17 times and joins the two halves, from what Israel may not eat to what it must eat “before the LORD” (vv. 23, 26) and share (v. 29).

**Against Leviticus 11:** Deuteronomy names 10 clean animals (vv. 4–5), 3 domestic and 7 wild, where Leviticus gives only the signs. Its list of forbidden birds has 21 names to Leviticus' 20. It allows no flying insects (v. 19) and drops the rules on touching carcasses.

Chapter 14 opens the subsection on a holy people (14:1–16:17): food, tithes, the year of release, firstlings, and the three pilgrim feasts. The tithe law reuses ch. 12's “place which he shall choose,” and its reckoning by years (“at the end of three years,” v. 28) leads straight into 15:1, “At the end of every seven years.”

**Later echoes:** Deuteronomy 26:12–15 gives the words a farmer says when the third-year tithe is done. Malachi 3:10, quoted by the risen Lord in 3 Nephi 24:10, calls for all the tithes to be brought “into the storehouse.”

traditions.text: The King James text lets an Israelite give meat from an animal that died of itself to the stranger, or sell it to a foreigner. The Church's footnotes show that the Joseph Smith Translation reverses both permissions in v. 21: thou shalt not give it, and thou shalt not sell it. The change brings the verse closer to Leviticus 17:15, which counts such meat as defiling for native and stranger alike.

A thematic link. In 1838 the Lord set the law of tithing for the Church as one-tenth of all members' interest annually, “a standing law unto them forever.” An earlier revelation provides that the storehouse, kept by the Church's consecrations, will care for widows, orphans, and the poor, the same people the third-year tithe feeds in vv. 28–29.

Resh Lakish reads the unusual verb of v. 1, *titgodedu*, two ways at once. It forbids cutting the body for the dead, and, heard as “do not form separate bands,” it forbids splitting the community into factions with rival practices. The debate that follows weighs when differing local customs divide Israel and when they do not.

The words “Ye are the children of the LORD” (v. 1) prompt a dispute. Rabbi Judah says Israel are called children only when they act as children should. Rabbi Meir answers that they are children either way, and lists verses that call Israel foolish, faithless, or corrupt sons, ending with Hosea's promise that they will be called sons of the living God. Sifre Deuteronomy records Judah's side of the same debate on this verse.

Philo reads the kid in its mother's milk as a law of compassion. It is monstrous, he says, for the milk that nourished the living animal to become the sauce for its dead body. Anyone who wants meat with milk can use the milk of another animal, since herds give plenty, so his reading allows what later rabbinic law forbids.

The school of Rabbi Ishmael notes that the Torah says “Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk” three times (Exodus 23:19; 34:26; and here). One verse forbids eating meat with milk, one forbids any benefit from it, and one forbids cooking it. The school of Rabbi Eliezer adds that because the rule follows the carcass law in v. 21, a carcass sold to a Gentile may not be cooked in milk first.

Tobit, a pious exile in Assyria, recalls the tithes he paid as a young man: the first tenth to the Levites who served in Jerusalem, a second tenth sold and the money spent in Jerusalem each year, and a third given to those it was due, as his grandmother Deborah had taught him. The second tenth is the tithe of vv. 22–26, turned into money for the journey.

Josephus also counts three tithes. A tenth beyond the Levites' share may be sold in the country, but the money must be spent on feasts and sacrifices in the holy city, so that Israel enjoys the fruits of the land in honor of the giver. Every third year a third tithe goes to those in want, widows, and orphans. His count matches Tobit's, as the translator Whiston noted, though later rabbinic law treated the poor tithe as replacing the second tithe in the third year.

The doubled verb of v. 22, *aser te'aser*, “thou shalt truly tithe,” is read as a pun: tithe (*aser*) so that you become rich (*titasher*). When Rabbi Johanan tells the young son of Resh Lakish to go and test it, the boy objects that Israel may not tempt the LORD (6:16). Johanan answers with his teacher's ruling that tithes are the one case where testing God is allowed, since in Malachi 3:10 God himself invites Israel to prove him with the tithe.

Irenaeus contrasts the tithe with Christian giving. Where the law enjoined tithes, he says, the Lord told his followers to share all their possessions with the poor, just as he deepened “Thou shalt not kill” into a ban on anger. The Jews consecrated a tenth of their goods, but those who have received liberty set aside all they have for the Lord's purposes, like the poor widow who gave her whole living.

15.overview:
At the end of every seven years a creditor is to cancel what a fellow Israelite owes him, a release proclaimed in the LORD's name; a foreigner's debt may still be collected. No one may refuse a loan because that year is near; Israel is to open its hand wide to the poor brother and give without a grudging heart. A Hebrew man or woman sold into service goes free in the seventh year, and not empty-handed, but with gifts from flock, threshing floor, and winepress, because Israel was once a slave in Egypt. One who chooses to stay has his ear pierced at the door and serves for ever. Firstborn male animals belong to the LORD and are eaten at the chosen place, unless blemished.

Verse 4 promises a land with no poor if Israel hearkens; v. 11 says the poor shall never cease out of the land. The chapter keeps both, and between them commands an open hand.

15.hermeneutics:
Babylonian kings also cancelled debts, but on their own schedule. A new king would proclaim *misharum*, “justice,” and the best preserved decree, from Ammi-saduqa (17th century BC), wipes out arrears and consumer loans of barley and silver owed by Akkadians and Amorites, the king's own people, and frees family members held for such debts. Loans made for trade were exempt, and the decree came when the king chose, usually early in his reign. Deuteronomy keeps the idea and removes the king. The release falls every seventh year by the calendar and is called “the LORD's release” (v. 2), and, like the Babylonian edict, it protects members of the community but not the foreigner (v. 3), who was most often a trader.

Credit was expensive. The Laws of Eshnunna, from about the same era, set interest at a fifth on silver and a third on grain, and a family that could not pay might hand over a son or daughter to work off the debt. In that world a loan made in the sixth year, soon to be cancelled, was close to a gift, which is the calculation v. 9 forbids: “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand.” The law asks the lender to absorb the loss, forbids interest between brothers elsewhere (23:19–20), and promises that the LORD will bless the one who gives (v. 10).

notes: **Release:** The root *shamat*, “release,” comes 6 times, all in vv. 1–9 (the noun *shemittah* 4 times, the verb twice). The chapter gives the seventh year its later Hebrew name.

**Brother and poor:** “Brother” occurs 7 times (vv. 2, 3, 7 twice, 9, 11, 12), and *evyon*, “poor” or “needy,” 6 times (vv. 4, 7 twice, 9, 11 twice). The debtor and the servant are both “thy brother.”

**Open hand, blessing:** “Thou shalt open thine hand wide” comes twice (vv. 8, 11), each time with the Hebrew verb doubled for emphasis. “Bless” comes 6 times (vv. 4 twice, 6, 10, 14, 18), so that the giver is told repeatedly he will not end up poorer.

Chapter 15 sits inside the subsection on a holy people (14:1–16:17). The third-year tithe of 14:28–29 fed the poor in town; this chapter widens that care to a seven-year cycle of released debts and freed servants. The firstlings of vv. 19–23, eaten “in the place which the LORD shall choose,” lead into the pilgrim feasts of ch. 16, kept at the same place.

**Later echoes:** Moses sets the public reading of the law “in the solemnity of the year of release” (31:10–11). Jeremiah 34:8–17 condemns Jerusalem for freeing its Hebrew servants and then taking them back, and v. 14 there quotes this chapter's seventh-year rule.

traditions.text: Enoch's city is described in words that fulfill v. 4: the Lord called his people Zion because they were of one heart and one mind, dwelt in righteousness, and “there was no poor among them.” Where Deuteronomy offers a land without poor as a promise tied to obedience, Moses 7 presents a people who reached it. That city, the chapter goes on, was in time taken up into heaven.

A thematic link to vv. 7–11. King Benjamin tells his people not to let a beggar's petition go in vain, and rebukes the man who says the poor have brought their misery on themselves and so stays his hand. His reason is that all are beggars before God, who supplies everything they have, much as v. 15 grounds generosity in Israel's own rescue from slavery.

After Christ's visit, the Nephites and Lamanites had all things in common, so that there were not rich and poor, bond and free. The account matches both halves of this chapter: no poor (v. 4) and no one held in service (vv. 12–18). The same pattern appears in Acts 4 (below).

Hillel the Elder saw people refusing to lend as the seventh year approached, the very sin v. 9 warns against. He created the *prozbul*, a declaration handing a loan over to the court, so that the debt survived the release and lenders would lend again. Sifre Deuteronomy grounds it in v. 3: “thine hand shall release” binds the creditor's own hand, not debts deposited with the court. The Mishnah adds that the sages are pleased with a debtor who repays after the seventh year anyway.

The rabbis set v. 4 against v. 11 and resolve the tension by obedience. When Israel does the will of God, the poor are found among others, and when it does not, the poor are found among Israel. The promise of v. 4 is also tied to the land: the blessing depends on living in it.

Philo counts the release among the honors Moses gave the number seven. Every seventh year debts are remitted, helping the poor and inviting the rich to humanity, since anyone's fortunes can change like the wind. He explains v. 3 by the names: fellow citizens are called brothers, joint heirs by nature, while strangers have no claim on that bond. He goes on to condemn lending at interest to the poor, which can double a debt and leave the borrower a beggar.

Josephus' digest of the laws given in Moab says borrowers should repay gladly, as if drawing on their own storehouse, and regulates pledges with care for the poor, returning a poor man's garment by sunset. It says nothing of debts cancelled in the seventh year. His silence fits Hillel's problem: by the first century, lenders and borrowers were finding ways to keep debts alive.

traditions.source: Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and John
traditions.text: When a woman pours costly ointment on Jesus at Bethany and some object that it could have been sold for the poor, he answers that the poor are with them always, words drawn from v. 11. Mark's version keeps more of the verse's force: “whensoever ye will ye may do them good.” The saying assumes, as Deuteronomy does, that the duty to the poor goes on, and Jesus sets his own coming death beside it as the one thing that would not.

Luke describes the first Jerusalem believers in language close to v. 4 in its Greek form: “neither was there any among them that lacked.” They were of one heart and one soul, and owners of land and houses sold them and laid the price at the apostles' feet for distribution to each as he had need. Moses 7 and 4 Nephi describe communities reaching the same state, and Moses 7 also calls Enoch's people “of one heart.”

The church manual's moral teaching reads like a commentary on vv. 7–10. Do not stretch out your hands to receive and draw them back from giving; do not hesitate to give, nor murmur when you give, for you will know who is the good repayer. Do not turn away the needy, but share all things with your brother and call nothing your own, since those who share what is immortal should share what is mortal.

16.overview:
Moses sets out Israel's three pilgrim feasts. Passover and the seven days of unleavened bread recall the night Israel left Egypt in haste. The Feast of Weeks comes seven weeks after the sickle first goes into the grain, and the Feast of Tabernacles follows the gathering of grain and wine. All three are kept “in the place which the LORD shall choose,” and every man comes with a gift as he is able. At v. 18 the subject turns to government: judges and officers in every town, who must not wrest judgment or take a gift. Two short bans follow, on a sacred pole beside the altar and a standing pillar.

Passover has moved. In Exodus 12 each household killed its lamb at home and marked its own doorposts with the blood. Here it may not be sacrificed “within any of thy gates” (v. 5), only at the chosen place.

16.hermeneutics:
A small limestone tablet from Gezer, usually dated to the 10th century BC, lays out the farmer's year by its work: two months of ingathering, two of sowing, two of late sowing, a month of hoeing flax, a month of barley harvest, a month of harvest, two months of tending vines, and a month of summer fruit. Israel's year was a year of crops. Deuteronomy ties two of its feasts to that work rather than to dates: Weeks is counted from the first cut of the sickle (v. 9), and Tabernacles comes when threshing floor and winepress are finished (v. 13). The pilgrimages fall where the farmer's year already had its pauses and its full barns.

The “grove” of v. 21 is in Hebrew an *asherah*, a wooden pole or tree linked with the goddess Asherah, and the “image” of v. 22 is a *matstsevah*, a standing stone. Both were common at shrines in Canaan and in Israel; Jacob himself set up a pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28:18). Inscriptions on storage jars at Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai (about 800 BC) invoke “YHWH of Samaria and his asherah,” and a tomb text at Khirbet el-Qom pairs the same names. Some Israelites evidently thought a pole beside the LORD's altar belonged there. Verse 21 forbids it exactly there, next to the altar.

Hammurabi's laws (§5) punish a judge who alters a verdict he has already sealed: he pays twelve times the claim and is publicly removed from the bench. Babylon policed its judges through the king's court. Deuteronomy speaks to the judge himself and gives him a reason, that a gift blinds the eyes of the wise (v. 19).

rows.text: No pole or pillar at the altar

notes: **The chosen place:** the phrase “the place which the LORD shall choose” (once “hath chosen”) occurs 6 times in vv. 1–17, at least once for each feast (vv. 2, 6, 7, 11, 15, 16).
**Sevens:** in the Hebrew of vv. 1–17, “seven” occurs 6 times and “weeks” 4 times. Weeks is itself seven sevens.

**Memory and joy:** Passover mentions Egypt four times and never says “rejoice.” Weeks and Tabernacles command rejoicing (vv. 11, 14, 15), and v. 12 brings Egypt back as the reason to include servants, Levites, strangers, orphans and widows.

Verses 1–17 close the section on a holy people's food, tithes, release and feasts that began at 14:1; the seven-year calendar of chapter 15 leads into the yearly calendar here. At v. 18 a new section begins on Israel's offices (16:18–18:22). Stephen Kaufman has proposed that the law code follows the order of the Ten Commandments, which would make 14:22–16:17 an expansion of the Sabbath and 16:18–18:22 of honoring father and mother, widened to all authority.
**Forward:** every seventh year, at Tabernacles, the law is to be read to all Israel at the chosen place (31:10–11).

traditions.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says that, though he was about seventy, he could not prove that the Exodus must be mentioned at night until Ben Zoma read v. 3. “The days of thy life” would mean only the days, Ben Zoma argued, so the added word “all” brings in the nights. The other sages answer that “all” adds the days of the Messiah. The exchange was later taken into the Passover Haggadah, where it is still read at the seder.

The Mishnah asks who must “appear before the LORD” (v. 16). Everyone is obliged except the deaf-mute, the mentally incompetent and minors, women and slaves, the lame, blind, sick and old, and anyone who cannot walk up to Jerusalem; the House of Hillel defines a minor as a child too young to hold his father's hand and climb the Temple Mount. To come “not empty” meant bringing a burnt offering and a festival offering of at least a fixed value in silver, and the Houses of Shammai and Hillel differ only on which of the two must be worth more.

Retelling the law, Josephus gives the three pilgrimages a social purpose as well as a religious one. Israelites from the farthest borders were to come to the temple city to thank God and pray, and also to “maintain a friendly correspondence with one another,” since people of one stock and one law should not be strangers.

For the judges of v. 18 Josephus gives a number the verse lacks: seven men in every city, chosen for their virtue, each with two officers from the tribe of Levi. Their rulings stand unless someone can show they took bribes, because cases must not be decided out of regard to gain or to the rank of the parties.

The Hebrew of v. 20 says literally “justice, justice shalt thou pursue.” One baraita reads the doubled word as one justice for judgment and one for compromise. Another says it means seeking out the best court of the generation, and lists where to go: after Rabbi Eliezer to Lod, after Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai to Beror Hayil, after Rabbi Akiva to Bnei Brak, and in Temple times to the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

Rava explains why a gift blinds (v. 19): once a judge accepts something from one side, he grows close to that party as to himself, and no one sees his own faults. The sages took the rule beyond money. Shmuel refused to hear a case brought by a man who had just given him a hand out of a ferry boat, and Ameimar refused one after a litigant brushed a feather from his head.

Philo says no grove was planted in the temple precincts, in keeping with the law, and gives three reasons. A true temple aims at austere holiness, not pleasure; the dung that makes trees grow has no place there; and fruit trees would draw the attention of the fickle away from the worship. His reasons are practical and moral; Deuteronomy's own concern is the asherah pole.

Paul reads the feast of unleavened bread as a picture of the church: “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us,” so the old leaven of malice and wickedness must be purged out. Believers are to keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. The seven days without leaven (vv. 3–4) become a whole life without malice, and the Passover victim becomes Christ himself.

Two of the New Testament's turning points happen at the pilgrim feasts of this chapter. At Pentecost, the Greek name for Weeks, Jews from every nation under heaven are gathered in Jerusalem when the Spirit comes, much as v. 16 would lead one to expect. At Tabernacles, on the last great day of the feast, Jesus cries out, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me.” John sets several chapters of Jesus' teaching at the pilgrim feasts in Jerusalem.

Justin tells the Jew Trypho that the lamb was roasted “in the form of the cross,” and that God allowed the Passover to be sacrificed only where his name was named because he foresaw that Jerusalem would be given over to enemies and the offerings would cease. Trypho concedes the point: the Passover lamb can no longer be sacrificed anywhere. The single-place rule of vv. 5–6 becomes, in Justin's hands, an argument that the old rites have ended.

17.overview:
After a ban on blemished sacrifices, Moses turns to the courts. Anyone accused of serving other gods, including the sun, moon and stars, must be investigated with care, and may be put to death only on the word of two or three witnesses, whose hands are first in the stoning. Cases too hard for the local judges go up to the priests and the judge at the chosen place, and their ruling is final. Last comes the law of the king. If Israel asks for one, he must be the LORD's choice and an Israelite, and must not multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold. He must write out a copy of the law and read it all his life.

The only positive duty this king is given is to read. He leads no army and hears no case in these verses; the law's aim is that his heart not be “lifted up above his brethren” (v. 20).

17.hermeneutics:
Ancient Near Eastern law collections came from kings. Hammurabi's prologue and epilogue present his laws as the just decisions of the king, inscribed on a stele so that a wronged man could have them read to him, and the other known collections were likewise issued in a ruler's name. Deuteronomy's king makes no laws at all. He receives a copy from the Levitical priests (v. 18) and is bound by it like any of his “brethren.” The usual order is reversed: the law stands over the king.

Hittite treaties ordered copies of the treaty laid up before the gods of each party, and the treaty of Suppiluliuma with Shattiwaza required it to be read aloud repeatedly before the king of Mittani and his people. Esarhaddon's succession treaties (672 BC) bound vassals to guard the sealed tablet and never alter it. In that world a written copy of the covenant was the document a ruler answered to. Israel's king keeps a copy of “this law” at his side and reads it daily, in the position of the vassal, with the LORD as the great king.

Horses meant chariotry, the costliest arm of an Iron Age army, and Egypt was a supplier (1 Kings 10:28–29). Royal marriages sealed alliances: the Amarna letters (14th century BC) record Pharaoh Amenhotep III taking daughters of the kings of Mittani and Babylon. Many wives meant many treaties and foreign courts at home, which is how 1 Kings 11:1–4 accounts for the turning of Solomon's heart.

rows.text: The local court: a case of idolatry

notes: **Right hand or left:** the people may not turn from the court's ruling “to the right hand, nor to the left” (v. 11), and the king may not turn from the commandment “to the right hand, or to the left” (v. 20). One line binds both the subject and the king.
**Multiply:** the Hebrew verb *rabah* occurs 4 times in vv. 16–17: twice for horses, once for wives, once for silver and gold.
**Presumption:** the man who acts “presumptuously” against priest or judge dies (vv. 12–13). The same Hebrew root returns for the prophet who speaks presumptuously (18:20, 22).

The section on Israel's offices runs from 16:18 to 18:22: judges (16:18–20; 17:8–13), the king (17:14–20), the Levitical priests (18:1–8) and the prophet (18:9–22). Norbert Lohfink described it as a kind of constitution in which each office is limited by the others. The worship cases of 16:21–17:7 sit inside it and show a local court at work.
**Forward:** Israel asks for a king “like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5), as v. 14 anticipates, and Solomon gathers the horses, gold and wives the law forbids (1 Kings 10:26–11:4).

traditions.text: A thematic parallel rather than a quotation: King Mosiah's case against kingship weighs the same dangers as vv. 14–20. If just men could always be kings, kings would be best, but one wicked king like Noah perverts all righteousness, so the Nephites are to choose judges and be judged by laws given “by the hand of the Lord.” Alma had already refused a crown because no one should think himself above another, close to the king of v. 20 whose heart must not be lifted up above his brethren.

The law given to the Church in 1831 applies the witness rule of v. 6 to Church discipline. A member accused of adultery is tried before two elders or more, and every word must be established by two witnesses “of the church, and not of the enemy.” The New Testament had already carried the same rule into church practice (Matthew 18:16).

The Hebrew of v. 18 asks the king to write “a copy of this law” (*mishneh ha-torah*). The Greek translators rendered it “this second law,” *to deuteronomion touto*. That phrase gave the book its Greek and English name, Deuteronomy.

The Temple Scroll rewrites vv. 14–20 as a much longer law of the king. It sharpens “neither shall he multiply wives” into one wife, taken from his father's house, who alone is with him all the days of her life. It also gives the king a guard of twelve thousand and a council of twelve princes, twelve priests and twelve Levites to advise him.

Philo explains why a foreigner may not rule: a stranger might drain the people's silver and gold and drive them from their land, while a kinsman would bring the scattered home. The king must copy the law with his own hand, because writing stamps the laws on the heart where reading lets them slip away. Philo imagines the king saying, “my sceptre shall be the book of the copy of the law.”

In Josephus's retelling Moses says aristocracy is the best constitution and Israel needs no governor but God. If they want a king, he must be one of their own nation, submit to the laws, and do nothing without the high priest and the senate. He is not to have many wives, great riches or many horses, and if he grasps at them he must be restrained.

The Mishnah puts numbers on the limits of vv. 16–17: no more than eighteen wives, only as many horses as his chariot needs, and only enough silver and gold to pay his soldiers. Rabbi Shimon says that even one wife who turns his heart is forbidden. The king writes his own Torah scroll and keeps it with him at war, in court and at his table, because v. 19 says “it shall be with him.”

Rabbi Yitzhak asks why the Torah rarely gives reasons for its commands. His answer: in two places it did, and the wisest of kings failed in both. Solomon reasoned that he could multiply wives without turning aside and multiply horses without sending the people back to Egypt, yet his wives turned his heart (1 Kings 11:4) and his chariots came out of Egypt (1 Kings 10:29).

Every seventh year at Tabernacles the king read Deuteronomy aloud in the Temple court, and the reading included this law of the king. When King Agrippa, of Herod's Edomite line, reached “thou mayest not set a stranger over thee” (v. 15), his eyes filled with tears. The crowd called out to him not to fear, because he was their brother.

On v. 11, “to the right hand, nor to the left,” the Sifre says Israel must obey the high court even if it tells them that right is left and left is right. Rashi repeats the saying and adds that obedience is all the more required when the court calls right right. The verse became a foundation for the authority of rabbinic courts.

Hebrews cites v. 6 directly: whoever despised Moses' law “died without mercy under two or three witnesses.” The writer argues from the lesser to the greater, that rejecting the Son of God deserves sorer punishment. In John, Jesus appeals to the same rule for himself, with the Father as his second witness.

18.overview:
The priests and the whole tribe of Levi receive no tribal land; the LORD and his offerings are their inheritance. Worshippers give the priest set portions of each sacrifice and the first of their grain, wine, oil and fleece, and a Levite who comes to the chosen place serves and eats alongside the rest. Moses then forbids the practices of the land's nations: passing a child through fire and eight kinds of divination and dealing with spirits. In their place the LORD will raise up a prophet like Moses, as the people asked at Horeb when they could not bear God's voice. A prophet who speaks presumptuously must die, and a word that does not come to pass is not the LORD's.

The promised prophet is the answer to the diviners. Verses 9–14 shut every road by which the nations sought hidden knowledge; vv. 15–22 open the one road Israel is given, a human voice carrying God's words.

18.hermeneutics:
In Mesopotamia divination was a learned profession. The *bārû* priest read the will of the gods in the liver of a sacrificed sheep, and long omen collections catalogued signs in the stars, in unusual births, in oil poured on water and in the flight of birds. Kings undertook nothing important without a favorable reading, and necromancers called up ghosts of the dead for counsel. Verses 10–11 name eight such practitioners (in the KJV: divination, observer of times, enchanter, witch, charmer, consulter with familiar spirits, wizard, necromancer) and reject the whole system as what “these nations” do (v. 14). The chapter does not deny that people want to know what is coming. It gives them a person instead of a technique.

Prophets were known outside Israel too. Letters from Mari on the Euphrates (18th century BC) report men and women, called *āpilum* (“answerer”) and *muḫḫûm* (“ecstatic”), who brought messages from gods to King Zimri-Lim. Officials often sent a lock of the prophet's hair and the fringe of his garment along with the report, and the king had the message checked by extispicy before acting on it. At Mari a liver was the test of a prophet. Deuteronomy has just forbidden that check, and it gives two others: a prophet who speaks in the name of other gods is condemned whatever happens (v. 20; 13:1–5), and one whose word does not come to pass has spoken presumptuously (v. 22).

notes: **Speaking:** in the Hebrew of vv. 17–22 the verb “speak” occurs 10 times and the noun “word” 6 times (vv. 18–22). The closing section is about whose words a prophet carries.

**Raise up:** “will raise up” comes twice, once in Moses' voice (v. 15, “like unto me”) and once in God's (v. 18, “like unto thee”). Both say the prophet will come from among Israel's “brethren,” the same term used for the king (17:15).

**Hearken:** “hearken” (Hebrew *shama*) links the units: the nations hearkened to diviners (v. 14), Israel shall hearken to the prophet (v. 15), and the one who will not hearken is answerable to God (v. 19).

Chapter 18 closes the section on Israel's offices (16:18–18:22) with the two that serve God most directly. Israel appoints judges and sets up a king, but the LORD chooses the priest (v. 5) and raises up the prophet (vv. 15, 18). The prophet law also completes 13:1–5, which dealt with a prophet who preaches other gods. Chapter 19 turns to homicide and refuge.
**Forward:** the book ends by saying that no prophet had yet arisen in Israel “like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (34:10), leaving the promise open.

traditions.text: Nephi quotes vv. 15 and 19 in a form close to Peter's in Acts 3: the people are to hear the prophet in all things, and those who will not hear him “shall be cut off from among the people.” He then names the prophet outright as the Holy One of Israel, who will execute judgment in righteousness.

Teaching the Nephites at Bountiful, the risen Jesus applies the verses to himself: “Behold, I am he of whom Moses spake.” He quotes them in the same expanded wording found in Acts 3:22–23 and 1 Nephi 22, so Peter, Nephi and the risen Jesus all cite v. 15 in one shared form.

When Moroni visited Joseph Smith in 1823, he quoted Acts 3:22–23 “precisely as they stand in our New Testament.” He said that prophet was Christ, but that the day when those who would not hear his voice should be cut off had not yet come, though it soon would. A revelation of 1831 repeats the warning and credits it to the prophet Moses.

Restoration scripture applies vv. 15–19 to Christ, but it also uses Moses as a pattern for later prophets. Joseph of Egypt foresees a latter-day seer who will be “great like unto Moses,” Joseph Smith receives revelations for the Church “even as Moses,” and the President of the High Priesthood is to be “like unto Moses.” These passages do not quote this chapter; they echo its idea of a prophet modeled on Moses.

Philo says Moses banished augurs, soothsayers and enchanters because they guess from the flight of birds and the entrails of victims, and that the true citizen must be “perfect” (v. 13) in the worship of God rather than in such arts. Since people long to know the future, Moses promised that a prophet would appear suddenly, inspired, saying nothing of his own. The prophets, Philo says, are interpreters of God, who uses their voices.

A single sheet from Qumran Cave 4 strings proof texts together with no comment: Deuteronomy 5:28–29 joined to 18:18–19, then Balaam's star (Numbers 24:15–17), then Moses' blessing of Levi (Deuteronomy 33:8–11). Scholars read the three as a coming prophet, king and priest. The Community Rule likewise tells the community to keep its first rules until a prophet comes, together with the Messiahs of Aaron and Israel.

The Samaritan text of Exodus 20 includes, right after the people's plea at Sinai, material from Deuteronomy including vv. 18–22, so the promise of a prophet like Moses is given at the mountain itself. Samaritans awaited a coming figure, the Taheb (“one who returns”), whom they tied to this promise. The same pairing of Deuteronomy 5 and 18 appears in 4QTestimonia.

The Mishnah defines the false prophet of v. 20: one who prophesies what he did not hear, or what was told to a different prophet, is executed by the court. Three others are left to Heaven under v. 19, “I will require it of him”: a prophet who suppresses his prophecy, one who disregards a true prophet's words, and a prophet who disobeys his own message.

Rashi reads “like unto me” as a pattern for a line of prophets: one like Moses, from among the people, raised up in his place, and so on from prophet to prophet through the ages. On v. 13 he explains “perfect” as walking with God wholeheartedly, trusting him rather than trying to probe the future. Where Christian readers saw one figure, Rashi saw an office.

Peter, preaching at the temple after healing a lame man, applies vv. 15 and 19 to Jesus and sharpens the warning: every soul that will not hear that prophet “shall be destroyed from among the people.” Stephen, on trial, cites the same verse to show that Moses himself pointed beyond his own law.

John shows the expectation alive among the people. Priests from Jerusalem ask John the Baptist whether he is “that prophet,” and he says no. After Jesus feeds the five thousand in the wilderness, the crowd decides he is “that prophet that should come into the world.” Many readers also hear v. 15's call to hearken in the voice at the transfiguration, “hear ye him” (Matthew 17:5).

In his Proof of the Gospel, Eusebius argues that no prophet after Moses was “like” him, citing 34:10, and then lists likenesses between Moses and Jesus. Both delivered a people, fasted forty days, fed multitudes in the wilderness, passed through the sea, had shining faces on a mountain, chose seventy and sent out twelve. His list is an early Christian reading of v. 15 as fulfilled point by point.

19.overview:
Once Israel holds the land, it must set apart three cities, with roads prepared to them, where someone who has killed a neighbor by accident can flee from the avenger of blood. The example is a woodcutter whose axe head flies off the handle. If the land grows, three more cities are added. A deliberate murderer who runs to such a city is fetched by the elders of his own town and handed over. One verse forbids moving a neighbor's landmark. Then comes the rule for witnesses: one is never enough, and a witness proved false suffers what he meant to do to the accused.

The famous “eye for eye” of v. 21 is aimed here at a lying witness. In Exodus 21 and Leviticus 24 the formula governs bodily injury; in Deuteronomy it sets the penalty for perjury, the same harm the witness “had thought to have done unto his brother” (v. 19).

19.hermeneutics:
Ancient law already separated accident from intent. Hammurabi's laws (§206–207) let a man who struck another in a quarrel swear that he did not strike deliberately, then pay the physician, or a fine if the victim died. The Hittite Laws (§3–4) set a lighter penalty when only the killer's hand, not his will, had sinned. What Deuteronomy adds is a place. Asylum elsewhere meant clinging to an altar, as Adonijah and Joab do (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28), and Exodus 21:13–14 still has the altar in view. Having put its one altar at a single chosen place, Deuteronomy supplies towns instead, spaced so that no slayer is overtaken “because the way is long” (v. 6).

Babylonian *kudurru* stones (about 1400–1000 BC) recorded grants of land and called down long curses on anyone who moved, hid or defaced them. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope tells its reader not to move the markers on the borders of the fields, a saying echoed in Proverbs 22:28 and 23:10. A boundary stone was a legal record set in the soil, and v. 14 adds that it was set by “they of old time” in the inheritance the LORD gave.

Hammurabi's code opens in the courtroom. An accuser who cannot prove a charge of murder is put to death (§1), and so is a witness in a capital case who cannot prove his testimony (§3). Babylonian talion, though, depended on rank: an eye for the eye of a free man (§196), silver for the eye of a commoner (§198). Deuteronomy applies its formula to the false witness without regard to rank; the measure is whatever the witness planned for “his brother.”

notes: **Threes:** “three” occurs 5 times in the Hebrew (vv. 2, 7, 9 twice, 15): three cities, three more, and up to three witnesses.
**Blood:** “blood” occurs 5 times in the refuge law (vv. 6, 10 twice, 12, 13). “Innocent blood” in vv. 10 and 13 brackets the case of the murderer who tries to hide in a refuge city.
**No pity:** “thine eye shall not pity” closes both the murderer's case (v. 13) and the false witness's (v. 21), and “put away” the evil or guilt (vv. 13, 19) repeats the refrain of 17:7, 12.

Chapter 19 opens the section on refuge, witnesses and war (19:1–21:9), turning from Israel's offices to the protection of life. If Stephen Kaufman's proposal is right, this stretch of the law expands “Thou shalt not kill.” The section closes with another case of innocent blood, the unsolved murder of 21:1–9.

**Backward and forward:** Moses has already set apart Bezer, Ramoth and Golan east of the Jordan (4:41–43), and Joshua names the western three, Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron (Joshua 20:7–8). Scripture never records the three extra cities of v. 9.

traditions.date: c. 559–545 BC; c. AD 400 (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: Book of Mormon writers apply the witness law of v. 15 to their own record. Nephi sets his testimony of the Redeemer beside Isaiah's and his brother Jacob's, saying that God establishes his word by the words of three, though he sends more witnesses still. Moroni, writing to the future translator, promises that three will be shown the plates by the power of God, and that “in the mouth of three witnesses shall these things be established.”

In a revelation to Oliver Cowdery during the translation of the Book of Mormon in 1829, the Lord gives him and Joseph Smith the keys of a gift and then repeats the rule of v. 15: every word is to be established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. The wording follows the New Testament form of the verse (Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1).

At the temple in Bountiful the risen Jesus quotes “an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth” as what is written, then tells his hearers not to resist evil but to turn the other cheek. His words match Matthew 5:38–39, delivered this time to a people still living under the law of Moses.

The Mishnah argues over v. 5. If an axe head slips from its handle and kills someone, Rabbi Judah the Prince says the slayer is not exiled to a refuge city, while the sages say he is. If a chip flies off the wood being split, the positions reverse. It also says roads to the cities were kept straight and paved, and two scholars went with the slayer to talk the avenger out of killing him on the way.

Expanding v. 3's command to prepare the way, the Talmud says the word “Refuge” was written on signs at every crossroads. Rav Hama bar Hanina draws a lesson from Psalm 25:8: if God marks the road for sinners who have killed, how much more will he guide the righteous.

When are false witnesses executed under v. 19? The Sadducees said only after the accused had actually been put to death, reading “life for life” strictly. The sages answered that v. 19 assumes the brother is still alive: the witnesses die if exposed after the verdict but before the execution.

Rashi, drawing on the Talmud and Sifre, fills in the practical details. The land was to be divided so that the distance from the border to the first city equaled the distance between cities and from the last city to the far border. The three extra cities of v. 8 wait for the day God gives the lands of the Kenite, Kenizzite and Kadmonite promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:19). Moving a landmark inside the land breaks two commands at once, the ban on robbery and this one.

Josephus says a single witness must never be believed, only three or at least two, and only those whose lives confirm their testimony. He excludes women and slaves as witnesses, a rule Deuteronomy does not state. A convicted false witness suffers the very punishment he sought for the other man.

The rabbis read “eye for eye” as money. Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai asks how a blind man who blinds another could be punished in kind, when the law must be the same for all. Josephus already allowed the injured party to accept money in place of the maimer's limb.

Philo reads v. 14 as guarding more than fields: customs are unwritten laws set by the ancients, and moving them is also forbidden. Josephus calls landmarks “a divine and unshaken limitation of rights” and warns that moving them leads to wars and to overturning the laws themselves.

Jesus builds v. 15 into the steps for settling a dispute: if a brother will not listen, take one or two more, so that every word is established by two or three witnesses. Paul applies the same verse to his third visit to Corinth, and 1 Timothy to accusations against an elder.

Against the Manichaeans, who set Moses against Christ, Augustine argues that the law of retaliation and the command to turn the other cheek are not opposed. The old law was meant to check hatred by holding revenge to the size of the injury, since an angry man who has been slightly hurt rarely stops there. It was “a covering to prevent the fire already kindled from spreading.” The gospel goes further by giving up even the just claim, as one forgives a debt that could lawfully be collected.

20.overview:
Israel is not to fear a larger army with horses and chariots. Before battle a priest tells the troops that the LORD goes with them to fight for them, and the officers send home four kinds of men: one with a new house not yet dedicated, one with a vineyard not yet eaten from, one betrothed but not yet married, and one who is afraid. A distant city must first be offered peace; if it accepts, it becomes tributary, and if it resists, it is besieged, its men killed and the rest taken as spoil. The cities of the six nations in the land are to be utterly destroyed. In a long siege, fruit trees may not be cut down.

The chapter limits war as much as it commands it. Its first word to an enemy city is peace (v. 10), and its last protects trees that will feed whoever lives there when the fighting is over.

20.hermeneutics:
In the Ugaritic epic of Kirta (13th century BC or earlier) the king musters an army so complete that the sick man is carried along and the newly married groom must go, driving his wife to another. The poem uses the scene to show how total the levy is. Deuteronomy turns the same scene around: the man who has not yet enjoyed his house, his vineyard or his bride is sent home (vv. 5–7), so that “another man” does not take what he began.

Assyrian kings boasted of cutting down orchards. Shalmaneser III records that he cut down the orchards around Damascus in 841 BC, and Sargon II's report of his eighth campaign (714 BC) describes felling the orchards and vineyards of Urartu. Fruit trees took years to replace, so destroying them punished a land long after its army was beaten. Verse 19 refuses the tactic, and v. 20 lets only trees not grown for food be cut for siege works.

The Moabite king Mesha, about 840 BC, records on his stele that he took the Israelite town of Nebo and killed all seven thousand of its men, women and children, because he had devoted it to his god Ashtar-Chemosh. His verb is the same root as the “utterly destroy” of v. 17 (*ḥrm*). Total destruction dedicated to a god was a known practice in the region, and Israel's neighbors used it against Israel. Deuteronomy confines it to the six nations named in v. 17 and gives its reason in v. 18: their worship would be learned.

rows.text: Two kinds of city: far off and near

notes: **Go home:** “let him go and return unto his house” comes 4 times (vv. 5, 6, 7, 8). The first three add “lest he die in the battle, and another man” enjoy what he began.
**Battle:** the Hebrew word for battle or war (*milchamah*) occurs 8 times, from the first verse to the last.
**Two kinds of city:** vv. 10–15 (cities “very far off”) and vv. 16–18 (“the cities of these people”) are set side by side, and v. 15 marks the line between them.

Chapter 20 sits inside the section on refuge, witnesses and war (19:1–21:9), between the homicide laws of chapter 19 and the unsolved murder of 21:1–9. Killing in war is placed among other killing: who must be sent home, who may be spared, and what may not be destroyed. Further war laws come later in 21:10–14, 23:9–14 and 24:5.

**Forward:** Joshua carries out the ban at Jericho and Ai (Joshua 6:21; 8:26), and the Gibeonites win a treaty by claiming to come from “a very far country” (Joshua 9:6, 9), exploiting the line drawn in v. 15.

traditions.text: Written as Missouri mobs drove the Saints from Jackson County, this revelation restates the rule of v. 10 as “the law that I gave unto mine ancients.” Israel was not to go to battle unless the Lord commanded, and was first to lift a standard of peace. If the offer was refused three times, they were to bring their testimonies before the Lord, who would then justify them in going to battle. The repeated offer matches the rabbinic reading of the siege law (Rashi, below).

A thematic link: as Zion's Camp neared Missouri, the Saints were told to sue for peace not only with those who had smitten them but with all people, to lift up an ensign of peace, and to make proposals for peace to their enemies. The word to the would-be army is the same as the first word of v. 10.

A thematic parallel: the Nephite war rule, like D&C 98, limits fighting to defense. The Lord had told them that if they were not guilty of the first offense nor the second, they need not let themselves be slain, and they were taught never to raise the sword except to preserve their lives. Mormon presents their wars as fought for homes, families and worship, not for power.

The priest of v. 2 becomes the priest anointed for war, who speaks in Hebrew. The Mishnah glosses each phrase of v. 3: do not faint at the neighing of horses, do not fear the clash of shields, do not tremble at the trumpets or the shouting. Your enemies come trusting in flesh and blood, as the Philistines trusted Goliath, but you come with the ark of the LORD.

The exemptions are widened: a man who bought, inherited or was given a house goes home, and so does one who planted as few as five fruit trees. Rabbi Akiva takes “fearful” at face value, while Rabbi Yose the Galilean says it means a man afraid because of his sins, and that the other exemptions exist so that he can leave without exposing himself. All this applies only to optional wars; in a commanded war even the groom leaves his chamber and the bride her canopy.

Philo gives two reasons for the exemptions of vv. 5–7. It would be hard for one man to labor and another to enjoy the fruit. And a man whose heart is at home would fight with his body while his soul was far from the battle.

Philo says Moses goes beyond all other lawgivers in humanity by forbidding Israel to cut down an enemy's fruit trees. Anger roused against men, he argues, should not fall on things innocent of all evil, and today's enemies may tomorrow send heralds to make peace. He extends the rule to ravaging enemy grain.

Josephus has Moses tell Israel to send ambassadors and heralds before any war, since it is right to use words before weapons. He sends home the timid and the men with new houses, vineyards and wives. The fruit trees, he says, were made for men, and “if they could speak, they would have a just plea against you.”

Rashi, following the Sifre, says vv. 10–15 concern optional wars, not the war against the seven nations, and that the offer of peace was to be repeated over two or three days. He reads the end of v. 19 as a question: is the tree of the field a man, able to retreat into the city before you, that it should suffer the siege? The KJV's parenthesis, “for the tree of the field is man's life,” takes the same Hebrew words differently.

The sages made v. 19 into a general ban on wasteful destruction. Rav forbade cutting down a palm still yielding a measure of dates, and Rabbi Hanina said his son died for felling a fig tree before its time. Rabbi Elazar held that even tearing one's clothes too much in mourning transgresses “thou shalt not destroy.”

A thematic echo: in Jesus' parable of the great supper, the guests excuse themselves because one has bought land, one has bought oxen, and one has married a wife, the kinds of new beginnings vv. 5–7 allow as reasons to leave the army. A few verses later a king who cannot win sends an embassy while the enemy is far off and asks conditions of peace.

Answering the Manichaean charge that Moses was cruel in war, Augustine argues that in wars carried on by divine command Moses showed not ferocity but obedience. The real evils in war, he says, are love of violence, revengeful cruelty, fierce enmity and the lust of power, not death itself. His argument became a foundation of Christian just-war thought.

21.overview:
When a murdered man is found in the open and the killer is unknown, the elders of the nearest town break a heifer's neck, wash their hands, and ask the LORD not to charge the blood to Israel. A soldier must give a captive woman a month to mourn before marrying her, and may not sell her if he sends her away. A father may not give the firstborn's double share to a favored wife's son. A defiant, drunken son may be stoned. An executed man hung on a tree must be buried that day.

Three of the five laws concern a man's own household, and each sets a limit on him. He may not sell a captive wife he has tired of, may not move the birthright to a favorite's son, and may not punish a rebellious son on his own authority. Father and mother together must bring the son to the elders at the gate.

21.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian law already held a community answerable for crimes on its ground. In the Code of Hammurabi (§§23–24), when a robber is not caught, the city and governor in whose territory it happened must repay the victim, and if a life is lost they pay one mina of silver to his kin. Measuring to the nearest town (v. 2) works on the same principle of liability by distance. Deuteronomy changes what is owed. No silver settles the matter; the town's elders swear their hands are clean, a heifer dies in a valley never plowed, and the priests ask the LORD to forgive, because the guilt rests on the land and the whole people.

The Middle Assyrian Laws (Tablet B §1) give the eldest brother two shares when brothers divide their father's estate. Deuteronomy assumes the same double portion (v. 17) and adds what the Assyrian rule does not address: a father's love for one wife cannot move it to her son. The case it describes is Jacob's household. Leah “was hated” (Genesis 29:31) and bore Reuben, and Rachel was loved and bore Joseph, who in the end received the birthright (1 Chronicles 5:1).

Assyrian kings displayed the bodies of rebels impaled on stakes outside captured cities, and Sennacherib's reliefs of the siege of Lachish show such stakes. The display was meant to last as a warning. Deuteronomy allows an executed man to be hung up but limits the display to a single day. The body must be buried before night, because a hanged man is “accursed of God” and would defile the land.

notes: **The middle three follow a household:** a man takes a wife (vv. 10–14), has two wives and their sons (vv. 15–17), then faces a grown son who will not obey (vv. 18–21).

**Repetition to watch:** The elders appear 6 times (vv. 2, 3, 4, 6, 19, 20). “Hated” (*senu'ah*) comes 4 times in vv. 15–17. The formula “so shalt thou put away” (*bi'arta*) closes the first case and the fourth (vv. 9, 21).
**Blood:** The word for blood comes 4 times in vv. 7–9, all in the oath and prayer over the heifer.

Verses 1–9 finish the laws about blood and war that began at 19:1. Like the refuge cities, the heifer rite keeps innocent blood from staining the land (19:10, 13; 21:9). Verse 10 repeats the opening of 20:1, “when thou goest forth to war,” but turns from the battlefield to the household and starts the family and neighbor laws that run to 25:19. Jewish reading names that whole portion *Ki Tetze* from this verse.
**Links:** Joshua follows v. 23 at Ai and Makkedah, taking the bodies down at sunset (Joshua 8:29; 10:26–27). Verse 17's “beginning of his strength” is Jacob's phrase for Reuben (Genesis 49:3).

traditions.text: Reads the elders' oath in v. 7 as a statement about hospitality. No one suspected the elders of murder; they mean the stranger did not leave their town without food or an escort. The Mishnah also records that the rite stopped once murderers became many and known, and names one Eliezer ben Dinai as an example.

His summary of the heifer law adds a step the text does not have: a diligent search for the killer, with rewards offered to anyone who will inform. Only when that fails do the leaders of the nearest city measure the distance and perform the rite. Their prayer asks that no such crime happen in the land again.

Treats the captive-woman law as a lesson in restraint and pity. The thirty days check the soldier's appetite and test whether his desire has any share in reason, and they give the woman time to grieve for her family. If he tires of her, the law forbids him to sell her or keep her as a slave and sends her away free.

The Talmud says the Torah permitted the captive marriage only as a concession to the evil inclination. Rashi builds on the order of the laws: the man who marries a captive out of desire will come to hate her (v. 15) and father a rebellious son by her (v. 18). The three laws become one warning story.

The Mishnah narrows the rebellious son to a boy just past puberty who has stolen from his parents to gorge on meat and wine. A teaching in the Talmud concludes that there never was such a son and never will be, and that the law was written to be studied for its reward. Rabbi Jonathan objects that he once saw one condemned and sat on his grave.

Gives the parents a speech of warning before any trial: they married in order to raise children who would care for them, and God, the father of all, shares in a parent's dishonor. Only if that fails is the son stoned and left in view for a day. He is buried at night, which Josephus says is how all the condemned are buried.

In the rabbis' reading the hanging comes after death: the body of a stoned blasphemer or idolater is hung briefly on a post and then untied at once. Rabbi Meir takes “curse of God” as God's own grief, as though the Divine Presence said “I am distressed” over the sinner's punishment. A Talmudic parable, repeated by Rashi, compares the hanged man to a king's twin brother whom onlookers mistake for the king.

Applies v. 22 to traitors: a man who informs against his people or hands them over to a foreign nation, or who flees to the nations and curses Israel, is hanged on the tree so that he dies. Many scholars read this as execution by hanging or crucifixion, the reverse of the Mishnah's order. The scroll keeps the same-day burial and calls the hanged accursed of God and men.

Describing how the Zealots left the high priest Ananus unburied, Josephus sets their act against Jewish custom. The Jews, he says, took such care over burial that they took down even the crucified and buried them before sunset.

Paul quotes v. 23 in a shortened form, “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree,” and argues that Christ became a curse for us to redeem us from the curse of the law. In Acts, Peter twice says Jesus was hanged on a tree, wording drawn from the same verse.

John reports that the Jewish leaders asked Pilate to break the legs of the crucified so the bodies would not remain on the cross over the Sabbath. The request applies v. 23, made more urgent by the feast, and matches the custom Josephus describes.

His Jewish partner in debate, Trypho, says the cross is his chief difficulty, since the law calls the crucified accursed. Justin answers that v. 23 does not mean God cursed Christ. It foretold the curses that Christ's opponents would speak against him and his followers.

Cites the captive-woman law to show that Moses' law joins humanity with self-control. The waiting period curbs lust, and cutting her hair tests whether reason or mere desire drives the marriage. His reading follows Philo's closely.

22.overview:
Short commands come first. An Israelite must return a brother's stray animal or lost property and help lift his fallen ox or ass. Men and women are not to wear each other's clothing. Whoever takes eggs or young from a nest must let the mother bird go. A new house needs a parapet on its roof, and seed, plow animals, and cloth are not to be mixed. Then come laws on marriage and sexual offenses: a bride falsely accused, adultery, a betrothed or unbetrothed young woman, and a father's wife.

The town and field cases (vv. 23–27) turn on whether the woman could be heard. In the town she is presumed to have consented because she did not cry out. In the field she is presumed to have cried with no one to save her, so only the man dies, and the law likens her to a murder victim (v. 26).

22.hermeneutics:
The Hittite Laws (§197) also let the place decide the case: if a man seizes a woman in the mountains, the offense is his and he dies; if in her house, the offense is hers and she dies. The Code of Hammurabi (§130) puts to death a man who lies with another man's betrothed virgin still living in her father's house, and lets her go free. Deuteronomy shares the old distinction between open country and settled space, and it states the reason. In the field no one could hear her cry (v. 27), so the doubt is resolved in her favor.

The Middle Assyrian Laws (A §55) require a man who seizes an unbetrothed virgin to pay her father three times a virgin's value in silver and to marry her, though the father may give her to someone else. Exodus 22:16–17 also leaves the father a choice. Deuteronomy sets the payment at fifty shekels and adds a rule found in neither code: the man “may not put her away all his days” (v. 29). It is the same loss of the right to divorce imposed on the husband who slanders his bride (v. 19).

Houses in Israel had flat roofs that served as living space. Rahab dries flax on hers, Samuel talks with Saul on a housetop, and David walks on his palace roof (Joshua 2:6; 1 Samuel 9:25; 2 Samuel 11:2). Hammurabi (§229) holds a builder liable with his life if a house he built collapses and kills the owner. Deuteronomy puts the duty on the owner instead. A fall from an unwalled roof brings blood guilt on his house (v. 8), as though he had shed it.

The word for the young woman (*na'arah*, KJV “damsel”) comes 14 times in vv. 15–29, and in all but v. 19 it is written without its final letter, the old spelling of the Torah, and read as *na'arah*.
