Part of the family and neighbor laws (21:10–25:19). The chapter has no heading of its own; it continues the run of household cases begun in 21:10. In Hebrew Bibles v. 30 is numbered 23:1, so there the sexual laws close the old chapter's last verse and open the next.

**Links:** Exodus 23:4–5 gives the same duty toward an enemy's straying ox or ass; Deuteronomy speaks of a brother. The tassels of v. 12 are explained in Numbers 15:39: Israel is to look on them and remember the commandments.

traditions.text: Calls sending away the mother bird the lightest of commands, costing no more than a small coin, yet the Torah promises long life for it; how much more, the rabbis reason, for the harder ones. Another passage silences a prayer leader who asks God to show the mercy he showed the bird's nest. The Talmud gives two reasons: such a prayer stirs jealousy among God's creatures, or it turns the King's decrees into mere expressions of mercy.
traditions.cite: m. Hullin 12:5; m. Berakhot 5:3; b. Berakhot 33b

traditions.text: Tells of a son whose father sent him up a building for chicks. He let the mother go and took the young, keeping both commands that promise long life, and fell to his death on the way down. Rabbi Jacob concluded that the promised reward belongs to the world to come, and one view says the sight of such a case led the sage Elisha ben Abuya to abandon his faith.

Explains the order of vv. 6–12 from an earlier midrash. Whoever keeps the small command about the nest will be rewarded with a new house that needs a parapet, then a vineyard, a field, and fine garments, because one good deed brings another.

Drawing on the earlier Sifre, reads v. 5 for its purpose. A woman dressing as a man or a man as a woman is forbidden as a way of passing unnoticed among the other sex for adultery. Rashi concludes that the Torah forbids only clothing that leads to such abomination.

Gives a reason for v. 11 that the text does not: wool woven with linen is reserved for the priests alone. The Mishnah points the same way, noting that wool and linen together are the only forbidden mixture in cloth and also the only materials priests wore in Temple service.

In his version of vv. 13–21, the bride's father, brother, or nearest kinsman defends her. A husband who accused her rashly is flogged and pays her father fifty shekels, where the text says a hundred. Josephus adds that a convicted priest's daughter is burned (compare Leviticus 21:9), and he separates consent from force in the later cases.

Explains why place matters in vv. 23–27: a city has courts, magistrates, and neighbors who would answer a cry, while the open country has none. He then warns judges not to make everything depend on the place, since a woman can be forced in the middle of a city and can consent far outside it. The deciding question is whether she cried out and resisted.

On the slandered bride, Philo pictures a husband who wants a divorce and invents a charge that cannot easily be disproved. If the accusation fails, he is fined and beaten, and the marriage is confirmed against his will. Philo adds a detail the text does not state: the wife may choose to stay with him or leave.

Works out the payments of vv. 28–29. A man who forces an unbetrothed girl owes her father compensation for pain, shame, and degradation besides the fixed fine, and he must marry her and may never divorce her, even if she is lame, blind, or afflicted with boils. The seducer, by contrast, pays less and need not marry her (compare Exodus 22:16–17).

Reads the ban on plowing with an ox and an ass together as care for the weaker animal, since the two are unequal in strength. He adds that one is clean and the other unclean, so the law keeps apart creatures that do not belong together, while still protecting the unclean one from harm.

Mary is found with child while betrothed to Joseph, the situation the laws of vv. 23–24 address. Matthew calls Joseph a just man who would not make her a public example and planned to divorce her quietly, before an angel tells him the child is of the Holy Ghost.

Uses vv. 1–4 to show the law's humanity: a found animal is a deposit to be kept and returned, even an enemy's. He reads the ox and ass of v. 10 two ways: as a ban on yoking anyone under another merely for his race, and as a figure for not assigning the Word's work equally to believer and unbeliever. Both readings build on Philo.

Arguing that Christians should stay away from the theater, he cites v. 5: God's law declares cursed the man who dresses in women's clothing. What then, he asks, must God think of the pantomime actor trained from youth to play women's parts?

23.overview:
The chapter opens with who may enter “the congregation of the LORD.” A man whose genitals are crushed or cut off may not, nor a *mamzer* (KJV “bastard”), nor any Ammonite or Moabite, because they withheld bread and water from Israel and hired Balaam to curse it. Edomites and Egyptians may enter in the third generation. The war camp is to be kept clean, since the LORD walks in it. Then come shorter laws: a runaway slave is given refuge, no Israelite may serve as a cult prostitute, interest is forbidden between Israelites, vows must be paid, and a passerby may eat from a neighbor's vineyard or grainfield but carry nothing away.

The reasons given for admission run against expectation. Egypt enslaved Israel, yet its people may enter, “because thou wast a stranger in his land” (v. 7). Moab and Ammon are barred for refusing food and water on the road.

23.hermeneutics:
Babylonian law protected the slave owner. The Code of Hammurabi (§§15–16) puts to death anyone who helps a palace slave out through the city gate or who hides a runaway slave and does not bring him out when the herald calls. Treaties between kings of the period often included clauses for returning each other's fugitives. Verses 15–16 reverse this. The escaped slave who reaches Israel is not handed back; he lives in whatever town he chooses, and no one may oppress him.

Lending at interest was normal and regulated. The Laws of Eshnunna (§18A) set the rate at one-fifth on silver and one-third on barley, and Hammurabi's code also fixed rates. Deuteronomy forbids interest of any kind between Israelites, on money, on food, or “any thing” (v. 19), and allows it only from the *nokhri*, the foreigner who comes for trade. The resident stranger (*ger*) is a different figure, protected elsewhere in these laws (24:14, 17).

KJV's “whore” and “sodomite” in v. 17 translate *qedeshah* and *qadesh*, literally “consecrated” woman and man. Texts from Ugarit list *qdšm* among temple personnel, and the Phoenician temple accounts from Kition on Cyprus list *klbm*, “dogs,” among those the temple paid; some read these as male cult servants, others as real dogs in a healing cult. Whether temples kept sacred prostitutes at all is now debated. Verse 18 sets “whore” beside *qedeshah* and “dog” beside *qadesh*. However the terms are taken, Israelites may not fill such roles, and their wages may not pay a vow in the LORD's house.

**Links:** Nehemiah 13:1–3 has vv. 3–5 read aloud and the mixed multitude separated from Israel. Yet Ruth the Moabitess marries into Judah and becomes David's great-grandmother (Ruth 4:13–17), and Isaiah 56:3–5 promises eunuchs a name in the LORD's house.

traditions.text: Reads v. 3 as barring Ammonite and Moabite men only, so their women may marry into Israel at once, while Egyptians and Edomites of both sexes wait three generations. Rabbi Shimon argues that Egyptian and Edomite women should also be admitted at once. The Talmud uses the same rule to defend David's descent from Ruth the Moabitess when it was challenged.

A convert named Judah the Ammonite asks the sages whether he may enter the assembly. Rabban Gamaliel cites v. 3 against him. Rabbi Joshua answers that Sennacherib of Assyria long ago mixed up the nations, so no one living is an Ammonite in the law's sense, and the sages admit him.

Asks why Egypt, which threw Israel's sons into the river, may not be abhorred (v. 7). His answer: the Egyptians were Israel's hosts in a time of need, when famine drove Jacob's family to them under Joseph. Edom, which met Israel with the sword (Numbers 20:18–20), is likewise not to be utterly rejected, because he is a brother.

Takes vv. 1–2 as a guard on the sacred assembly, barring the mutilated, effeminate men, and the children of harlots. He then says this passage, if any in scripture, invites an allegorical reading. The excluded become types of false thinkers: those who deny the ideas, the atheists, and those who worship many gods.

In his digest of the law, eunuchs are to be shunned as men who destroyed their power to have children, and no one may castrate men or animals. He reads the “price of a dog” in v. 18 literally, as the fee for mating a hunting or sheep dog, which may not be offered to God any more than a harlot's hire.

Describes the Essenes keeping the latrine rule of vv. 12–13 with care. Each new member receives a small paddle-like hatchet; they dig a pit a foot deep in a remote spot, cover themselves with a cloak, and fill the pit afterward. On the Sabbath they do not relieve themselves at all.

Retells vv. 15–16 as a law about suppliants. A slave who flees a savage master, or one he fears, has taken refuge at your hearth, and it is not holy to give up a suppliant. Philo adds a fallback the text lacks: if he cannot be kept, he should be sold to another master rather than sent back.

Widens the “brother” in v. 19 to every fellow citizen and countryman, since it is not just to breed offspring from money as a farmer does from cattle. The lender who takes back only the principal gains something better than interest: the borrower's gratitude and a good name.

Forbids lending to a fellow Hebrew at interest on food or drink, since it is unjust to profit from a countryman's misfortune. The lender should count the borrower's gratitude, and the reward God gives for kindness, as his gain, the same reasoning Philo gives.

Extends vv. 24–25 to everyone who passes ripe fruit: the owner should let them eat their fill, whether they are countrymen or strangers, and be glad of the chance to share. Where the rabbis narrow the verses to hired laborers, Josephus widens them to any traveler.

The rabbis read vv. 24–25 as a hired laborer's right. The Talmud derives from these verses that a worker harvesting a vineyard or a field may eat from the crop while he works, and the Mishnah sets the limits of when and what he may eat.

traditions.text: Jesus' hungry disciples pluck ears of grain as they walk through a field, which v. 25 allows. The Pharisees object only because it is the Sabbath, and Luke adds that they rubbed the grain in their hands.

An Ethiopian eunuch, returning from worship in Jerusalem, reads Isaiah in his chariot. Philip teaches him, and the eunuch asks what hinders his baptism and is baptized. Readers have long set the scene beside v. 1 and Isaiah 56:3–5.
Like Philo, he takes the brother of v. 19 to include anyone of the same race, mind, and faith. God's own interest on such loans, he says, is paid in mildness, gentleness, and generosity.

In a treatise against usury he asks who the foreigner of v. 20 is and answers that it is the enemy whom one may lawfully fight. Where there is a right of war, he concludes, there is a right of interest, so the verse gives no license to charge interest to neighbors.

24.overview:
A man who divorces his wife gives her a written bill and sends her away, and if her second marriage ends, he may not take her back. A new husband is spared war and other duty for a year. Short laws follow on debt, labor, and justice: no millstone taken as a pledge, death for kidnapping a fellow Israelite, care with skin disease as the priests teach, a lender who waits outside for his pledge and returns a poor man's cloak by nightfall, wages paid the same day, each person put to death only for his own sin, and harvest left in the field for the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.

In Hebrew, vv. 1–4 are one long case. The divorce, the remarriage, and the second divorce or death are all conditions; the only command comes at the end, that the first husband may not remarry her. The law takes divorce as a given and regulates its aftermath.

24.hermeneutics:
Divorce was ordinary in Israel's world and the codes regulated it. The Code of Hammurabi (§§137–141) sets what a divorced wife takes with her, and the Middle Assyrian Laws (A §37) let a husband send his wife away with a gift or with nothing, as he wishes. Fifth-century BC Jewish marriage contracts from Elephantine in Egypt use “hate” as the legal word for ending a marriage, the same verb used of the second husband in v. 3. Deuteronomy adds a written bill handed to the woman. It gave her proof of her release, so she could “go and be another man's wife” (v. 2).

An ostracon from Mesad Hashavyahu, a fort near Yavneh-Yam on the coast, preserves a 7th-century BC appeal from a harvest worker to a local official. He says that Hoshavyahu son of Shobai took his garment after he finished his reaping, and he asks for it back. Whatever law he had in mind, the letter shows that a poor laborer's cloak could be seized and that he could petition for its return, the situation of vv. 12–15 and 17.

Mesopotamian law sometimes punished one family member for another's crime. In Hammurabi's code, if a man strikes a pregnant woman and she dies, his own daughter is put to death (§§209–210); if a builder's house collapses and kills the owner's son, the builder's son is killed (§§229–230). Verse 16 rules out that kind of substitute justice in Israel's courts: fathers do not die for sons or sons for fathers.

notes: **The vulnerable three:** The stranger, the fatherless, and the widow appear together 4 times (vv. 17, 19, 20, 21), and the stranger once more in v. 14.

**Remember:** *Zakhar* (“remember”) comes 3 times (vv. 9, 18, 22). Both justice laws close the same way: remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt, therefore I command thee to do this thing (vv. 18, 22).
**Pledges:** The verb for taking a pledge (*chaval*) brackets the debt laws at v. 6 and v. 17, and the noun for the pledge comes 4 times in vv. 10–13.

Part of the family and neighbor laws (21:10–25:19). Verses 1–5 finish the marriage laws of ch. 22; from v. 6 the chapter turns to debt, labor, and the poor, and the closing harvest law leads into the firstfruits of ch. 26.

**Links:** King Amaziah spares the children of his father's murderers, citing v. 16 (2 Kings 14:6). Jeremiah 3:1 uses vv. 1–4 to ask whether unfaithful Israel can return to the LORD. Ruth the Moabitess gleans in Boaz's field (Ruth 2:2–3).

traditions.text: At the temple in Bountiful the risen Jesus quotes the rule of v. 1, that a man who puts away his wife must give her a writing of divorcement. He answers that whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, causes her to commit adultery, and that whoever marries the divorced woman commits adultery. The words match the Sermon on the Mount (below).

A thematic link, not a quotation. The second article states that “men will be punished for their own sins,” and not for Adam's transgression. It applies to humanity as a whole the principle v. 16 sets for Israel's courts.

Records the classic dispute over the “uncleanness” (*ervat davar*) of v. 1. The house of Shammai allows divorce only for sexual misconduct. The house of Hillel allows it even for a spoiled dish, and Rabbi Akiva even if he finds a woman more beautiful, since the verse also says “she find no favour in his eyes.”

States the law in the broadest terms: a man who wants to divorce his wife “for any cause whatsoever” must give her a written assurance that he will not take her back, so that she is free to remarry. The Pharisees' question to Jesus, whether divorce is lawful “for every cause,” uses the same phrase (Matthew 19:3).

Reads vv. 1–4 as a law against a woman's return to her first husband whether her second husband divorces her or dies. She broke her first bond and chose new attachments, he says, so she may marry any man rather than him, and the man who takes her back shows a want of manly resolve.

Turns vv. 10–13 into procedure. A creditor may take a pledge only through an agent of the court, never by entering the debtor's house. If the debtor has two of a utensil, the creditor takes one, and he must return a pillow at night and a plow by day.

His version of the pledge laws separates rich debtors from poor ones. A creditor may keep a rich man's pledge until the loan is repaid, but a poor man's must come back before sunset, especially a garment he sleeps in. He extends v. 6 to every tool of the mill, so that no debtor loses the means of getting his food.

Reads the millstones of v. 6 as teeth, since the Greek word for the millstone also means a molar. Taking them in pledge, like knocking out a slave's teeth, robs a man of the means to eat, so the law calls it taking his life in pledge.

Admires the lender who waits outside for his pledge and the harvest laws of vv. 19–21. Leaving sheaves, olives, and grapes teaches the rich to be generous and lets the poor glean their neighbors' fields as if they owned them, like a father who shares the goods of the prosperous children with the poor ones.

Adds a moral to v. 16. Children are not to be punished for their parents' faults but pitied for being born to wicked parents, and fathers should not bear the blame for sons who reject the teaching they were given.

Asked why Moses commanded a writing of divorcement, Jesus answers that Moses allowed it because of the hardness of their hearts, but from the beginning it was not so. He points back to Genesis, where God made them male and female to be one flesh, and treats remarriage after divorce, except for fornication in Matthew, as adultery.

Answering the Manichean Faustus, who set Jesus against Moses, Augustine argues that the bill of divorce was meant to slow divorce down. A man had to go to the scribes to have it written, and they could advise him and try to reconcile the couple, so the law and Jesus' teaching point the same way.
Cites the rule of v. 15, to pay the poor man's wages daily, as part of the law's humanity. A poor worker kept waiting for his pay, Clement reasons, loses heart for the work ahead.

Warns the rich that the withheld wages of the reapers who harvested their fields cry out, and the cries have reached the ears of the Lord. The image echoes v. 15, where the unpaid worker may cry to the LORD against his employer.

25.overview:
A guilty man may be beaten, but with no more than forty strokes, so that a brother is not degraded. The ox treading out grain is not to be muzzled. If a man dies childless, his brother is to marry the widow and give the dead man an heir; if he refuses, she pulls off his sandal and spits before him at the gate. A woman who seizes the genitals of a man fighting her husband loses her hand. Weights must be honest. Last comes Amalek, who struck Israel's weary stragglers on the way out of Egypt; once Israel has rest, it must blot out Amalek's memory.

The chapter is about names that last or vanish. The levirate marriage exists so that the dead man's name is “not put out of Israel” (v. 6). Amalek's remembrance is to be blotted out, yet Israel is told both to remember and not to forget what Amalek did (vv. 17, 19).

25.hermeneutics:
Marrying a dead man's widow within his family was known beyond Israel. The Hittite Laws (§193) pass a widow to her husband's brother, then to his father, then to the father's brother, and the Middle Assyrian Laws also provide for such marriages. Deuteronomy limits the duty to brothers living together and gives it one purpose: a son who will carry the dead man's name and keep his inheritance. It also gives the brother a way out, at the cost of public shame. The sandal was a sign of claim to property, as Ruth 4:7 explains and as Psalm 60:8 pictures in “over Edom will I cast out my shoe.” The widow pulls it off at the gate, and his house is known as the one whose shoe was loosed.

The Middle Assyrian Laws (A §8) treat the same case as vv. 11–12: a woman who injures a man's testicle in a quarrel loses a finger, and a further clause, damaged on the tablet, sets a harsher penalty if both are harmed. Deuteronomy takes the hand. Outside the talion rule of 19:21 it is the only cutting of the body its laws prescribe, and the same formula, “thine eye shall not pity,” goes with both.

Egyptian wisdom shared the concern with honest scales. The Instruction of Amenemope (chapter 16) warns against tampering with the balance and falsifying the weights, and Proverbs 11:1 calls a false balance an abomination. Merchants could carry a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling, the “great and small” of vv. 13–14. Amos 8:5 accuses traders of making the ephah small and the shekel great.

**Strokes:** The verb for striking (*nakah*) comes 4 times in vv. 2–3, and forty is the limit.
**Forgetting:** “Thou shalt not forget” (v. 19) uses the verb of 24:19, the forgotten sheaf. That verb occurs only in these two verses in chs. 24–25.

The last chapter of the family and neighbor laws (21:10–25:19) and of the long run of statutes that began in ch. 12. Chapter 26 turns to the firstfruits ceremony and the covenant's sealing. The closing command to remember Amalek once Israel has rest looks ahead to life in the land.

**Links:** Exodus 17:14 first orders Amalek's remembrance put out; Saul's failure to carry it out costs him the kingdom (1 Samuel 15:2–3). The levirate duty drives the stories of Tamar (Genesis 38) and Ruth, and the Sadducees' question to Jesus (Matthew 22:24).

traditions.text: Joins the end of v. 2 to the start of v. 3 to read “by number, forty,” meaning a number near forty, and sets the maximum at thirty-nine lashes. Rabbi Judah holds out for a full forty. The court also judges how many blows the man can survive, always in a number divisible by three, and stops if he cannot bear more.

Rava uses the thirty-nine lashes to make a point about the sages' standing. People rise when a Torah scroll passes, he says, yet fail to rise for a great scholar, though the scroll says forty and the sages reduced it by one.

Admires v. 4 as one law in harmony with the rest, like a singer in a trained chorus. The ox plowed the field before the sowing and now threshes the harvest, so it should share in what it helped produce. He moves at once to the ox and ass that may not plow together (22:10).

Explains v. 4 in plain terms: it is unjust to keep fellow-laboring animals from the fruit of their own work. He places it among the harvest laws, beside the gleanings left for the poor and the passerby's right to eat.

Gives the levirate law a social purpose: families will not die out, estates stay among kin, and widows find comfort in marrying their husbands' nearest relatives. If the brother refuses, the woman protests before the elders, looses his sandal, and spits in his face. Josephus adds that she may then marry whomever she pleases.

Describes the refusal ceremony, *halitzah*, as a court performed it. The elders first advise the brother whether to marry or release her. She then recites v. 7 and he recites v. 8, both in Hebrew, before she draws off his shoe and spits on the ground before him.

Asks whether the son of v. 6 must be given the dead brother's actual name, Joseph for Joseph or John for John. A teaching answers no: comparing Genesis 48:6, “called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance,” the rabbis take the name to mean the dead man's inheritance.
Lists vv. 17–19 among the four special Torah readings of the season of Adar. They are read on the Sabbath before Purim, the feast that celebrates the defeat of Haman.

Counts the command of v. 19 among three duties Israel took on when it entered the land: to appoint a king, to cut off Amalek's descendants in war, and to build the Temple. A teaching sets the order from other verses: the king first (Exodus 17:16), then Amalek, then the Temple once the LORD gives rest from all enemies, as he did for David (Deuteronomy 12:10–11; 2 Samuel 7:1–2).

Has Moses, at the end of his life, charge Israel not to forget the Amalekites' injuries in the wilderness and to make war on them once settled in the land. In his account of Esther he calls Haman, the Agagite of Esther 3:1, an Amalekite who hated the Jews because his nation had been destroyed by them. The link explains why the Amalek reading falls before Purim.

Reads the order of the chapter as a warning: if you use false weights (vv. 13–16), expect an enemy like Amalek (v. 17). On “he met thee by the way” (v. 18) he offers a midrash on the Hebrew *qarekha*: Amalek cooled Israel off, like a man who leaps into a scalding bath no one else dared enter and makes it seem cool to others.

Quotes v. 4 to argue that those who preach the gospel may live by it. He asks whether God cares for oxen and answers that the law was written for our sakes, so that the plowman plows in hope. 1 Timothy cites the verse again alongside the saying “The labourer is worthy of his reward.”
Among his sufferings he lists that five times he received “forty stripes save one” from the Jews. The number reflects the same practice of stopping at thirty-nine that the Mishnah later records.

The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, cite vv. 5–6 and pose a case of seven brothers who marry the same widow in turn. In the resurrection, they ask, whose wife will she be? Jesus answers that they know neither the scriptures nor the power of God, for in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage.

26.overview:
Once Israel is settled in the land, each farmer is to bring the first of his harvest in a basket to the place the LORD chooses. Before the priest and the altar he recites a short history: a wandering Syrian father went down to Egypt, the family grew into a nation, the Egyptians enslaved them, the LORD brought them out and gave them this land. Then he sets the basket down and feasts with the Levite and the stranger. Every third year, after giving the tithe to the Levite, stranger, fatherless and widow, he declares he has done it all and asks God to bless Israel. The law code closes as both sides declare the covenant “this day.”

Listen to the pronouns. The farmer was never in Egypt, yet he says the Egyptians “afflicted us” and the LORD “brought us forth” and “thou, O LORD, hast given me” the land. The Exodus is told as his own story.

26.hermeneutics:
Egypt's Book of the Dead, chapter 125, gives the speech a dead person makes before Osiris and his judges: a long list of wrongs not done, “I have not…,” among them shorting the temple offerings. Verses 13–14 use the same form: “I have not transgressed,” “I have not eaten,” “neither have I taken away,” “nor given.” The setting is the reverse. The Egyptian confession is spoken in the hall of the dead to win a place in the afterlife; Israel's is spoken by a living farmer at harvest, about food given to the poor, and asks only for blessing on the people and the land (v. 15).

The last denial is “nor given ought thereof for the dead.” Across the region families fed their dead. In Mesopotamia the *kispu* was a regular meal of food and drink set out for dead ancestors, and texts from Ugarit also speak of meals for the dead. The farmer swears that none of the holy portion went to that use, nor was eaten while he was mourning, when contact with death made food unclean (compare Hosea 9:4, “the bread of mourners”). The tithe belongs to the living: the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.

The recital opens with an Aramean, the KJV's “Syrian.” Arameans appear in Assyrian records from about 1100 BC as tribal peoples of upper Mesopotamia and Syria, and Genesis places Israel's kin among them: Rebekah and Laban are called Syrians of Padan-aram (Genesis 25:20; 31:20). Israel's founding story begins with a landless outsider, which gives weight to the man now standing in his own field with a basket of its fruit.

notes: The first speech tells what God has done; the second, what the worshiper has done. Each ends on the same phrase about the land.

**This day:** vv. 16, 17 and 18 each say “this day.” In vv. 17–18 Israel “avouched” the LORD and the LORD “avouched” Israel. That form of the verb (*he'emir*) occurs here and nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible.
**Give:** the verb *natan* comes 11 times in vv. 1–15. The LORD gives the land, the farmer gives the tithe, and once (v. 6) the Egyptians “laid upon us” hard bondage.

Chapter 26 closes the law code of chapters 12–26. The code opened by sending Israel to “the place which the LORD your God shall choose” (12:5), and its last ritual sends the farmer there with his basket (v. 2). Verses 16–19 seal the code with mutual vows before Moses turns, in chapter 27, to the ceremony across the Jordan.
**Related recitals:** the father's answer to his son in 6:20–24 tells the same story of Egypt and the land, and Joshua retells it at Shechem before the people renew the covenant (Joshua 24:2–13, 25).

traditions.text: The Greek translators read v. 5 as “my father abandoned Syria,” so the story starts with Jacob leaving Aram behind rather than with his hardship there. Philo's retelling follows this reading, while the rabbis read the same Hebrew letters as a threat from Laban (see Sifre below). The opening words were already read more than one way before the Christian era.

Philo calls this rite the feast of the basket. The landowner either recites a hymn or listens to it: the nation's founders left Syria for Egypt, grew from few to many, were oppressed, and were rescued with signs and wonders and given a most fertile land. Like the Mishnah below, he allows for a worshiper who only hears the words.

His summary of Moses' laws joins the two rites into one visit. The farmer brings his ripe fruits and blesses God for the land; before going home he stands before the temple, gives thanks for deliverance from Egypt, testifies that his tithes are paid, and asks God to keep giving good things to all the Hebrews.

Describes the Second Temple procession: villagers gathered overnight, an ox with gilded horns and an olive crown went ahead, and a flute played to Jerusalem, where even King Agrippa carried his own basket on his shoulder to the temple court. The bringer recited from v. 3 with the basket on his shoulder; at “a Syrian ready to perish” he lowered it, the priest waved it, and he finished the passage.

At first those who could recite did so, and others repeated the words after a reader. When people who could not recite stopped coming out of embarrassment, the sages ruled that the words be read aloud for everyone to repeat, so that no one would be shamed at the altar. The same care shows in the next mishnah, where the rich bring baskets of silver and gold and the poor baskets of peeled willow.

Sorts the chapter's two speeches by language. The tithe declaration of vv. 13–15 may be said in any language, like the Shema and grace after meals. The firstfruits recital of vv. 5–10 must be said in Hebrew, alongside the priestly blessing and the blessings and curses of Gerizim and Ebal in the next chapter.

The pronouns of the recital raised a legal question. A convert brings firstfruits but does not recite, the Mishnah rules, since he cannot say the land was sworn “unto our fathers” (v. 3). For the same reason converts do not make the tithe declaration of vv. 13–15, having no inheritance in the land.

Reads the tithe declaration phrase by phrase. “Neither have I forgotten them” means I did not forget to bless God over the tithe; “I have hearkened” means I brought it to the temple. The prayer of v. 15 is taken as a bargain: we have done what you decreed, now do what you promised, and bless us with children, dew and rain.

The Mishnah says Yohanan the high priest abolished the tithe declaration. The Talmud explains why: since Ezra the first tithe had gone to priests rather than Levites, so no one could truthfully say “given them unto the Levite” (v. 13). The rite ended because the words no longer matched the practice.

At the Passover meal a father answers his son's questions by beginning with disgrace and ending with praise, expounding from v. 5 to the end of the passage. The firstfruits recital thus became the core of the Passover Haggadah, still read at Jewish tables.

Reads v. 5 as “a Syrian destroyed my father”: Laban the Syrian meant to wipe out Jacob's family when he pursued him (Genesis 31). God counted the intent as done, so the verse speaks as if it happened. “With a few” means the seventy souls who went down to Egypt. This is the reading of the Passover Haggadah, against the Septuagint's.

Where v. 18 says the LORD has avouched Israel to be “his peculiar people,” the Greek has *laos periousios*, a people of his own possession. Titus 2:14 uses the same phrase for the church, a people Christ purifies to himself. 1 Peter 2:9 gives the church Israel's titles in the same spirit, though its Greek draws on other verses.

27.overview:
Moses and the elders give orders for the day Israel crosses the Jordan. They are to set up great stones on Mount Ebal, coat them with plaster, and write on them all the words of the law “very plainly.” Beside them they are to build an altar of uncut stones, offer burnt and peace offerings, and eat and rejoice. Six tribes will stand on Mount Gerizim to bless and six on Mount Ebal to curse, and the Levites will call out twelve curses. After each one, all the people answer “Amen.”

Notice what the curses aim at. The first falls on the man who sets up an idol “in a secret place” (v. 15), the tenth on the one who strikes his neighbor “secretly” (v. 24). Most of the twelve are wrongs no court is likely to see, and by saying Amen each Israelite calls the curse down on himself if he does them.

27.hermeneutics:
At Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, a text about “Balaam son of Beor” was written in ink on a plastered wall around 800 BC, and plaster inscriptions also survive at Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai. Writing on plaster was a known way to put words on public display in this region. It was cheaper than carving and could hold a long text, but it was fragile: both texts survive only in pieces. Verses 2–8 ask for that kind of display, a whole law spread across plastered stones at the entrance to the land, written large enough to read.

The Hittite military oath (CTH 427) has an officiant hold up objects and pronounce what will happen to a soldier who breaks his oath, such as a broken arrow for broken weapons. After each curse the men reply, “So be it.” Verses 15–26 work the same way, with “Amen” in place of “so be it,” and every Israelite pronounces the curse on himself. Deuteronomy drops the props and the witnessing gods. Its curses also aim at hidden wrongs among neighbors, where the Hittite oath aims at disloyalty to the king.

Babylonian boundary stones (*kudurru*) recorded land grants and ended with curses on anyone who moved or defaced them, and the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope warns against moving the markers at a field's edge. Verse 17 puts the same crime on Israel's list, one of only twelve, and 19:14 calls the landmark something “they of old time have set.” Moving a stone at night was a theft no witness saw, which is why it belongs among these curses.

notes: **Twelve and twelve:** “Cursed” (*arur*) opens each of vv. 15–26, 12 times, and “Amen” closes each, 12 times. Twelve tribes stand to hear them.
**In secret:** the Hebrew *basseter*, “in secret,” comes twice, in the first curse (v. 15) and the tenth (v. 24), marking the theme of the list.

The twelfth curse is different in kind. It names no single act but covers every word of “this law,” a summary of everything before it. The blessings promised from Gerizim (v. 12) are never spoken in the chapter.

Chapter 27 breaks into Moses' speech. The law code ends at 26:19, and 28:1 picks up again in the same voice, but here the narrator speaks of Moses in the third person, first with the elders (v. 1) and then with the Levitical priests (v. 9). With 11:26–32 it brackets the law code with the Gerizim and Ebal ceremony.

**Forward:** Joshua builds the altar on Ebal of stones no iron touched, writes a copy of the law on the stones, and reads the blessings and cursings with half the people before each mountain (Joshua 8:30–35).

traditions.text: The Church's footnotes to vv. 24–25 point to Moses 5:29–31, where Cain swears secret oaths with Satan and takes the name Master Mahan, “that I may murder and get gain.” The two curses here fall on exactly that pair, striking a neighbor secretly and taking pay to kill the innocent. In Moses 5:36 Cain himself is then cursed from the earth.

The Church's footnote to v. 9, where Israel becomes the people of the LORD “this day,” points to King Benjamin's people. After they enter a covenant to obey God's commandments, Benjamin tells them that because of it they are called the children of Christ, for “this day he hath spiritually begotten you.” In both a people becomes the Lord's on a named day by a spoken covenant.

The Samaritans' Torah reads “Gerizim” where the Jewish text reads “Ebal” in v. 4, so the altar stands on their holy mountain. It also adds a commandment after Exodus 20:17 and Deuteronomy 5:21, built from 11:29–30 and 27:2–7, to set up the stones and altar on Gerizim. Each side has accused the other of changing the text; many scholars now think the Samaritan reading may be the older one, though others defend “Ebal.” The Samaritan woman's “our fathers worshipped in this mountain” (John 4:20) is the same dispute.

Retells the command with details of his own: the altar is to face the rising sun, near Shechem, with Gerizim on the right and Ebal on the left. Moses, he says, wrote the blessings and curses on the altar itself, on each side, and after that day no other sacrifice was ever offered on it, because it was not lawful.

Describes the ceremony: six tribes on each summit, the priests around the ark in the valley, the Levites around the priests. The Levites turned toward Gerizim and said each line as a blessing, blessed is the man who does not make an idol, then turned toward Ebal and said it as a curse, and both sides answered Amen to each. The Mishnah supplies the blessings the chapter leaves unspoken, and says the law was written on the stones in seventy languages, so that “very plainly” (v. 8) meant for every nation.

The Dead Sea community renewed its covenant every year with a ceremony built on this chapter. The priests blessed the men of God's lot, the Levites cursed the men of Belial's lot, and all who entered answered “Amen, Amen.” Like Deuteronomy's list, the curses reach the hidden heart, the one who enters the covenant while keeping idols inside.

Paul quotes v. 26 in the Greek form, “Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things” written in the law. The Hebrew has neither “every one” nor “all”; the Septuagint adds both, and the added “all” carries Paul's point that no one keeps the whole law. A few verses later he says Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse (Galatians 3:13).
Builds on Paul's use of v. 26. The whole human race is under this curse, Justin tells Trypho, since no one has kept all the law, and the Father willed that his Christ take on the curses of all.

His gazetteer of biblical places puts Gerizim and Ebal near Jericho, by Gilgal (taking 11:30 literally), and says the Samaritans are wrong to point to the two mountains at Neapolis (Shechem). His reason: those mountains stand too far apart for people on one to hear the other. The identification with the Shechem peaks, held by the Mishnah and Josephus, is the one most follow today.

On Ebal's northeast slope Adam Zertal excavated an Iron Age I structure (pottery c. 1220–1000 BC) with burned bones of young bulls, goats and fallow deer, and identified it as Joshua's altar. Aharon Kempinski read it as a watchtower within a small village, and others accept a cult place but not the link to Joshua. There is still no consensus on what the structure was.

A folded lead piece sifted from Zertal's old dump piles was announced in 2022 as a curse tablet naming Yahweh, dated to the Late Bronze Age. Other scholars dispute that any letters can be read, and some suggest it is a fishing or net weight. Until a full, peer-reviewed reading wins acceptance, it cannot be treated as evidence for this chapter.

28.overview:
Moses sets out what follows from obeying or refusing the LORD. If Israel hearkens, blessings will “overtake” them: blessed in city and field, in children, crops and herds, in coming and going; enemies scattered, rain in season, lending to nations and never borrowing, the head and not the tail. If Israel refuses, every blessing turns to a curse, and the list runs on for fifty more verses: disease, drought, defeat, madness, another man taking a man's wife, house and vineyard, exile with their king, a far nation whose siege drives parents to eat their children, and scattering among all peoples.

Watch where the curses end. The last threat is a return to Egypt in ships, to be offered as slaves where no one will buy (v. 68). Along the way come the “diseases of Egypt” (v. 60) and a people “left few in number” who had been as the stars (v. 62). Point by point, the Exodus runs backward.

28.hermeneutics:
Esarhaddon of Assyria made his vassals and officials swear loyalty to his heir in 672 BC, and the oath tablets end with a long run of curses. In one stretch, Sin clothes the oath-breaker with leprosy; Shamash takes away his eyesight so he walks about in darkness; Ninurta feeds his flesh to the eagle and vulture; and Venus makes his wife lie in his enemy's lap while strangers divide his goods and his sons lose his house. Verses 26–33 run through the same matters in nearly the same order: carrion birds, skin disease, blindness and groping in darkness, a betrothed wife taken, house, vineyard and herds seized, sons and daughters given to another people. Tigay notes that only the order is shared, and the wording differs too much to show copying; Crouch doubts any direct link. The striking change is that no gods are listed. In the treaty each god sends his own plague. Here “the LORD shall smite thee” covers them all.

In 2009 another copy of the same oath was found at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey, the seat of an Assyrian province. It lay in the inner room of a temple, beside a pedestal on which it seems to have been displayed. These oaths were sacred objects, kept before the gods. Judah was an Assyrian vassal in these years: Esarhaddon names “Manasseh, king of Judah” among the western kings he summoned to supply his palace, and some scholars think Manasseh swore this very oath. Readers who knew such oaths would hear chapter 28 as a covenant of the same kind, with the LORD in the place of the great king and the law placed beside the ark as its witness (31:26).

notes: **Proportion:** the blessings take 14 verses (vv. 1–14); the curses take 54 (vv. 15–68).
**Mirror lines:** “Blessed” (*baruk*) comes 6 times in vv. 3–6 and “cursed” (*arur*) 6 times in vv. 16–19, with the same subjects. The curses swap the middle two lines, basket before offspring.

**Refrain:** the curse panel keeps returning to destruction. The verb *shamad*, “destroy,” comes 7 times (vv. 20, 24, 45, 48, 51, 61, 63), most often in “until thou be destroyed.” Egypt is named 3 times (vv. 27, 60, 68).

Chapter 28 ends Moses' second address (4:44–28:68). The blessing and the curse were announced in 11:26–28 and staged on Gerizim and Ebal in chapter 27; here they are spelled out. The Hebrew Bible ends the chapter with one more verse (28:69), which the KJV prints as 29:1.

**Forward:** Daniel prays in Babylon that “the curse is poured upon us” as written in the law of Moses (Daniel 9:11). Moses himself answers the chapter in 30:1–3: when the blessing and the curse have both come, Israel can return and be gathered.

traditions.text: Nephi quotes the prophet Zenos on the people at Jerusalem who will turn their hearts aside and reject the God of Israel. They will wander in the flesh and perish, and “become a hiss and a byword, and be hated among all nations.” The wording follows v. 37, where Israel becomes an astonishment, a proverb and a byword among the nations. Zenos, a prophet known only from the brass plates, also foresees the scattered house of Israel remembered and gathered (1 Nephi 19:15–16), much as Deuteronomy 30 answers this chapter.

Abinadi's warning to King Noah's people draws on the same curses. They will be brought into bondage, smitten and slain, and “the vultures of the air, and the dogs” will devour their flesh. The Church's edition links the passage to v. 26, the carcass left to the birds and beasts with no one to frighten them away. Abinadi goes on to threaten famine, pestilence and the loss of crops to insects (Mosiah 12:4–7), much as vv. 21–22 and 38–42 do.

Moroni explains the decree for the Jaredites' promised land: whoever possesses it must serve God “or they shall be swept off” when they are ripened in iniquity. Like vv. 63–64, it ties a people's hold on a land to obedience and makes losing the land the final curse. The Book of Mormon applies the covenant pattern of this chapter to a second land and a second people, and Ether's closing chapters show it carried out.

The prophets of Jerusalem's fall reuse this chapter's words. Jeremiah threatens “a nation from far” whose language Judah will not understand, eating up its harvest and its flocks (compare vv. 49–51), and says the exiles will be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth and become a proverb, the words of vv. 25 and 37. Lamentations then reports that compassionate women boiled their own children in the siege, the horror of vv. 56–57 come true.

The exiles' confession in this apocryphal book says the Lord has confirmed his word against them. Nothing under heaven, they say, matches what was done in Jerusalem, where parents ate the flesh of their sons and daughters, just as the law of Moses had written. It reads the siege of vv. 53–57 as fulfilled in Babylon's siege of Jerusalem.

Writing after Rome had burned the temple, Josephus says Moses foretold it: if Israel broke the law, their land would be filled with enemy weapons, their cities overthrown, their temple burnt, and they would be sold as slaves to men with no pity. Yet God would restore the cities and the temple, and they would lose these things “not once only, but often.” He sets this prophecy among Moses' last speeches, beside the blessings and the song.

Abaye distinguishes the two curse chapters. Leviticus 26 is in the plural and Moses spoke it from the mouth of God, so its reading may not be split between readers; this chapter is in the singular and Moses said it on his own, so it may be. When one reader stammered over these curses, Rav Huna let him stop and another continue. A teaching credited to Ezra sets this chapter to be read before the New Year, so the year ends with its curses.

Argues that Leviticus 26 foretells the Babylonian exile and this chapter the Roman one. He points to the nation from far whose tongue Israel will not understand (v. 49), the scattering to the ends of the earth (v. 64), sons and daughters taken by another people (v. 32), and v. 68, fulfilled, he says, when Titus filled ships with captives. The Talmud's distinction between the two chapters becomes a distinction between two exiles. He adds that this chapter, unlike Leviticus 26, sets no end to the exile.

Reads the verb of v. 68 as reflexive: Israel will offer themselves for sale as slaves, and still no one will buy, because their enemies will have decreed their death. On this reading the last curse is worse than slavery, since even being bought would have meant survival.

Quotes v. 66 in a form close to the Hebrew, “your life shall be hanging before your eyes,” and adds that they would not believe their life. He reads it as Moses foretelling the Word, the one who made them, hanging on the tree while his own people did not believe in him. The KJV's “hang in doubt” hides the image this reading depends on.

29.overview:
A heading names “the words of the covenant” made in Moab, besides the one made at Horeb. Moses reminds Israel of what they saw in Egypt, though the LORD has not yet given them “an heart to perceive,” and of forty years in which their clothes never wore out. Now all Israel stands before the LORD, from the captains to the water carriers, wives, children and strangers, to enter the covenant and its oath. Moses warns against anyone who hears the curse and still promises himself peace. Later generations will see the land burned like Sodom and ask why: Israel forsook the covenant. The chapter closes: the secret things belong to the LORD, the revealed things to us and our children.

Notice who is bound. The covenant is made with those standing there “this day,” and also “with him that is not here with us this day” (v. 15). Every later reader is counted as present in Moab.

29.hermeneutics:
Hittite vassal treaties of the 14th–13th centuries BC open with history before they give commands. In his treaty with Duppi-Teshub of Amurru, Mursili II first recounts how his father dealt with Duppi-Teshub's grandfather Aziru and how Mursili himself set Duppi-Teshub on the throne, and only then lists what the vassal owes. Verses 2–8 do the same: Egypt, the wilderness, the defeat of Sihon and Og, and the land given to two and a half tribes, then “Keep therefore” (v. 9). The Hittite treaty also reaches past the people in the room, promising the throne to the vassal's future heir and binding the vassal to the king's descendants. Verses 14–15 stretch the oath the same way, to those “not here with us this day.”

Ashurbanipal's annals (c. 643 BC) tell how Arab tribes broke their oath to Assyria. Famine came, they ate the flesh of their children, and every curse written in their oath fell on them. Then the people of Arabia asked one another why such evil had befallen Arabia, and answered: because we did not keep the great oaths sworn to Assur. Verses 24–28 use the same pattern. The nations ask, “Wherefore hath the LORD done thus unto this land?” and the answer is a broken covenant. Here the oath is sworn to the LORD, not to a king, and the question is put in advance as a warning. The same question and answer return in 1 Kings 9:8–9 and Jeremiah 22:8–9.

The same annals boast that Ashurbanipal scattered “salt and sihlu” (a thorny plant) over the provinces of Elam, and Abimelech sowed Shechem with salt (Judges 9:45). Salt marked ground meant to stay barren. Verse 23's land of “brimstone, and salt, and burning,” where no grass grows, is that kind of land.

notes: **This day:** *hayyom* comes 8 times (vv. 4, 10, 12, 13, 15 twice, 18, 28). The present moment in Moab is the chapter's anchor.

**Covenant and oath:** “covenant” (*berit*) comes 7 times (vv. 1 twice, 9, 12, 14, 21, 25), and *alah*, the sworn oath that carries a curse, 5 times (vv. 12, 14, 19, 20, 21). “Written in this book” comes 3 times (vv. 20, 21, 27).
The movement narrows and widens: from all Israel (vv. 10–15) to one man, woman, family or tribe (v. 18), then out to the whole land and the nations watching it (vv. 22–28).

Verse 1 is a hinge. Hebrew Bibles count it as 28:69, closing the laws and curses; the KJV makes it the heading of chapter 29. Its form, “These are the words…,” matches the headings at 1:1 and 4:45, and it opens the covenant in Moab (chs. 29–30), set beside the one made at Horeb (5:2–3).

**Forward:** the closing saying is answered in 30:11, where the commandment “is not hidden from thee.” Joshua later gathers the tribes at Shechem and asks them to “choose you this day” (Joshua 24:15).

traditions.text: Verse 20 warns that the LORD will blot out the name of the one who turns away, and the Church's footnote points to Alma's sermon at Zarahemla. Alma tells those who want to follow the good shepherd to separate from the wicked, whose names “shall be blotted out” and not numbered among the righteous. Both speak to a covenant people that includes some who only appear to belong, and both leave the blotting out to God rather than to the community.

In the days of Coriantor, prophets warn the Jaredites that without repentance the Lord will bring utter destruction on them and “bring forth another people to possess the land.” The Church's footnote links this to v. 28, where the LORD roots Israel out and casts them into another land. In the Book of Mormon the covenant warning is played out on another continent.

The yearly covenant ceremony of the Dead Sea community quotes vv. 19–20 almost word for word. Priests and Levites curse the one who enters the covenant with idols in his heart, who hears the covenant's words and blesses himself, saying he will have peace though he walks in his own stubbornness. All the curses of the covenant will cling to him and God will set him apart for evil, the language of v. 21, and everyone answers “Amen, Amen.” The ceremony was to be repeated every year for as long as the dominion of Belial lasted.

Judges warned a man about to swear in court that the oath was taken in the court's sense, not his own, just as Moses told Israel in Moab that their oath was bound to God's understanding and his. From “him that is not here with us this day” (v. 15) the Talmud adds that later generations and future converts were included. Rashi, following Midrash Tanchuma, reads the verse the same way, since everyone then alive was already standing there.

Counts the covenants made over the commandments: one at Sinai, one on the plains of Moab (citing v. 1, the Hebrew 28:69), and one at Gerizim and Ebal. Multiplying blessings and curses, general and particular, the sages reckon 48 covenants for every commandment in the Torah. Rabbi Shimon replaces Gerizim and Ebal with the Tent of Meeting. On this count the covenant in Moab is a full covenant in its own right, as v. 1 says, not a mere repetition of Sinai.

On “unto this day” (v. 4) Rashi passes on a tradition: when Moses gave the written law to the Levites, the other tribes protested that they too had stood at Sinai and did not want the priests to claim it as theirs. Moses rejoiced, saying that only today had they shown a heart to know the LORD. The complaint was proof of the heart v. 4 says they lacked.

In Hebrew scrolls dots stand over the words “unto us and to our children” in v. 29. Rashi explains the verse and the dots together: the community is not punished for a person's hidden sins, which belong to God, but must deal with open ones. The dots show that even open sins were not charged to the whole people until they crossed the Jordan and took the oath at Gerizim and Ebal, becoming responsible for one another.

Paul joins v. 4 with Isaiah 29:10: God gave them a spirit of slumber, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, unto this day. He uses it to explain why most of Israel had not accepted Jesus while a remnant had. Moses' “unto this day” in Moab becomes Paul's own day. Later in the chapter Paul insists the blindness is partial and will end, when all Israel shall be saved (Romans 11:25–26).

The Greek of v. 18 speaks of a root springing up “with gall and bitterness.” Hebrews 12:15 warns the church against any root of bitterness springing up to defile many, and in Acts 8:23 Peter tells Simon the sorcerer he is in the gall of bitterness. Both apply Moses' warning about one hidden apostate to a member of the Christian community. Hebrews ends the same chapter with another line from Deuteronomy, that God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29; Deuteronomy 4:24).

30.overview:
Moses looks past the curses of chapters 28–29 to a day when Israel, scattered among the nations, remembers and turns back to the LORD. Then the LORD will turn their captivity, gather them from the farthest places, bring them home, and circumcise their hearts so they can love him with all their heart and soul. The commandment, Moses says, is neither hidden in heaven nor beyond the sea; it is in their mouth and heart. He ends by setting life and death, blessing and cursing before them, with heaven and earth as witnesses, and urges them to choose life.

Set v. 6 beside 10:16. There Israel was told to circumcise the foreskin of its own heart; here the LORD promises to do it himself, after the exile. The chapter holds both at once: a choice Israel must make today, and a change of heart that only God can work.

30.hermeneutics:
Hittite vassal treaties of the 14th and 13th centuries BC close by calling the gods to witness, and the lists end with the world itself: mountains, rivers, springs, the great sea, heaven and earth, winds and clouds. The treaty Mursili II made with Duppi-Teshub of Amurru is a standard example. Moses calls the same pair in v. 19 (also 4:26; 31:28), with a difference: there is no roster of gods to name, only the sky and the ground. A listener who knew the form would hear v. 19 as the formal seal on a sworn covenant, with witnesses that outlast every generation.

Assyria made mass deportation a tool of empire. From Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC) onward whole populations were moved across the empire, and in 722 BC the people of Samaria were sent to Halah, the Habor, and the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6). Babylon did the same to Judah. Verses 1–5 speak to people in exactly that state, driven out as far as “the outmost parts of heaven” (v. 4). Treaty curses end with the rebel ruined and offer no way back; this covenant writes the return into its own terms.

Mesopotamian stories put life-giving knowledge out of reach. Gilgamesh crosses the sea and the waters of death to find Utnapishtim and learn how to escape death, then loses the plant he carries home. Adapa is summoned up to heaven and refuses the bread and water of life offered to him there. Verses 12–13 name the same two journeys, up to heaven and across the sea, and declare neither one necessary.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence from promised return (vv. 1–10) to present choice (vv. 11–20).
notes: **Return:** The verb *shuv* (return, turn) comes 7 times in vv. 1–10 (vv. 1, 2, 3 twice, 8, 9, 10). Israel turns back, and God turns back to Israel. The KJV hides two of them as “call them to mind” (v. 1) and “turn thy captivity” (v. 3). The verb does not appear in vv. 11–20.
**Today:** “This day” comes 7 times (vv. 2, 8, 11, 15, 16, 18, 19), pulling a promise about the far future back into the present decision.
**Heart:** *levav* comes 8 times, three of them in v. 6.

The chapter closes the covenant in Moab that began at 29:1 and with it Moses' long speeches. The witnesses and the call to choose (vv. 19–20) are his last words of exhortation; from 31:1 the book turns to narrative and his final arrangements.

**Echoes:** Joshua sets the same choice before Israel at Shechem: “choose you this day whom ye will serve” (Joshua 24:15). The promise of v. 6 returns in the prophets as a new heart and the law written within (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26).

traditions.text: Book of Mormon prophets repeatedly use the language of vv. 15 and 19. Lehi teaches that people are free to choose liberty and eternal life or captivity and death, and Jacob tells his people the same. Samuel the Lamanite adds that God has given them knowledge so “that ye might choose life or death,” matching v. 11's claim that the commandment is not hidden.

Nephi and Jacob describe a gathering on the pattern of vv. 1–5: scattered Israel is brought back “to the lands of their inheritance.” Deuteronomy ties the return to Israel turning back to the LORD; these passages name that turning as coming to know their Redeemer, Christ.

In the Kirtland Temple, Moses appeared and committed to Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery the keys of “the gathering of Israel from the four parts of the earth.” The link is thematic: the prophet who foretold the gathering in vv. 3–4 is the one who hands over its keys.

A wisdom poem in this book of the Apocrypha asks who has gone up into heaven to bring wisdom down, or crossed the sea to find her, borrowing the two journeys of vv. 12–13. It then names her: wisdom is “the book of the commandments of God,” and those who keep it will live. Paul later reworks the same verses (Early Christian below).

Philo paraphrases vv. 11–14: the good is not across the sea or at the ends of the earth, and no one needs wings to reach heaven for it. He reads the mouth, the heart, and the doing of v. 14 as speech, intention, and action, and says happiness comes when the three agree.

Philo also expands vv. 1–5. When the scattered confess their sins, he says, they will be freed in a single day even at the ends of the earth, and will come from Greece, barbarian lands, and the islands to one place, led by a divine vision seen only by them. It is one of the fullest early readings of the chapter as a future ingathering.

In the dispute over the oven of Akhnai, Rabbi Eliezer calls on miracles and finally a voice from heaven to support his ruling. Rabbi Yehoshua answers with v. 12, “It is not in heaven”: the Torah was given at Sinai, and decisions now follow the majority of the sages. Elijah later reports that God smiled and said his children had defeated him.

Gives several readings of vv. 12–13. One: if the Torah were in heaven you would have to climb after it, so spare no effort to learn it. Rabbi Yohanan's: it is not found among the haughty, who lift themselves to heaven, nor among traders always traveling overseas with no time to study.

This midrash has Moses use v. 12 as a warning: do not say that another Moses will arise and bring another Torah from heaven, because none of it was left there. When the people ask where it is, then, Moses answers that it is near, in their mouth and heart. The reading makes the Torah given through Moses complete and final, a point the Bava Metzia story applies to heavenly voices.

Rashi notices that v. 3 says literally that the LORD “will return” with the captivity, not that he will bring it back. Following the Talmud, he reads it to mean that God's presence goes into exile with Israel and returns when they are redeemed. He adds that the gathering is so hard that God must take each exile by the hand, as Isaiah 27:12 says Israel will be gathered “one by one.”

Paul quotes vv. 12–14 and reads them through Christ. No one need go up to heaven to bring Christ down, or into the deep to bring him up from the dead; the near word in mouth and heart is “the word of faith, which we preach.” Where Baruch identified the near thing with the law, Paul identifies it with confessing Jesus and believing God raised him.

In his defense of free will, Origen cites Moses' words as proof that people choose for themselves: God sets before them “the way of life and the way of death.” His version blends v. 15 with the command to choose in v. 19, and he sets it beside Micah 6:8 and Isaiah 1:19–20.

31.overview:
Moses, now 120, tells Israel he will not cross the Jordan; the LORD will go before them, and so will Joshua. He charges Joshua in front of the people, writes down the law, hands it to the priests and elders, and orders it read to the whole nation every seventh year at the Feast of Tabernacles. At the tabernacle the LORD appears in the pillar of cloud, foretells that Israel will turn to other gods after Moses dies, and commands a song to stand as a witness against them. Moses writes the song, has the book of the law placed beside the ark, and recites the song to the assembly.

The chapter gives a people about to lose Moses three things to carry on without him: a leader, a book, and a song. The LORD expects failure and says so plainly. The book and the song are put in place beforehand so that, when disaster comes, Israel will recognize why.

historicalContext.text: The chapter speaks of Moses in the third person and records him writing “this law” and “this song” (vv. 9, 22, 24). Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars connect Deuteronomy's core with the law book found under Josiah (2 Kings 22).

31.hermeneutics:
Hittite kings kept treaty tablets in temples and had them read aloud. The treaty Suppiluliuma I made with Shattiwaza of Mitanni (14th century BC) says that one copy lies before the Sun-goddess of Arinna and another before the storm god Teshub, and that the text must be read at regular intervals before the king of Mitanni and his people. Deuteronomy treats its covenant document the same way: it is kept at the ark, the holiest object Israel had, and read in public every seven years (vv. 9–13, 26). The audience is different. A treaty was read to a vassal king and his court; this law is read to men, women, children, and the resident foreigner (v. 12), so that the whole people, not only its rulers, are bound and taught.

In 672 BC the Assyrian king Esarhaddon summoned his vassals and officials and made them swear loyalty to his chosen heir, Ashurbanipal, so that the succession was fixed while he was still alive to enforce it. A copy of that oath found in 2009 in a temple at Tell Tayinat, in southern Turkey, appears to have been set up there as a sacred object. Moses settles his succession the same way, in public and before his death: he names Joshua before all Israel (v. 7), presents him at the tabernacle (v. 14), and the LORD himself gives the charge (v. 23). When Moses dies, no one can claim the leadership was left open.

notes: **Be strong:** *chazaq* comes 3 times, once to all Israel (v. 6) and twice to Joshua (vv. 7, 23). The LORD's own charge in v. 23 repeats Moses' words from v. 7, and Joshua 1:6–9 takes them up again.
**Witness:** The noun *'ed* comes 3 times: the song is a witness twice (vv. 19, 21) and the book once (v. 26). “Song” (*shirah*) comes 5 times.
**Hidden face:** The verb “hide” comes 3 times in vv. 17–18; v. 18 doubles it (“I will surely hide my face”).

Narrative takes over after the long speeches, and the book's last section begins: Moses' final arrangements, the Song (ch. 32), the Blessing (ch. 33), and his death (ch. 34). Verse 30 introduces the Song and 32:44 closes it, so this chapter is the frame for the poem that follows.

**Forward:** Joshua reads the law before all Israel, women, children, and strangers included (Joshua 8:34–35). Josiah reads the found book of the covenant to all Judah (2 Kings 23:2), and Ezra reads the law day by day through the Feast of Tabernacles (Nehemiah 8:18).

traditions.text: Nephi reasons that his people could not keep the law of Moses unless they had it in writing, and the plates of brass held the law and “the five books of Moses.” His concern is the one behind vv. 9–13: a law must be written down and kept to be obeyed. The Church's Bible Dictionary cites this passage as reaffirming that Moses wrote the five books that bear his name.

King Benjamin tells his sons that without the plates their people would have “suffered in ignorance,” since Lehi could not have remembered everything he taught his children. The link to vv. 12–13 is thematic: a written record lets each generation teach the next.

In his summary of Moses' laws, Josephus has the high priest stand on a raised platform every seventh year at the Feast of Tabernacles and read the laws to all the people, women, children, and servants included. The purpose, he says, is that the laws be “engraven in their souls” and kept in memory. The Mishnah (next entry) gives the reading to the king instead.

Describes the seventh-year assembly of vv. 10–13 as the Second Temple practiced it: a wooden platform in the Temple court, the scroll passed from hand to hand up to the high priest, and the king reading selected parts of Deuteronomy. When King Agrippa reached 17:15, “thou mayest not set a stranger over thee,” he wept for his Edomite descent, and the people called out that he was their brother.

Rabbis disagree over where the book of v. 26 was placed. Rabbi Meir works out the ark's dimensions in handbreadths to show that two handbreadths were left beside the tablets, where Moses' scroll lay inside the ark. Rabbi Yehuda puts it outside, on a shelf at the ark's side and later on the chest the Philistines sent back, and both appeal to the phrase “in the side of the ark.”

Rava draws a command from v. 19, “write ye this song”: every Jew should write a Torah scroll of his own, even one who has inherited a scroll from his parents. The song Moses was told to write becomes, in this reading, the whole Torah that contains it.

Asked by sectarians to prove resurrection from the Torah, Rabban Gamaliel cites v. 16, “thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, and rise up.” His opponents answer that “rise up” belongs with the next words, so that it is the people who rise up to stray, and the Talmud reports they did not accept the proof. The passage shows early readers searching the books of Moses for the doctrine.

Asks why v. 2 says “this day” and answers that Moses turned exactly 120 on the day he spoke. God completes the years of the righteous to the day, the rabbis say, so Moses was born and died on the same date. Other passages fix that date as the seventh of Adar.

Philo praises Moses for passing over his own two sons and his priestly nephews and choosing Joshua, his companion and pupil from youth. He describes Moses taking Joshua by the right hand, leading him before the assembly, and urging him to be strong, with no trace of envy. For Philo the scene is a pattern for every ruler who comes after.

This early midrash says God told Moses to give Joshua a spokesman and let him teach while Moses was still alive, so no one could later say he had kept silent in his master's lifetime. It also reports that Moses was pained that none of his own sons rose to lead, and that God consoled him with the reminder that Aaron's sons were like his own.

Urging contentment, the writer quotes God's promise “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee,” the promise Moses gives Israel and Joshua in vv. 6 and 8 and the LORD repeats in Joshua 1:5. A charge to a new leader becomes a promise to every believer.

Justin points out that Joshua's name is the same as Jesus' in Greek, and that Moses gave him the name. Because Joshua, not Moses, led the people into the land and divided it by lot, Justin reads him as a figure of Christ, who will gather the dispersed and give them a lasting inheritance.

32.overview:
Moses recites a long poem. He summons heaven and earth to listen, praises the LORD as the Rock whose ways are just, and charges Israel with corruption. He recalls how the Most High divided the nations, kept Jacob as his own portion, found him in the wilderness, and fed him richly. Jeshurun grew fat, kicked, and turned to new gods, so God hides his face and sends hunger, plague, beasts, and the sword. He holds back from wiping them out lest their enemies boast, then turns on those enemies and avenges his servants. Afterward Moses urges Israel to set their hearts on these words, and the LORD sends him up Mount Nebo to see the land and die.

This is the witness promised in 31:19–21: a song given before the apostasy it describes, so later Israel would find its own history already sung.

32.hermeneutics:
At Ugarit on the Syrian coast (14th–13th century BC), the high god El presides over an assembly of divine sons, and one myth counts seventy sons of his consort Athirat (KTU 1.4 vi 46). Verse 8 pictures the Most High dividing the nations and setting their borders, and the received Hebrew ends “according to the number of the children of Israel.” A Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran (4QDeutj, 1st century BC) reads “sons of God” there instead. Most Septuagint manuscripts read “angels of God,” and an early papyrus (P. Fouad 266) reads “sons of God,” which the Göttingen critical edition prints. On the Qumran reading, each nation is assigned to a heavenly being while the LORD keeps Jacob for himself (v. 9), and the verse fits the divine council language Israel's neighbors used, now subordinate to one God.

The curses of vv. 23–24 use names a Canaanite listener would know. The word the KJV renders “burning heat” is *Resheph*, a god of plague and war worshiped at Ugarit and in Phoenicia and Egypt, where he was shown with spear and shield. In the Song he is one of the LORD's arrows (v. 23), with no power of his own. Verse 17 makes a similar move: the *shedim*, “devils,” to whom Israel sacrificed share their name with the Akkadian *shedu*, a protective spirit, and the Song dismisses them as “not God.”

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the poem moves in sequence from summons through accusation and judgment to vindication.
notes: **Rock:** *tsur* comes 8 times in vv. 1–43: five times of the LORD (vv. 4, 15, 18, 30, 31), twice of the enemies' gods (vv. 31, 37), and once of the flinty rock that yields oil (v. 13).
**Jeshurun:** this rare name for Israel appears in v. 15 and twice more in the next chapter (33:5, 26); elsewhere only in Isaiah 44:2.
**Speaker:** From v. 20 God speaks in the first person, and the poem's climax is his oath, “I live for ever” (v. 40).

The Song proper (vv. 1–43) is framed by narrative: 31:30 introduces it and v. 44 says Moses spoke it with Hoshea, that is, Joshua. Verses 45–52 close Moses' speaking and turn toward his death, a command carried out in 34:1–5.
**Backward:** vv. 48–52 repeat the command of Numbers 27:12–14, with the same reason, Meribah. **Forward:** Isaiah opens with the same summons to heaven and earth (Isaiah 1:2).

traditions.text: Moroni warns against smiting and judging others, citing “what the scripture says”: judgment belongs to the Lord, and vengeance also, and he will repay. The wording rests on v. 35, the same verse Paul quotes in Romans 12:19.

Nephi calls the LORD “the rock of my salvation,” and his brother Jacob urges his people to come to the God who is the rock of their salvation, the title of v. 15. Helaman tells his sons that the rock is their Redeemer, Christ, as Paul names the rock that followed Israel (1 Corinthians 10:4). These are shared titles rather than quotations of the Song.

The Greek translation gives v. 43 a longer opening than the Hebrew: the heavens rejoice with him, “and let all the angels of God worship him,” and then the nations rejoice with his people. Hebrews 1:6 quotes the added line about the angels.

A small Qumran manuscript preserving the end of the Song gives v. 43 a form close to the Greek. It calls the heavens to rejoice with him and all the gods to bow down to him, lines the received Hebrew lacks. It is Hebrew evidence that the Septuagint's longer verse was not the translator's invention.

Ben Sira restates vv. 8–9: when the nations of the earth were divided, God set a ruler over every people, “but Israel is the Lord's portion.” The ruler of each nation is left vague, but the line fits the reading of v. 8 found at Qumran (see Hermeneutics).

Jubilees says God placed spirits in authority over the many nations to lead them astray, but set no angel or spirit over Israel, because he alone is their ruler. It is the sharpest early statement of the idea behind vv. 8–9, with the nations' heavenly rulers turned hostile.

The Aramaic paraphrase of v. 8 holds both readings together. The Most High cast lots among the seventy angels who are princes of the nations, and fixed the nations' borders by the seventy souls of Israel who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:27).

Josephus calls the Song a poem composed in hexameter verse, the meter of Greek epic, which Moses read to the people and left to them in the holy book. It contained a prediction of what would happen later, and Josephus says everything has come to pass as it foretold and is still happening to his people.

Compares v. 1 with Isaiah 1:2, which reverses the verbs. Moses, close to heaven, said “give ear” to the heavens and “hear” to the earth; Isaiah, closer to earth, did the opposite. Rashi, drawing on this midrash, adds why heaven and earth were chosen: Moses was mortal, and the covenant needed witnesses that would outlive him.

In the Temple the Levites sang the Song at the additional Sabbath offering, divided into six sections. The sections begin at vv. 1, 7, 13, 19, 27, and 36, and the Talmud gives a memory aid made of the first letter of each opening word. The same six divisions, it says, are used when the Song is read in the synagogue.

Paul quotes the Song three times in Romans. Verse 21, God provoking Israel to jealousy by “a foolish nation,” explains the Gentiles' faith; v. 35 forbids Christians to take revenge; and v. 43 in its Greek form has the Gentiles rejoicing with God's people.

Hebrews quotes the Greek form of v. 43, “let all the angels of God worship him,” as God's word when he brings his firstborn into the world, proving the Son greater than angels. Later it quotes vv. 35–36 on vengeance and judgment as a warning to believers.

The victors standing beside the sea of glass sing “the song of Moses” together with the song of the Lamb. Their words, praising God's great works and his just and true ways, echo the Song's opening praise of the Rock whose work is perfect and whose ways are judgment (v. 4). Moses' song of witness has become a song of victory.

Justin quotes v. 43 in its Greek form as a prophecy that the nations would rejoice with Israel. He then quotes vv. 7–9 with the children of Israel as the measure of the nations' borders, and notes that the Seventy translated the line “according to the number of the angels of God.” He accepts the Jewish reading because his argument works either way, which shows both readings were current in the 2nd century.

33.overview:
Before his death Moses blesses the tribes. A hymn opens the poem: the LORD comes from Sinai, Seir, and Paran with holy ones, gives a fiery law, and becomes king in Jeshurun. Short blessings follow. Reuben is to live; Judah's cry is to be heard; Levi receives the Thummim and Urim and the duty to teach and offer; Benjamin dwells safely; Joseph gets the richest land and the horns of the wild ox; then Zebulun and Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher. A closing hymn praises the God of Jeshurun, the eternal refuge, and Israel saved by the LORD.

Set beside Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49), the weight has shifted. Levi, cursed there with Simeon for violence, is now the priestly tribe, praised for loyalty that put God before family (v. 9). Simeon is not named at all, and none of the sayings is a rebuke.

33.hermeneutics:
Several early Hebrew poems bring the LORD out of the south: from Seir and the field of Edom (Judges 5:4), from Teman and Mount Paran (Habakkuk 3:3). Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud, a way station in the northern Sinai of about 800 BC, invoke “YHWH of Teman” alongside “YHWH of Samaria.” Verse 2 belongs to that tradition. The God of Sinai rises out of the southern desert and marches toward his people, and the blessing opens with that march before it names a single tribe.

In the Ugaritic myths the storm god Baal's standing title is “rider of the clouds.” Verse 26 gives the God of Jeshurun the same role, riding the heavens to help his people, and Psalm 68 uses the phrase of the LORD (68:4, 33). In the closing hymn the title claims for Israel's God what the neighbors credited to Baal, down to the dew that drops from his heavens (v. 28).

The KJV's “unicorns” (v. 17) translates *re'em*, the wild ox or aurochs, called *rimu* in Akkadian. Mesopotamian kings hunted it as royal game, and Tiglath-pileser I (c. 1100 BC) boasts in his annals of killing wild bulls in the land of Mitanni. A hearer would take Joseph's firstborn bull, with horns that gore the nations, as an image of royal strength. The two horns are then named as Ephraim and Manasseh, the tribes that dominated the later northern kingdom.
