close.text: None like the God of Jeshurun

notes: **Frame:** Jeshurun is named only at the two ends (vv. 5, 26). The frame speaks of the LORD and all Israel; the middle goes tribe by tribe.
**Weight:** Levi (vv. 8–11, 55 Hebrew words) and Joseph (vv. 13–17, 54 words) take 109 of the 230 words in the tribal sayings (vv. 6–25). Judah gets a single verse.
**Missing:** Eleven sons of Jacob are named and Simeon is absent. Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh appear inside his blessing (v. 17).
A new heading, “this is the blessing” (v. 1), sets the chapter apart between the Song and Moses' death. It is his last speech, and 34:1 moves straight to Nebo.

**Backward:** Jacob's deathbed blessing (Genesis 49) is the model, and v. 16 repeats its words on the crown of Joseph's head (Genesis 49:26). Levi's reward looks back to the golden calf, when the Levites stood with Moses against their own kin (Exodus 32:26–29), the loyalty v. 9 describes.

traditions.text: Speaking of the elders of the Church who would not yet settle in Zion, the Lord says “they shall push the people together from the ends of the earth.” The words come from Joseph's blessing in v. 17, and the revelation applies the gathering power of Joseph's horns to missionary work.

Moroni told Joseph Smith that two stones in silver bows, fastened to a breastplate, made up what is called the Urim and Thummim, and that possessing and using them made a person a seer in former times. D&C 17 links them to the brother of Jared. The connection to Levi's Thummim and Urim (v. 8) is thematic: Deuteronomy gives the oracle to the priestly tribe without describing it.

The Greek reads the hard end of v. 2 as “on his right hand were his angels with him,” where the KJV has “a fiery law.” That reading puts angels at the giving of the law, an idea the New Testament repeats (Early Christian below).

The book opens by reworking v. 2: the eternal God will tread upon the earth, on Mount Sinai, and come with ten thousands of his holy ones to judge. Here the march from Sinai is moved to the end of days. Jude 14–15 quotes this passage as Enoch's prophecy.

A single sheet of proof texts from Qumran quotes Levi's blessing (vv. 8–11) alongside the promise of a prophet like Moses (18:18–19) and Balaam's star and sceptre (Numbers 24:15–17). The community seems to have read Levi's Urim, teaching, and altar as marks of a coming priestly leader beside a prophet and a king.

Philo describes Moses near his departure as already being changed from body and soul into pure mind. Inspired, he prophesied no longer to the nation as a whole but to each tribe separately, and Philo says some of these predictions had already come true, which gave confidence in the rest. Tribes that differed in birth and mother, he adds, fittingly received different oracles.

Reads v. 2 as revelation from every side: Sinai, Seir, and Paran give three directions, and Habakkuk 3:3 supplies the fourth, Teman. Another reading has God speaking the Torah in four languages, Hebrew from Sinai and Roman (Latin) from Seir, identified with Edom and Rome.

Rashi finds Simeon hidden in Judah's blessing: “Hear” (*shema*) in v. 7 echoes Simeon's name, and Simeon's land lay inside Judah's (Joshua 19:9). Why no separate blessing? Moses held Shittim against the tribe, where a Simeonite prince led the sin at Peor (Numbers 25:14).

The Targum expands “Let Reuben live, and not die” (v. 6): may he live in this world and not die the second death that the wicked die in the world to come. The phrase “second death” also appears in Revelation 20:14 and in Book of Mormon teaching (Alma 12:32).

The Talmud says that as soon as a child can speak, the father should begin teaching him Torah. The first verse he learns is v. 4, “Moses commanded us a law,” followed by the opening line of the Shema. A line from Moses' last blessing becomes a child's first words of scripture.

The Talmud assigns the reading of “And this is the blessing” (chs. 33–34) to the second day of the Eighth Day of Assembly, as kept outside the land of Israel, with Solomon's dedication prayer as the prophetic reading. That day later became Simchat Torah, when the yearly cycle finishes with Moses' blessing and death and begins again at Genesis 1.

Three New Testament writers say the law came through angels. Stephen tells the council they received it “by the disposition of angels”; Paul says it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator; Hebrews calls it the word spoken by angels. The Greek of v. 2, with angels at God's right hand at Sinai, is the clearest scriptural basis for the idea.

Justin quotes Joseph's blessing (vv. 13–17) and reads the horns of the unicorn as the cross. The upright beam rises like one horn and the crossbeam ends like two more, and with these the nations are pushed together from one end of the earth to the other. D&C 58:45 also reads the pushing as a gathering.

34.overview:
Moses climbs from the plains of Moab to the top of Pisgah on Mount Nebo. The LORD shows him the land, from Gilead to Dan, across to the western sea, and down to the Negev and Zoar, and tells him this is the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: he may see it but not go over. Moses dies there at 120, his eyes undimmed and his strength unabated, and is buried in a valley in Moab; no one knows his grave. Israel mourns thirty days, and Joshua, full of wisdom because Moses had laid hands on him, takes the lead.

The last verses look back from a distance: “unto this day” (v. 6) and “there arose not a prophet since” (v. 10). The Torah ends outside the promised land, with the promise in sight and its greatest prophet laid to rest by the LORD where no one can find him.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: The chapter narrates Moses' death and looks back from a later time (vv. 6, 10). The Talmud records two views: Joshua wrote the last eight verses, or Moses wrote them in tears at God's dictation (Bava Batra 14b–15a).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its core to the 7th century BC, with additions in the 6th.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: End of the fortieth year after the Exodus (1:3): about 1406 BC by 1 Kings 6:1, or the 13th century BC on the later date. Josephus dates the death to 1 Adar (Antiquities 4.8.49), the Talmud to 7 Adar (Kiddushin 38a).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The top of Pisgah on Mount Nebo, opposite Jericho; burial in a valley facing Beth-peor (v. 6). The Book of Mormon reads this as the Lord taking Moses to himself (Alma 45:19), and the Church teaches that Moses was translated.

34.hermeneutics:
Mount Nebo rises about 800 meters above sea level at the edge of the Moabite plateau, and its western spur looks down on the Jordan valley, Jericho, and the north end of the Dead Sea. On a clear day the hills around Jerusalem are visible. Dan in the far north and the western sea are not; the central hills block them. The list in vv. 1–3 runs around the whole land, north, west, and south, then back to the valley below, so what the LORD shows Moses is more than any eye could take in from that height.

Nebo was a disputed town. On the Mesha Stele (c. 840 BC), the king of Moab says his god Chemosh told him to take Nebo from Israel; he killed its people and dragged objects belonging to YHWH before Chemosh. Readers in the time of the kings knew this ground as Moabite, held by Israel only for a while. Moses dies “in the land of Moab” (vv. 5–6), outside the land he led Israel toward.

Families across the ancient Near East kept up offerings for their dead, the Mesopotamian *kispu*, and the tomb of a famous man could become a shrine. Deuteronomy itself forbids giving holy food “for the dead” (26:14). A grave that no one can find leaves nothing to visit and nothing to feed, and the founder of Israel's law cannot become the center of a cult of the dead.

No prophet since like Moses

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence from the view to death, burial, mourning, succession, and epitaph.
notes: **Name:** “Moses” occurs 9 times in 12 verses. The chapter keeps him at the center to the last line.
**Epitaph:** vv. 10–12 sum up his life in two parts: the LORD knew him “face to face,” and he did signs and wonders before Pharaoh and in the sight of all Israel.
**Book frame:** Deuteronomy opens with Moses speaking “on this side Jordan” (1:1) and ends with him buried on the same side, the land still ahead.

The last chapter of Deuteronomy and of the five books of Moses. Verse 1 carries out the command of 32:48–52, and v. 9 ties back to Joshua's commissioning (31:7–8, 23; Numbers 27:18–23). Verses 10–12 close the Torah with a verdict on Moses' whole life.
**Forward:** Joshua 1:1–2 begins “after the death of Moses.” **Backward:** v. 10 answers 18:15–18; the prophet like Moses had not yet arisen when these words were written.

traditions.text: When Alma disappears and no one knows of his death or burial, the record notes a saying that he was taken up by the Spirit or buried by the Lord, “even as Moses.” Mormon then states that “the scriptures saith the Lord took Moses unto himself” and supposes Alma was received the same way. The Church's footnote to v. 5 points to this passage and to the topic of translated beings.

The Church teaches plainly that Moses did not die as v. 5 reports: “Moses was a translated being.” He needed a body of flesh and bones to confer priesthood keys on Peter, James, and John at the Mount of Transfiguration, before Christ's resurrection. On April 3, 1836, he came to the Kirtland Temple and conferred the keys of the gathering of Israel on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery.

Josephus has Moses dismiss the elders on Mount Abarim and, while still speaking with Eleazar and Joshua, disappear when a cloud suddenly stands over him. Moses wrote in the holy books that he died, Josephus explains, for fear people would say that he had gone to God because of his great virtue. The account sits close to Alma 45:19 and to the Restoration teaching.

Philo calls the end of the Torah its most wonderful part. As Moses stood ready to fly away to heaven, he was inspired to prophesy his own death and burial while still alive, telling how no one knew his tomb because he was buried by immortal powers, not mortal hands, and how the nation mourned him for a month.

A story tells of the Roman authorities sending men to Beth-peor to find Moses' grave: to those standing above it seemed below, and to those below it seemed above. Rabbi Hama son of Rabbi Hanina adds that even Moses does not know where he is buried, and that he was buried facing Beth-peor to atone for Israel's sin there (Numbers 25).

Taking v. 6 to mean that God himself buried Moses, the Talmud makes it a model for human conduct. Just as God clothed the naked, visited the sick, and comforted mourners, so he buried the dead, and Israel is to walk in his ways by doing the same.

Verse 5 says Moses died “according to the word of the LORD,” literally by the LORD's mouth, and the rabbis read this as death by a divine kiss. The Angel of Death had no power over him, and the same is said of Aaron, whose death uses the same phrase (Numbers 33:38), and of Miriam. Even Moses' death is told as an act of closeness to God.

The Targum fills v. 6 with angels. Michael and Gabriel spread a golden bed, other angels lay Moses on it, and God's Word leads him four miles and buries him opposite Beth-peor, so that Israel would remember their sin whenever they looked at Peor. Michael's role recalls the dispute over Moses' body in Jude 9 (Early Christian below).

Reads the view from Nebo as a view of the future: God showed Moses the land at peace and under its oppressors, and the line of kings from Ruth of Moab. On v. 10 it says no prophet like Moses arose in Israel, but one did among the nations, Balaam, and then lists how their prophecy differed.

Jude mentions that Michael the archangel disputed with the devil over the body of Moses and would only say, “The Lord rebuke thee.” Origen names the source as a book called the Ascension of Moses, a work now mostly lost. The tradition grows from the hidden grave of v. 6.

Clement repeats a tradition that Joshua, lifted up by the Spirit with Caleb, saw Moses double as he was taken up: one Moses with the angels and another honored with burial in the mountain ravines. Clement uses it to show that not everyone perceives the same truth.

Hebrews recalls God's praise of Moses as faithful in all his house as a servant (Numbers 12:7), the closeness that v. 10 calls knowing the LORD face to face. It accepts that verdict and still sets Christ above Moses, as a Son over the house and as the builder is above the house he builds.
